posts.title: How Thermo Fisher Scientific built AI-powered patient matching on AWS
posts.summary: Learn how Thermo Fisher Scientific built an AI-powered patient-matching platform on AWS, modernizing its clinical trial recruitment data foundation and using AWS Countdown Premium to de-risk the production launch.
posts.content:
Clinical trial recruitment is often described as a patient-matching challenge. In practice, it is much broader. Patient Recruitment teams need to understand where potential participants are in the recruitment journey, how sites are performing, which geographies may offer the strongest opportunities, and whether enough patients may meet increasingly complex study criteria. The answers often sit across different systems, datasets, surveys, questionnaires, consent records, marketing interactions, and operational workflows.

For Thermo Fisher Scientific, improving that experience required more than introducing a new application. It required rethinking the data foundation supporting patient recruitment and creating a more scalable way to turn recruitment data into actionable insights.

Using AWS, Thermo Fisher Scientific established a modern patient recruitment data foundation which brings together and curates data for analytics and AI-enabled use cases. Built on this foundation are complementary capabilities including Patient Recruitment’s Central Insights Hub (CIH), which provides recruitment analytics and operational visibility, and Patient Match AI, Thermo Fisher Scientific’s proprietary tool, that supports self-service patient search, feasibility assessment, and cohort discovery through natural-language interaction.

The impact is particularly visible in cohort discovery. Questions that could previously involve days or even weeks of analysis and back-and-forth with technical teams can now be explored and refined in minutes, giving recruitment teams a faster path from a question to an actionable patient population.

As these capabilities moved toward production, Thermo Fisher Scientific also worked with AWS Countdown Premium to strengthen operational readiness, support launch activities, and reduce risk during a critical stage of the transformation.

The challenge

Over time, patient recruitment data had grown across multiple systems and use cases. Patient information, surveys and questionnaires, recruitment funnel activity, marketing interactions, consent information, site data, and other operational datasets did not always exist in a single, consistent form.

That fragmentation created several challenges.

Recruitment teams needed faster ways to identify and refine relevant patient populations across large volumes of records. They also needed a clearer view of recruitment performance across studies, sites, and geographies. At the same time, the organization wanted to introduce AI-enabled capabilities without compromising data quality, privacy, governance, or compliance.

Existing processes often depended on specialized technical teams to translate business or clinical questions into database queries, retrieve the appropriate data, validate the results, and then repeat the process as criteria changed.

For a simple question, that approach could be manageable. For complex cohort discovery involving multiple clinical, demographic, geographic, or consent-related criteria, it could become a lengthy iterative process.

Thermo Fisher Scientific therefore faced two connected challenges: modernizing the patient recruitment data environment and making that data easier for business users to explore and act on.

Building the data foundation first

Rather than treating AI as a layer that could simply be added to existing systems, the team started with the data. Thermo Fisher Scientific established a modern patient recruitment data foundation on AWS to bring together information from previously disconnected sources and prepare it for downstream analytics and intelligent applications.

The new foundation standardizes and curates data from sources such as patient profiles, surveys, questionnaires, recruitment funnel activity, marketing information, consent data, and other recruitment datasets. Data transformations help create more consistent structures and reusable datasets for applications that depend on them.

This approach provides an important separation of concerns: source systems continue to serve their operational purposes, while curated datasets are prepared specifically for analytics, reporting, and AI-driven workloads.

For the business, the result is a more trusted and reusable source of recruitment information. For technology teams, it creates a scalable foundation that can support multiple products instead of building separate data pipelines for every new use case.

Turning recruitment data into operational insight with Central Insights Hub

One of the capabilities supported by this broader modernization is Central Insights Hub (CIH), Thermo Fisher’s in-house custom UI layer built using open-source technologies.

CIH is a centralized clinical trial recruitment analytics platform that helps teams understand how recruitment efforts are performing across studies.

Through interactive dashboards and visualizations, users can follow the recruitment journey from initial patient engagement through milestones such as pre-screening, referral to a study site, consent, enrollment, and randomization.

The platform brings together views of patient progression, site activity, recruitment timelines, geographic performance, and other operational measures. As CIH has evolved, additional capabilities have expanded visibility into areas such as recruitment costs, participant demographics, disqualification trends, site-patient engagement, and marketing-channel performance.

This gives recruitment teams a common place to identify bottlenecks, compare activity across sites and countries, understand where additional attention may be required, and make more timely decisions.

CIH shows how recruitment is performing and where teams should focus.

Making cohort discovery self-service with Patient Match AI

Patient Match AI, an internal tool within Thermo Fisher, addresses a different, but complementary, challenge: helping users quickly determine which patient populations may be relevant to a recruitment need.

Instead of asking a technical team to manually construct database queries, users can describe what they are looking for in natural language.

For example, a user may begin by asking for the number of patients who meet a broad clinical condition. They can then progressively refine that population by age, geography, diagnosis, treatment history, demographic characteristics, consent or contactability criteria, and other available attributes.

The intended experience follows a straightforward progression:

COUNT → REFINE → TARGETED LIST → EXPORT

Users can start by understanding the size of a potential population, refine the criteria as they learn more, and then move toward a targeted patient cohort when appropriate.

This changes the working model from a series of handoffs to a more interactive, self-service experience.

Tasks that previously could require several rounds of analysis over days or weeks can, for many common feasibility workflows, now be explored in minutes. Recruitment teams can test assumptions, adjust criteria, and understand how those changes affect the potential population without restarting the process each time.

Patient Match AI also supports aggregate insights and visualizations, helping users better understand the composition of a cohort before progressing to governed workflows when patient identity information is required.

Privacy, governance, consent, contactability, and personally identifiable information (PII) controls, consistent with applicable regulatory requirements, remain an important part of the design. The objective is not unrestricted access to patient data, but a faster and more intuitive way to work within established recruitment and governance processes.

Architecture overview

The following diagram shows how data moves from source systems through the curated data foundation into Patient Match AI and Central Insights Hub, and the key AWS services involved at each stage.

Figure 1: How data moves from source systems through the curated data foundation into Patient Match AI and Central Insights Hub

The solution uses a cloud-native architecture on AWS that combines managed services for data storage, transformation, orchestration, analytics, AI workloads, and application delivery.

Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) provides scalable storage for recruitment data, while AWS Glue supports data transformation and cataloging. AWS Step Functions orchestrates multi-stage data processing workflows, and Amazon Athena runs analytical queries across curated datasets.

The analytics layer uses Apache Iceberg tables on Amazon S3, providing a flexible foundation for large-scale analytical workloads and supporting continued growth in both data volume and use cases.

A key architectural principle is the separation of operational application workloads from analytical processing. Complex cohort and eligibility queries can therefore run across large volumes of patient profiles without placing the same workload on transactional application databases.

Thermo Fisher’s identity resolution and profile consolidation processes also help bring together records originating from multiple systems, reducing duplication and establishing a more consistent view for downstream recruitment use cases.

The outcome is not simply a collection of cloud services. It is an architecture designed so that data can be ingested, curated, queried, and reused across analytics and AI capabilities without rebuilding the underlying foundation for every product.

Source systems include patient profiles, surveys and questionnaires, recruitment funnel activity, marketing and consent data, and site and operational data. These sources are ingested into the data foundation. There, AWS Step Functions orchestrates multi-stage processing, Amazon S3 provides storage, and AWS Glue handles transformation and cataloging. An identity resolution step consolidates profiles and reduces duplication.

Curated data then flows into two separated stores. Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) holds identity, health, and operations data. The team selected it as the closest managed equivalent to the MongoDB database they had previously relied on. Amazon S3 with Apache Iceberg tables, queried through Amazon Athena, holds the analytics data.

These curated datasets feed the intelligence layer. Central Insights Hub provides recruitment analytics, and Patient Match AI supports natural-language cohort discovery through a COUNT, REFINE, TARGETED LIST, and EXPORT workflow. Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) hosts the API layer, and AWS Lambda performs patient match scoring. Results reach recruitment teams for feasibility, cohort discovery, and site, geographic, and funnel performance analysis. Throughout, privacy, governance, consent, contactability, and PII controls remain part of the design.

Preparing for production with AWS Countdown Premium

Building technology was only part of the journey. Moving a large-scale recruitment capability into production required confidence that the architecture, capacity, operating procedures, and support model were ready for launch.

Thermo Fisher Scientific engaged AWS Countdown Premium from the testing phase onward.

AWS Countdown Premium is an engineer-led support service that provides designated expertise and guidance across critical phases of cloud projects. For this engagement, that support helped the team prepare for launch in four key areas.

Designated engineering expertise

A specialist engineer selected from a team of AWS experts served as a consistent technical point of contact and developed a deeper understanding of the Patient Match AI architecture.

That continuity was valuable when working through complex technical issues. Rather than rebuilding context for each support interaction, the team could work with an engineer who was already familiar with the system and could coordinate access to additional AWS subject matter experts when needed.

One example from the engagement:
Pipeline design review: An AWS specialist engineer reviewed key design decisions ahead of launch. The patient scoring logic moved away from retrieving every record before ranking, and the pipeline was parallelized before sorting and querying. For long-running external calls in AWS Step Functions, the team adopted the wait-for-callback pattern, so they pay only for state transitions and not for idle wait time.

Operational readiness and proactive planning

The engagement focused on identifying potential issues before production rather than waiting for them to appear during launch.

Pre-event reviews, capacity planning, operational runbooks, and decision frameworks helped the team validate that the environment was prepared to support large-scale patient recruitment workloads.

Another example from the engagement:
AWS Glue readiness review: An AWS Glue specialist reviewed the team’s extract, transform, and load (ETL) jobs in non-production and shared written recommendations before launch. The team also received guidance on reading Apache Iceberg tables through the AWS Glue Iceberg REST endpoint and on putting AWS Glue Studio visual jobs under source control.

Support during go-live

During launch, coordinated AWS support provided another layer of technical coverage for troubleshooting and issue resolution.

For a production system supporting clinical recruitment workflows, this helped the team move through go-live with greater confidence and a clear escalation path for issues requiring AWS expertise.

Post-launch stabilization

Support continued beyond the initial deployment.

This provided continuity as the team monitored production behavior, addressed early issues, and transitioned from launch activities into normal operations.

Results

By combining a modern cloud architecture with support from AWS Countdown Premium, Thermo Fisher Scientific achieved several key outcomes:

  • Unified patient data – More than 20 million patient profile records, about 1.6 TB, were brought together from previously separate sources, including patient profiles, surveys, questionnaires, recruitment funnel data, marketing information and consent data.
  • Self-service cohort discovery – With Patient Match AI, recruitment teams can find and refine patient populations by asking questions in plain language, and the shared test queries run in under six seconds against the full dataset.
  • Faster feasibility analysis – Cohort analysis now takes minutes as opposed to days for many common feasibility and patient discovery workflows.
  • More timely insights – Recruitment data is kept up to date continuously, so it is available right away for AI-driven patient search and shortly afterward for analytics dashboards.
  • Modernized data foundation – The move to a data foundation built on AWS reduces reliance on the earlier Snowflake-backed dashboard environment.
  • Successful production launch – Patient Match AI went live in production in Q2 FY26. AWS Countdown Premium supported the launch through an architecture review, readiness reviews for Amazon DocumentDB and AWS Glue, and expert guidance on workflow design and query optimization over a four-month engagement.
  • Designated engineering support – A dedicated Countdown Premium engineer worked with the Amazon DocumentDB service team and specialists to tune the database, cutting estimated processing time by more than 3x.
  • Lower launch risk – Testing at full scale against the complete 20 million record dataset exposed query performance problems early, so they could be fixed before go-live.

Looking ahead

The broader value of this transformation goes beyond any single application. Thermo Fisher Scientific has established a modern, curated patient recruitment data foundation that can support different types of experiences, from operational analytics in Central Insights Hub to AI-powered cohort discovery through Patient Match AI, and that shared foundation creates an opportunity to continue evolving recruitment capabilities without repeatedly rebuilding the underlying data infrastructure.

More importantly, it changes how recruitment teams can work with data.

Instead of waiting for information to move through multiple technical handoffs, teams can increasingly interact with trusted recruitment data directly, using dashboards to understand what is happening and natural-language tools to explore what may be possible.

Conclusion

Thermo Fisher Scientific’s modernization of its patient recruitment environment, including a modern, curated patient recruitment data foundation, Central Insights Hub (CIH), and Patient Match AI, demonstrates how organizations can combine modern data architecture, analytics, and AI capabilities to solve complex, high-stakes business problems.

By using AWS services for data management, orchestration, analytics, and AI, the team created an environment that makes recruitment information easier to access, understand, and act on. Processes that once required substantial manual analysis can now be more timely, interactive, and self-service.

AWS Countdown Premium played an important role in de-risking the transition to production. Designated engineering support, proactive planning, launch assistance, and post-launch stabilization helped the team move these capabilities into production with greater confidence and operational readiness.

For Thermo Fisher Scientific, the result is more than a technology modernization. It is a foundation for helping recruitment teams move from data to insight, and from insight to action, faster.

Other organizations have used AWS Countdown Premium for similar initiatives, from improving manufacturing operations to seamless website migration and accelerating critical cloud migrations.

To learn more about how AWS Countdown Premium can support your next critical cloud initiative, reach out to your AWS account team.

posts.title: Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon
posts.summary: How Meta's Reality Labs brought Cuttlefish and its QEMU backend to macOS and Apple silicon. [...] Read More... The post Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon appeared…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Hadrien Zalek, Joe Knox, Alex Chong, Marcel Apfelbaum How Meta's Reality Labs brought Cuttlefish and its QEMU backend to macOS and Apple silicon.

Meta’s Reality Labs builds products such as AI glasses. Emulators provide us with a way to scale development and testing without relying on scarce physical hardware.

Testing software for non-phone Android devices depends on how closely a virtual device reproduces the software behavior of the physical product. While a lightweight emulator like Goldfish gets you part of the way, differences from the real device can hide bugs until later in development. This lack of fidelity also erodes trust in device emulation, increasing reliance on scarce physical hardware.

Cuttlefish is the Android Open Source Project’s (AOSP’s) virtual-device framework for testing Android software against virtual hardware. It boots the same system images as real hardware and runs a realistic software stack against virtual hardware. This enables Cuttlefish to more closely track a physical device’s behavior than a lightweight emulator does.

Unfortunately, Cuttlefish is only supported on Linux, and our application and library developers work on Macs with Apple silicon. This forced us to support Goldfish and Cuttlefish side by side.

We knew if we could consolidate onto a single Cuttlefish-based platform, we could give all of our developers the benefit of the same high-fidelity virtual device. The challenge was porting the stack to make Cuttlefish run natively on macOS.

The Impact of Fragmentation

Maintaining dual emulator platforms imposed a heavy operational burden: It drained computing resources, created confusion for developers, and slowed down the emulator team. Every tool required support for two separate platforms, while infrastructure and engineering capacity were divided between them. Furthermore, developers had to choose an emulator target based on how they worked: Goldfish ran everywhere but had less fidelity while Cuttlefish needed Linux.

The AOSP mirrors this exact divide: Goldfish targets application developers, whereas Cuttlefish serves Android platform developers. So long as we maintained that division, we would suffer the effects of fragmentation.

The Stack and the macOS Gaps

Cuttlefish is the orchestration layer, while the component that actually runs the guest OS is a virtual machine monitor (VMM). On Linux, Cuttlefish normally uses crosvm but previously included support for QEMU as an alternative VMM. That integration had become inactive over time. To enable native Apple silicon support on macOS, we revived QEMU support.

Many of Cuttlefish’s virtual devices use vhost-user backends, separate processes that provide virtio devices to QEMU over a socket. The architecture is clean, but large parts of it were written with a hard Linux assumption. Three of those assumptions break on macOS. The vhost-user machinery is gated to Linux and won’t build or run. The Apple hypervisor imposes resource limits QEMU didn’t expect. Finally, the native display, build, and signing paths didn’t exist. We tackled all three.

Making vhost-user Portable Beyond Linux

The most structurally important changes were in QEMU’s vhost-user path. The frontends, libvhost-user, and the contrib backends such as vhost-user-blk were all gated to Linux. We relaxed those build restrictions so the vhost-user frontends and libraries can build on macOS as well as Linux. This lets Cuttlefish’s device backends hand off to QEMU on a Mac the same way they do on Linux. Without this, the higher-fidelity device model that makes Cuttlefish worth using isn’t available outside Linux.

Living Within Hypervisor.framework

On Apple silicon, QEMU accelerates through HVF (Hypervisor.framework) instead of KVM. QEMU’s HVF backend did not track enough memory regions for larger Cuttlefish configurations. We increased its tracking-slot count so those configurations could run correctly.

A Usable Native Display

Local application development requires an interactive display allowing developers to view and engage directly with the virtual device. To enable direct interaction and bypass reliance on the WebRTC interface, we transitioned to QEMU’s native Cocoa display. The changes include:

  • BGRA Pixel Format Support: Enables accurate display rendering to eliminate visual artifacts on Apple silicon.
  • Mouse-Click-as-Touch: Translates pointer actions into touch input for interacting with touchscreen devices.
  • Custom Geometry Options: Adds the -g flag to graphic_console_init for display configuration.

We also enabled the unstable Rutabaga structs needed to match the Rust-side graphics ABI in gfxstream/rutabaga configurations.

Building and Signing on Apple Silicon

Finally, there was the build and packaging work: initial Darwin build support, building QEMU for arm64 on macOS, and toolchain fixes. The macOS builds also needed the JIT entitlement in addition to support for code signing and notarization. On the Cuttlefish side, we added macOS host support so the framework’s orchestration builds and runs on a Mac instead of assuming a Linux host.

The Benefits

By moving to a unified platform, we cut maintenance requirements, reduced infrastructure needs, eliminated redundant tooling, enhanced fidelity, and ensured developers run the exact same Cuttlefish virtual devices used across CI.

A single platform also made it easier to support capabilities on a shared stack, including:

  • Bluetooth pairing and connectivity.
  • Wi-Fi.
  • Cellular.
  • 3D graphics.
  • Over-the-air (OTA) update testing to exercise over-the-air update flows against a virtual device.
  • Fastboot.
  • Snapshotting to save and restore device state in CI and development flows.

Beyond supporting Reality Labs engineers, this identical virtual device is shared with external developers building for our ecosystem. This alignment guarantees that third-party teams test against the exact same Cuttlefish-based platform we use to develop and validate the OS itself.

With AI agents playing a growing role in Android development, validation execution and runtime behavior is just as essential as code generation. Virtual devices empower both engineers and automated agents to operate concurrently within isolated environments, facilitating application execution and rapid iteration. By enabling instant state resets and repeated test runs, teams eliminate dependencies on shared physical hardware and prevent workflow interruptions. Ultimately, high-fidelity emulation ensures these continuous feedback loops are both rapid and meaningful.

Giving Back to the Community

Although we built this for development within Reality Labs, the macOS support is useful beyond our products. We’re sharing our work with the community so other developers can build on the QEMU and AOSP foundations that enabled our work.

We’re distributing the work in two parts:

  • qemu-wearables: a Meta-maintained fork of QEMU carrying our commits.
  • cuttlefish-wearables: a set of patch files, with instructions for patching Android/AOSP.

The repositories contain our QEMU changes and the Cuttlefish patch series, along with build and patch-application instructions.

We’re also exploring ways to contribute these changes upstream to QEMU and AOSP. In the meantime, developers can use our fork and patch set.

Acknowledgements

This project relies on the foundations laid by the QEMU and Cuttlefish/AOSP communities. We are particularly grateful for the vsock-user implementation created by Stefano Garzarella, which directly enabled our macOS integration.

Special thanks also go to Olya Arkhangelskaia and Tom Care at Meta for their foundational work bringing Cuttlefish to macOS, and to Jeffrey Effendy for improvements to the native Mac developer experience and subsequent productization work.

posts.title: Modular regression testing framework built on AWS for large-scale systems
posts.summary: Regression testing must catch behavior changes before they reach production, yet synthetic tests miss real-world edge cases. This post walks through a modular framework, built on AWS, that replays a sample of production…
posts.content:
For services handling high-stakes operations such as financial transactions, order processing, or eligibility decisions, regression testing has to catch behavior changes before production deployment. Traditional integration tests help, but they can suffer from unreliable dependencies that cause false positives and slow down deployment pipelines. In this post, I walk through how I built an automated regression testing framework for my team using AWS services. Each run of the framework is a simulation: it replays a sample of production traffic against the new code and compares the results to validate that changes do not break existing functionality.

To build this framework, you need a service whose requests and responses you can capture to a stream such as Amazon DynamoDB Streams, a pre-production environment that can receive replayed requests, and a deployment pipeline with a gate that can read an Amazon CloudWatch alarm.

Minimally invasive design

The framework’s power lies in its modular design. Components fit between existing blocks in your system with minimal changes to your core business logic. Stateless systems need no changes. Stateful systems add a check that recognizes replayed requests and skips side effects. The same components capture, replay, and validate traffic at the API gateway, between microservices, or at internal service boundaries.

Focus: Regression detection

This framework specifically targets no-impact validation, confirming that code changes do not break existing behavior. It does not test new business logic. A/B testing and user acceptance testing handle that. Instead, the framework gives engineering teams confidence that refactors, upgrades, and feature-flagged deployments maintain existing functionality.

Scope and applicability

The framework works best with computation-heavy, stateless systems, where replaying a request produces the same output without side effects. Examples include pricing calculators, validation engines, eligibility decision engines, and data transformation pipelines.

Stateful systems need more coordination. These include transaction processing (payments, orders, inventory) and non-idempotent writes that would create duplicate records or notifications. They also include randomized logic such as A/B assignment, and multi-step workflows such as shopping carts, where each request depends on earlier state. “Handling stateful dependencies” later in this post covers patterns for these systems.

Proven results

In more than 6 months of production use in our system, the framework caught five regressions that would have affected customers, with zero false positives that blocked valid deployments. Teams can set alarms on the share of replayed requests whose results match production (commonly 99.9 percent) to block potentially problematic deployments. This maintains faster deployment velocity through automated quality gates. The framework also standardizes testing approaches across all AWS Regions, which gives consistent validation regardless of deployment location.

Use cases: When and why to simulate for regression detection

The framework addresses three critical scenarios where engineering teams need confidence that code changes do not break existing functionality:

1. Refactoring and technical upgrades

Teams refactoring internal logic or upgrading dependencies need confidence that behavior hasn’t changed. Post-deployment monitoring only catches issues after they affect customers. Simulation provides pre-deployment validation with zero customer impact.

Example: A team upgraded their data processing algorithm’s internal data structures for performance. Unit tests passed, and simulation verified that complex real-world request patterns still produced identical business logic outputs across all Regions.

2. Feature toggle deployments

Code deployed behind feature flags creates a unique challenge: the code is deployed but not yet active. Engineering teams need confidence during the deployment phase, whereas product teams monitor the feature after toggle activation using standard product metrics.

Example: A team added a new validation rule behind a feature flag. Simulation ran against the new code path using production traffic, validating that the deployment itself didn’t introduce regressions before the product team turned on the feature.

3. Validating impact boundaries for significant changes

When product teams predict a change will affect a specific percentage of requests, engineering teams need confidence in that boundary. The change should not affect other request types.

Example: Product predicted a business rule change would affect 15 percent of requests in specific Regions. Simulation confirmed 14.2 percent impact within the predicted request patterns and 0 percent impact on other request types, validating that the change didn’t break functionality outside its intended scope.

Architecture overview: Versatile component-based design

Figure 1 shows the framework. When a deployment reaches the deployment gate, the pipeline publishes an event to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS). Amazon SNS delivers it to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. An AWS Lambda function reads the queue and starts the AWS Step Functions workflow. The workflow turns replay on and off. While replay is on, the replay function reads captured requests from the Amazon DynamoDB stream and sends them to the new code. It logs a match result for each request to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. A CloudWatch alarm on the match fraction tells the deployment gate whether to promote the deployment.

Figure 1: Regression testing framework architecture

Component insertion flexibility

The framework is designed to be versatile. Each component can be positioned to capture inputs and outputs at any system boundary:

  • API level: Capture HTTP requests and responses at gateway or service endpoints.
  • Service level: Capture inter-service communication and message passing.
  • Database level: Capture query inputs and results for data layer validation.
  • Message queue level: Capture message processing for event-driven architectures.

You can compare end-to-end outputs or scope the comparison to one block of business logic. Anything after that block, such as formatting or downstream API calls, falls outside the comparison.

Tech stack and rationale

I chose managed AWS services to keep operational overhead low and to pay only for the resources each simulation consumes:

  • AWS Step Functions: Visual workflow orchestration with built-in error handling and state management for coordinating timed operations.
  • AWS Lambda: Serverless execution with automatic scaling. Pay only for actual simulation time.
  • Amazon DynamoDB: Low-latency access to production request data with global tables for multi-Region support. (Note: We used DynamoDB as part of our existing tech stack. You can adapt the framework to the storage system you currently use.)
  • Amazon CloudWatch: Unified logging, metrics, and alarming. Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights supports complex queries without additional infrastructure.
  • Amazon SNS and Amazon SQS: Reliable publish/subscribe messaging for pipeline integration with retry logic and dead-letter queues.

Component 1: Traffic capture – universal storage with complete parameter logging

Core function: Captures actual production request documents and their associated responses, not synthetic data or mocks. This complete production dataset is what makes regression detection accurate by replaying the same requests that flowed through the production system with all their complexity and edge cases.

Key challenge: Capturing all parameters and context needed to reproduce the component’s behavior accurately. Missing any input parameter, request context, or metadata can lead to inaccurate replay and false regression signals.

Apply domain-specific knowledge to identify and capture all inputs your system needs for accurate replay. This includes obvious parameters (request body, headers) and less obvious context (user session state, feature flags, regional settings, timestamps). The completeness of your capture directly determines replay accuracy.

Storage flexibility: The framework design works with any storage system that can generate events:

  • Amazon DynamoDB Streams: For document-based systems.
  • Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) and Amazon Aurora: Using database triggers or change data capture.
  • Amazon Kinesis Data Streams: For high-throughput event streaming.
  • CloudWatch Logs: For API gateway or application-level capture.
  • Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK): For Kafka-based architectures.

Component 2: Replay engine – running simulated production traffic against test environments

Core function: Takes batched production requests from storage streams and invokes test environment APIs with the same parameters, capturing responses for comparison.

Key challenge: The system needs to distinguish replayed traffic from production traffic. Without this distinction, replayed requests would be processed identically to production requests, leading to duplicate processing and unintended side effects.

The replay engine solves this by attaching simulation IDs to every replayed request:

// Add simulation markers to every replayed request
request.addProperty("simulationId", simulationId);
request.addProperty("isSimulation", true);

Component 3: Comparison engine – domain-specific output analysis

Core function: Compares specific business logic outputs between production and simulation responses to calculate match fractions. The engine extracts the outputs you’ve chosen to focus on and determines whether they match within acceptable thresholds.

Key challenge: Determining what to compare for your specific application. This requires deep domain knowledge. You need to identify which outputs represent your core business logic as opposed to downstream formatting, third-party variations, or environmental differences that do not indicate actual regressions.

Before logging, reduce each response to the fields that carry your business logic, and normalize them so equivalent outputs compare equal, for example by dropping timestamps and sorting lists. The replay engine compares the reduced results and logs one JSON line for each request. Each line has a numeric match field that is 1 when the results are equal and 0 when they differ or the replay fails. Both results stay in the line for investigating mismatches:

{"SimulationId": "<simulationId>", "match": 1, "prod": "<reduced production result>", "sim": "<reduced simulation result>"}

CloudWatch Logs Insights discovers fields in JSON log events, and the query averages match for one simulation:

filter SimulationId = "<simulationId>"
| stats avg(match) as matchFraction

When the replay completes, run the query and publish the match fraction as a custom CloudWatch metric for the deployment gate’s alarm. The implementation reference at the end of this post shows a Lambda function that does this. What constitutes a meaningful comparison depends on your system architecture and business requirements. For the full query language, see the CloudWatch Logs Insights query syntax.

Component 4: Orchestration – CI/CD pipeline integration

Core function: Manages the timing and coordination of simulation components: starts traffic capture, waits for sufficient data collection, stops capture, evaluates results, and provides pass or fail decisions for deployment gates.

Key challenge: Integrating simulation results into continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines as reliable quality gates. Deployments need automated pass or fail decisions based on simulation outcomes, not only monitoring data that requires manual interpretation.

Deployment events reach the AWS Step Functions workflow through Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS, and a Lambda function that starts the execution, with retries and error handling.

Replay starts and stops by enabling and disabling the event source mapping between the capture stream and the replay function. Lambda can take several minutes to stop or restart polling after the mapping changes. The workflow waits a few minutes after stopping replay before it evaluates results. When replay is enabled again, the mapping can resume with records captured while it was off. Set a maximum record age on the mapping to skip stale records, and use reserved concurrency on the replay function to cap the burst.

A CloudWatch alarm on the match fraction blocks the deployment when it falls below your threshold. In AWS CodePipeline, for example, an entry condition with a CloudWatchAlarm rule on the production stage blocks promotion while the alarm is in the ALARM state. Otherwise, the pipeline promotes the deployment. The implementation reference at the end of this post shows the state machine definition and the start and stop functions.

Simulation traffic controls and production safety

Critical safeguards prevent overwhelming test environments and maintain production safety:

// Hard limits prevent accidental overload
if (props.trafficFraction > 0.1) throw new Error('Traffic fraction too high');
// Concurrency controls limit resource usage
reservedConcurrentExecutions: 3

Typical configuration: 5 percent traffic replay with 200-record batching provides sufficient coverage while maintaining system stability.

Handling stateful dependencies

As noted in “Scope and applicability,” systems with stateful components can use this framework with additional patterns.

1. Idempotency controls

Services in the simulated logic path can use the simulation IDs described in Component 2 to detect replayed requests. They then skip stateful operations (database writes, notifications, external API calls) while still returning a response.

// Service checks for replay
if (!request.isSimulation()) {
    database.write(result);
    notificationService.send(result);
}

For services that need further isolation, simulation IDs can also be used to route simulation traffic to separate test instances or maintain separate simulation state.

2. Deterministic randomization

For systems using randomization (A/B assignment, sampling, shuffling), use the simulation ID as a seed:

// Production: true randomization
Random rand = new Random();
// Simulation: deterministic based on request
if (request.isSimulation()) {
    rand = new Random(request.getSimulationId().hashCode());
}

This makes simulation responses reproducible and comparable.

When to reconsider

If adding idempotency infrastructure creates an ongoing maintenance burden that exceeds the value of automated regression testing, consider whether this framework is the right fit. Manual testing or alternative validation approaches might be more practical for your system.

Cost and operational efficiency

The framework’s own Lambda functions, logging, streaming, and orchestration cost little. The primary cost driver is your own system processing replayed requests, which varies based on your architecture. The following is a breakdown of the framework costs only. Prices shown are for the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region as of October 2026. To estimate your own costs, use the AWS Pricing Calculator.

Cost components:

  • Lambda executions: $0.0000166667 per GB-second plus $0.0000002 per request.
  • CloudWatch Logs: $0.50 per GB ingested plus $0.03 per GB stored (monthly).
  • CloudWatch Logs Insights: $0.005 per GB scanned per query.
  • Step Functions: $0.025 per 1,000 state transitions.
  • DynamoDB Streams: no read charge when standard AWS Lambda functions read the stream (Lambda Managed Instances incur Streams charges).
  • Amazon SNS and Amazon SQS: $0.40–$0.50 per million requests.

Example calculation (24-hour simulation, 5 percent of 100,000 daily requests):

  • 5,000 replayed requests × 1 second average duration × 256 MB = about $0.02 Lambda cost.
  • 5,000 log entries × 5 KB average = 25 MB logs = about $0.013 ingestion plus about $0.001 storage.
  • DynamoDB Streams reads: $0 (included in the preceding Lambda cost).
  • One evaluation query scanning 25 MB = about $0.0001 Logs Insights.
  • Step Functions and messaging costs = about $0.01.

Total estimated cost: about $0.05 for this example scenario.

Multi-Region deployment multiplies costs by the number of Regions. Higher traffic volumes scale proportionally. For example, 500,000 daily requests (25,000 replayed) cost approximately $0.25 per simulation.

Scale the calculation based on your traffic volume and simulation frequency. Most importantly, the confidence to deploy faster and the hours saved on manual validation far exceed the simulation costs.

Getting started: Phased implementation approach

Build the framework in three phases. Each phase is usable before the next one starts.

Phase 1 – Core components: Set up traffic capture with your chosen event source, create a replay engine with simulation IDs, implement centralized output analysis with structured logging, and build orchestration with Step Functions.

Phase 2 – Automated verification: Design a match fraction calculation with business logic for filtering variances, create CloudWatch Logs Insights queries, and set up CloudWatch alarms for quality gates.

Phase 3 – Full automation: Integrate with deployment pipelines, deploy across multiple Regions, build monitoring dashboards, and tune thresholds based on real data.

Implementation reference

posts.title: Scale distributed AI workloads with Ray and Anyscale on Amazon EC2
posts.summary: Building multimodal AI/ML pipelines on Amazon EC2 means scaling distributed compute, controlling costs across stages, and keeping up with new models and hardware. This post shows how the Ray-powered Anyscale application…
posts.content:
If you are building multimodal artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) pipelines on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) that process text, video, and audio, you have likely hit at least one of these challenges. Scaling from a single instance to distributed compute without rewriting code, managing costs across training, fine-tuning, and inference, and keeping up with an evolving network of models, frameworks, and hardware are among the biggest challenges AI engineers face today. These challenges compound when each pipeline stage has distinct compute, networking, and storage requirements, and multiple teams own separate parts of the workflow.

This post shows how the Ray-powered Anyscale application on AWS helps you tackle these challenges. You will learn how to: deploy Ray across three AWS compute options based on your operational requirements, optimize costs by matching heterogeneous instance types to each pipeline stage, and scale from prototype to production without code changes.

How Anyscale builds on Ray

Ray Core is the distributed computing foundation underlying the entire framework. It provides primitives for parallelizing Python workloads across clusters, handling task scheduling, fault tolerance, and autoscaling. Ray AI libraries are built on top of Ray Core. As a result, custom workloads that don’t fit a standard pattern can still use the same distributed infrastructure.

Ray Data ingests and transforms datasets at scale, feeding processed data into training, tuning, and inference stages. Ray Train orchestrates distributed multi-node jobs with built-in fault tolerance, supporting foundation model fine-tuning across architectures such as Llama and Mistral with automatic selection of data-parallel, model-parallel, or pipeline-parallel strategies. Ray Tune parallelizes hyperparameter experiments across large clusters. Ray Serve runs production inference endpoints with dynamic batching, automatic scaling, and multi-model deployment support. Ray RLlib supports distributed reinforcement learning workloads, including reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for large language model (LLM) alignment.

Anyscale on AWS

Many AWS customers already run self-managed Ray clusters on Amazon EC2. Anyscale builds on that foundation as a fully managed service that deploys within your AWS account, integrating with your existing Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) networks, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and compliance frameworks. The application handles cluster management, autoscaling, and cost controls so you can focus on workloads rather than infrastructure.

AWS and Anyscale together address three dimensions of production AI/ML: cost-efficient infrastructure spanning the full Amazon EC2 portfolio, a Ray-on-Anyscale stack that scales reliably from experimentation to production, and an integrated framework that reduces friction at every stage of development. With Anyscale, you can map each pipeline stage to the appropriate instance type. Intel and AMD-based instances handle preprocessing, tokenization, and feature extraction. AWS Graviton-based instances cover preprocessing, worker nodes, embedding generation, and lightweight inference where price-performance matters. NVIDIA GPU instances and AWS Trainium handle training and fine-tuning. AWS Inferentia serves high-throughput inference endpoints. Amazon EC2 Spot Instances run automatically for batch training, preprocessing, and hyperparameter sweeps.

Anyscale deployment architecture on AWS

Three deployment options provide flexibility based on operational requirements:

Amazon EC2 with Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) provides direct compute control and high-performance inter-node networking.

Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with EFA supports containerized workloads.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod delivers managed large-scale foundation model training with built-in cluster resiliency.

Regardless of the deployment path, Ray libraries handle distinct pipeline stages. Ray Data orchestrates preprocessing across CPU-only instances, AWS Graviton-based instances, GPU instances, and Spot Instances. Ray Train, Ray Serve, and Ray RLlib handle distributed training, inference serving, and reinforcement learning on NVIDIA GPU instances and AWS AI chips.

Figure 1: Anyscale on AWS architecture

Anyscale runs a hosted control plane that sends instructions to an operator deployed in your AWS environment. The data plane (Amazon EC2 instances, storage, and networking) stays in your account, and Anyscale manages Ray cluster lifecycle without direct access to your data.

Option A: Amazon EC2

Amazon EC2 supports the full pipeline without constraint. This makes it the recommended default for teams running EC2-based workloads who want to scale into AI/ML without retooling their operations. Ray Data runs preprocessing on cost-efficient instance types including Spot Instances and Graviton processors. Ray Train handles distributed training on GPU and Trainium instances with EFA. Ray Tune runs hyperparameter search across CPU and GPU instances. Ray Serve deploys inference on Inferentia or Graviton. Ray supports reinforcement learning through RLlib on GPU instances, and RLHF workflows run through frameworks such as OpenRLHF.

Anyscale manages instance lifecycle, provisioning and terminating nodes based on demand. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) handles datasets, checkpoints, and model artifacts. Amazon FSx for Lustre provides parallel file system throughput for training jobs with repeated large-dataset reads. EFA is available on supported instance types for multi-node training.

Option B: Amazon EKS

Amazon EKS runs the same full pipeline within a Kubernetes environment. This makes it the right choice if your organization already manages Kubernetes and wants Ray to share the same infrastructure and tooling. The Anyscale operator deploys Ray nodes as pods, and Ray libraries run identically to the Amazon EC2 path at the application layer.

Karpenter handles node autoscaling, provisioning GPU nodes for training, Graviton nodes for preprocessing and inference, and Spot Instances for batch workloads. Ray Serve benefits from Kubernetes-integrated zero-downtime upgrades for production inference deployments. The tradeoff: Amazon EKS adds container orchestration complexity and requires custom configuration for the Anyscale operator.

Option C: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is purpose-built for resilience-critical stages where multi-week runs on large GPU or Trainium clusters make node failures expensive. It continuously monitors cluster health, automatically replaces unhealthy nodes, and resumes from the last checkpoint without manual intervention. HyperPod supports both Slurm-orchestrated and Amazon EKS-based clusters, and now supports the full model development lifecycle including inference deployment. Amazon SageMaker Studio integration adds experiment tracking and model management.

Native integrations shared by EC2, EKS, and HyperPod

Networking and storage

EFA provides low-latency, high-bandwidth inter-node communication for distributed training on all three deployment paths. Amazon S3 is the primary store for datasets, checkpoints, and artifacts. Ray Data pipelines read directly from Amazon S3-based data lakes. Amazon FSx for Lustre integrates with S3 for parallel file system throughput. Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) covers shared file access for workspaces and notebooks.

Security and compliance

Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) network isolation, IAM role-based access control, and AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption at rest and in transit apply regardless of deployment path. Data stays within your AWS account and encryption keys remain under your control. This architecture supports compliance with frameworks including HIPAA and SOC 2 without changes to Ray workload code.

Observability

Anyscale monitoring provides workload-specific dashboards covering training progress, pipeline throughput, and request latency. Grafana dashboards are accessible from the Anyscale console. Amazon CloudWatch handles AWS metrics, logs, and alarms. Prometheus supports custom metrics collection for teams with existing monitoring pipelines.

Each deployment path follows the same workflow: Ray Data feeds processed data to Anyscale Runtime, Ray Train orchestrates training, Ray Serve handles inference through Amazon API Gateway, and Ray RLlib supports reinforcement learning.

Cost optimization and provisioning

Right-sizing compute per stage

AWS Graviton-based instances deliver strong price-performance for CPU-bound Ray workloads across preprocessing, embedding generation, and lightweight inference. PyTorch inference on Graviton3 C7g instances shows up to 50% cost savings versus x86 equivalents (Tomaz Berisa, n.d.). Graviton4 adds 30% better compute per core and 75% more memory bandwidth than Graviton3 (AWS, n.d.). Graviton also runs small language models (1–7B parameters) cost-efficiently for generative AI inference.

Intel-based instances provide strong x86 price-performance for tokenization, batch transforms, and workloads requiring broad framework compatibility. AMD-based instances deliver strong performance for CPU-intensive preprocessing, feature engineering, and inference workloads requiring maximum throughput per core. NVIDIA GPU instances provide high throughput for distributed training, fine-tuning, and large-model inference.

AWS Trainium2 delivers 30–40% better price-performance than comparable GPU instances for training at scale (AWS, n.d.). AWS Inferentia2 provides up to 4x higher throughput and 10x lower latency than its predecessor for production inference. Ray auto-detects accelerator types, so Anyscale routes each workload stage to the appropriate hardware without manual configuration.

Spot Instances with Ray fault tolerance

Anyscale keeps head nodes on On-Demand and runs workers on Spot with automatic fallback. Ray Data retries failed tasks on replacement nodes. Ray Train resumes from checkpoints, achieving up to 60% savings on distributed training. Ray Serve proactively migrates replicas on the 2-minute preemption warning.

Capacity Blocks and On-Demand Capacity Reservations

For scheduled training runs requiring capacity availability, Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks reserve 1–64 accelerated instances for up to six months, bookable eight weeks in advance. Each block supports up to 512 GPUs or 1,024 Trainium chips, placed in Amazon EC2 UltraClusters with petabit-scale networking. Anyscale machine pools reference capacity reservations directly with priority-ordered fallback: Capacity Block, then Spot, then On-Demand. On-Demand Capacity Reservations (ODCRs) provide open-ended capacity availability.

Combined provisioning strategy

Anyscale runs two-layer autoscaling: Ray Serve scales replicas on request metrics while the cluster autoscaler provisions and terminates nodes. The recommended purchasing stack starts with AWS Compute Savings Plans, saving up to 66% across Graviton, GPU, Trainium, and Inferentia. Layer on Spot for fault-tolerant batch jobs, Capacity Blocks for scheduled training, and On-Demand for burst.

Getting started: From prototype to production

Your path follows four phases, each building on the last without code changes:

Phase 1: Validate locally (1–2 days). Start with Ray on a single Amazon EC2 instance or your laptop. Build your data pipeline and training loop, and validate model quality before touching distributed infrastructure.

Phase 2: Scale data (1–2 weeks). Deploy Ray Data with AWS Graviton and Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to process your full dataset at scale, with Spot Instances reducing preprocessing costs by up to 90% (AWS, n.d.).

Phase 3: Scale training (2–4 weeks). Choose your deployment option: Amazon EC2 for maximum flexibility, Amazon EKS for Kubernetes-native environments, or Amazon SageMaker HyperPod for resilience-critical runs. Scale training across multiple GPUs or AWS Trainium instances with EFA.

Phase 4: Deploy inference (1–2 weeks). Deploy Ray Serve for model serving with autoscaling configured to your traffic patterns.

The same code runs across all four phases. Moving from a single instance to a multi-node cluster requires only configuration changes managed by Anyscale.

Conclusion

Ray and Anyscale on AWS provide a practical path from prototype to production across the full AI/ML pipeline. Three deployment options address different operational requirements: Amazon EC2 for maximum flexibility, Amazon EKS for Kubernetes-native environments, and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod for resilience-critical training. With heterogeneous clusters mixing Amazon EC2 Spot Instances, AWS Graviton, NVIDIA GPUs, AWS Trainium, and AWS Inferentia, you can match compute to each pipeline stage. The same Ray code runs from a single instance to a multi-node cluster without modification, and Anyscale handles cluster management, fault tolerance, autoscaling, and resource orchestration.

Your next steps depend on where you are today:

  • Already running Ray on AWS – deploy Anyscale through the AWS Marketplace for managed autoscaling, cost controls, and governance.
  • New to distributed ML – start with the Anyscale documentation on a single Amazon EC2 instance, then scale out.
  • Evaluating Anyscale – explore the Ray quickstart for architecture guides and tutorials.

For more on the AWS services covered in this post, see the documentation for Amazon EC2, Amazon EKS, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, AWS Trainium, AWS Inferentia, and AWS Graviton.
