posts.title: Inside an enterprise AI agent: A governed, observable loop architecture
posts.summary: This post lays out a five-layer reference architecture for governed, observable enterprise AI agents on AWS: an API gateway, a five-phase agent runtime, a knowledge and state tier, platform services, and a cross-cutting…
posts.content:
An enterprise AI agent isn’t a bigger chatbot. A chatbot answers one message at a time. An agent keeps working toward a goal: it reads what the user is asking for, breaks the work into steps, pulls in the knowledge it needs, weighs the evidence, calls external tools, and checks the results before it decides whether to keep going or hand back an answer. Every one of those steps touches real systems and real data, so governance, observability, and trust controls must live at each step. Most chatbot designs don’t provide them.

This post lays out a reference architecture for that kind of agent, organized as five layers: an API gateway that handles identity and policy, a five-phase agent runtime (Understand, Plan, Retrieve, Reason, and Act and Observe), a knowledge and state tier that gives the agent memory, a platform-services layer for models and tools, and a trust and control framework that runs across all of them. Each layer maps to AWS managed services. We also cover the design patterns that work and the mistakes we have seen teams make.

Enterprises are moving past single-turn question-and-answer interfaces for business reasons. They want to automate more of the routine work so their people can spend time elsewhere, ship products and customer experiences faster, and get more done without adding headcount. Those goals justify the investment, but reaching them requires moving from single-turn chatbots to agents that can carry out multi-step work on their own. That jump brings new problems to solve in orchestration, memory, and governance, and the rest of this section is about what those problems demand of the architecture.

From chatbots to agents

Enterprise AI is shifting from systems that answer a question and stop to agents that plan, use tools, and come back with an outcome you can verify. The difference is the loop. Rather than returning one response, an agent cycles through understanding, planning, retrieval, reasoning, and action, and it keeps cycling until it either reaches the user’s goal or decides a human needs to step in.

At AWS re:Invent 2025, Werner Vogels said that the developers who succeed think in systems and build with precision. The teams pulling ahead with agents aren’t the teams that moved first or chose the newest model. They are the ones who treat the whole thing as a system and understand that a choice made in one layer shows up in every layer around it.

What is an AI agent? An AI agent uses a foundation model (FM) as its reasoning core and adds tools, memory, and guardrails so it can take on work that takes more than one step. Where a single-turn chatbot answers and forgets, an agent holds onto state, reasons across several steps, and acts in systems outside itself.

The enterprise imperative: Governed, observable, trustworthy, cost-aware

A capable model is the more straightforward part. Running agents in an enterprise means putting governance, observability, trust controls, policy enforcement, and cost controls around every step they take. Cost matters as much as capability: many enterprises find token spend growing faster than the productivity gains it delivers, so an agent must also be designed to spend inference where it adds value. That is what this architecture is built to do:

  • Governed – Every action clears a policy gate, an approval workflow, or a guardrail before it runs.
  • Observable – Each step emits a trace (latency, tokens, tool status, and execution path) for later audit.
  • Trustworthy – Confidence scoring, evaluations, and human checkpoints sit between the agent and the user.
  • Iterative – The loop sharpens its understanding on each pass as tool results come back.

What this post covers

What follows is a reference architecture for enterprise AI agents on AWS, walked through layer by layer from the first request to the verified result, with diagrams, the AWS services that implement each piece, and the patterns worth copying and avoiding. The aim is to give architects and engineering leaders a shared vocabulary and a mental model for designing these systems.

The AWS Well-Architected Framework Generative AI Lens organizes generative AI workloads around six pillars (operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability), each with its own practices and controls. We split the agent into layers that line up with those pillars, so every layer owns a clear responsibility that traces back to a recognized standard instead of a one-off choice. Teams can change, secure, and scale one layer without disturbing the others while keeping the end-to-end governance the Lens requires.

Layered architecture design

The design is layered and loop-based, with five tiers that each do one job. The agent runtime sits in the middle. It’s a five-phase loop that turns a user’s goal into a verified outcome. Around it sit the layers for knowledge, platform services, trust controls, and the governance that cuts across everything.

Reference architecture diagram

Figure 1 shows the five layers together. Read it top to bottom: the API gateway takes the request and enforces identity and policy, then the flow moves down through the agent runtime, the knowledge and state tier, and the platform services, with the trust and control framework running alongside on the right.

Figure 1: Inside an enterprise AI agent, reference architecture

Design principles

Five principles shaped this design, and each one left a mark on the layers you will see later in concrete ways. Zero trust is why identity context travels through every phase of the loop. Observable by default is why there is a dedicated step-level tracing tier instead of leaning on application logs.

These principles aren’t ad-hoc. They come directly from the AWS Well-Architected Framework Generative AI Lens. The Lens’s security guidance maps closely to the following five principles. Least-privilege access across models, data stores, endpoints, and workflows is what zero trust and defense in depth rest on. Securing the data and the traffic between components is separation of concerns in practice. Watching and enforcing the boundaries between the control and data planes is observable by default doing its job. And constraining what the agent is allowed to do, through guardrails and clear limits, is where fail-safe defaults come from. Because it builds on the Lens, this design follows recognized AWS guidance rather than a single team’s convention. It also reflects what AWS Professional Services has implemented and run in production with enterprise customers across industries such as retail and technology: lessons learned in the field that we apply on every engagement, not a set of theoretical best practices. For the full security guidance, see the Generative AI Lens security pillar in the AWS Well-Architected documentation.

PrincipleDescriptionZero trustEvery request is authenticated and authorized before reaching the runtime. User identity flows through every phase.Defense in depthMultiple layers of controls (API gateway, policy gate, trust and control, governance) facilitate no single point of failure.Separation of concernsEach architectural layer has clear boundaries and responsibilities. Knowledge is separated from compute. Trust is separated from execution.Observable by defaultEvery step produces telemetry. Tracing, metrics, and logs are first-class architectural concerns, not afterthoughts.Fail-safe defaultsWhen uncertain, the agent defaults to the safest action: clarify with the user or escalate to a human.

Layer 1 of 5 · Entry point: API gateway, identity, and policy (see Figure 1)

Every interaction starts with a user goal: a request in plain language that kicks off the loop. Before it reaches the runtime, it goes through the API gateway and the identity and policy layer, where the zero-trust posture is enforced.

User goal

The user goal starts with a business objective that drives the top-level intent, stated in natural language. It might be as small as “What was our Q3 revenue?” or as involved as “Book a meeting with Sarah, check her calendar availability, and send a summary of our last project discussion.” The agent’s first job is to read that intent and work out the most efficient way to deliver it.

API gateway

The API gateway is the front door for every interaction. It terminates TLS, routes requests (REST, plus WebSocket for streaming responses), applies rate limits, and validates input. On AWS, this is usually Amazon API Gateway with WebSocket APIs for real-time streaming.

Identity and authentication

No request reaches the runtime unauthenticated. The identity layer checks OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens, resolves who the caller is, and attaches their context (role, permissions, organization, and session ID) to the request. That context rides along through every later phase, so each tool call and data lookup stays within the caller’s permissions.

Policy enforcement

The policy layer handles role-based access control (RBAC), tool-level permissions, data scoping, and usage quotas. It decides which tools the agent might call for a given user, which data it might touch, and how many tokens it might use in a session.

ComponentResponsibilityAWS serviceAPI gatewayTLS termination, request routing, WebSocket streaming, rate limitingAmazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer (ALB)IdentityToken validation, OAuth 2.0/OIDC, user context injection, session managementAmazon Cognito, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)PolicyRBAC, tool permissions, data scoping, usage quotasIAM policies, AWS Organizations

Design principle: Zero trust. The gateway authenticates and authorizes every request before it reaches the runtime. The user’s identity, role, and permissions ride on the session context and stay with the request through every phase of the loop.

Layer 2 of 5 · Agent runtime: the five-phase cognitive loop (see Figure 1)

The runtime performs the core work of the agent. It runs a continuous loop of five phases that track how a careful professional handles a hard task: understand what is being asked, plan an approach, gather the information you need, reason through the choices, then act and watch what comes back before going around again. (see Figure 2)

A note on the model. We aren’t claiming a new theory of agent cognition here. These five phases combine proven ideas under one vocabulary. They draw on the sense, plan, act loop from robotics, the reasoning and acting pattern from ReAct prompting, and the self-reflection step from approaches such as Reflexion (a technique in which the model critiques its own previous attempt and uses that feedback to improve the next one). The enterprise contribution is naming the phases out loud, so you have a clear place to attach governance, observability, and trust controls at each one. If you already think in three or four steps, say plan, act, observe, these phases map directly onto that model.

Figure 2: The five-phase cognitive loop: Understand, Plan, Retrieve, Reason, Act and Observe

Passes through the loop can end in a final answer, or they can go around again with new evidence from a tool result, an error to handle, or extra context. This ability to refine its work separates an agent from a single large language model (LLM) call.

Phase 1: Understand (intent, context, and constraints)

Understand is the agent’s perception step. It reads the user’s input and pulls out three things:

  • Intent – What the user is actually trying to do. The agent classifies the request type (retrieve information, perform an action, or generate content) and identifies the domain.
  • Context – A working picture built from several sources: the conversation so far (short-term memory), the user’s profile and permissions from the gateway, session state, and relevant history from earlier interactions (long-term memory).
  • Constraints – The boundaries it has to respect: time limits, data access tied to the IAM role, token budgets, which tools are available, and organization-specific policies.

On AWS. Understand usually runs on Amazon Bedrock with a foundation model such as Anthropic Claude or Amazon Nova doing the intent classification. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock. The system prompt carries the agent’s persona, its tools, and its behavioral guardrails, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails filter the input before the model ever sees it.

Phase 2: Plan (decompose, select tools, and define success criteria)

With the intent clear, the agent moves to Plan, where the foundation model breaks the goal into steps.

Sub-stepDescriptionOutputDecomposeBreak the user’s goal into a sequence of sub-tasks. Complex goals might require multiple tool calls and intermediate reasoning steps.Ordered task graph (directed acyclic graph, or DAG)Select toolsFor each sub-task, select the appropriate tool(s) from the tool registry using tool descriptions and few-shot examples.Tool-to-task mappingSuccess criteriaDefine what “done” looks like for each sub-task. The Reason phase uses this to evaluate whether a tool call succeeded.Evaluation rubric

No tool runs straight from the plan. Each call first passes through the tool gateway and policy enforcement layer, which checks permissions, inspects the input parameters, applies governance policy, and confirms the request is within budget.

Re-planning. Plan is not a one-shot step. When Reason sees that a sub-task failed or came back wrong, the agent can revise the plan by reordering the task graph, choosing a different tool, or splitting a stubborn step into smaller ones.

Phase 3: Retrieve (knowledge, memory, and session state)

In Retrieve, the agent grounds its reasoning in facts from three sources:

  • Knowledge base (Retrieval Augmented Generation, or RAG) – Semantic search over enterprise documents using embeddings and vector retrieval, with reranking for precision and access filtering for security.
  • Memory – Short-term (the conversation buffer), long-term (preferences and facts it has learned), and episodic (how past tasks turned out).
  • Session state – The current interaction’s tool-result cache, intermediate computations, and external API responses.

The RAG pipeline runs in four stages:

  1. Query rewriting: Optimize the natural language query for search, optionally generating multiple queries for different facets.
  2. Embedding and search: Embed the query and match against the vector index using approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search.
  3. Reranking: A cross-encoder model reranks initial results for precision, filtering out false positives.
  4. Access filtering: Results are filtered based on the user’s identity and data access policies.

On AWS. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the fully managed RAG capability. It handles chunking, embedding with Amazon Titan Embeddings, and vector storage in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless. For memory, Amazon DynamoDB holds session state and Amazon ElastiCache caches recent results for low-latency reads.

Phase 4: Reason (model routing, decide, and reflect)

Reason is where the model turns evidence into a decision. With the retrieved context in hand, it does three things:

  • Model routing – Pick the right model for this step. Simple work goes to smaller, faster models. Complex reasoning goes to a larger, more capable model. That keeps cost and latency down, and it’s one of the most effective cost-optimization levers in the architecture.
  • Decision – Combine what was retrieved with the plan to decide the next tool call, the parameters to pass, whether the plan needs changing, or whether to ask a clarifying question.
  • Reflection – Look at the result of each action. Did the call succeed? Does the output match what was expected? Does the plan need to change?

Anti-pattern: Infinite loops. Knowing when to stop is a core design problem. With no safeguards, an agent can get stuck reasoning in circles. The usual defenses are a cap on iterations, a timeout budget, classifying errors as transient or permanent, and a path to escalate to a human. Getting this wrong costs more than one unfinished task. A looping agent keeps calling the model and its tools, so token spend and compute climb with every wasted pass and nothing gets done. The effects compound. Latency rises and service level agreements (SLAs) slip. Downstream APIs and model endpoints absorb redundant load, which can trigger throttling for other workloads. The user waits on a request that never completes, which erodes the trust this architecture exists to protect. Caps on iterations, time, and tokens, plus an escalation path, keep a confused agent from turning into a runaway bill.

Phase 5: Act and observe (APIs, code, data, and MCP tools)

Act and Observe is where the agent reaches into the outside world. It carries the most governance risk because it changes real systems.

  • Tool execution – The agent calls external tools through standard interfaces (REST APIs, code sandboxes, data connectors, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools) and logs every call with its full request and response.
  • Observation – Each result is parsed, validated, and fed back into context: structured returns, error messages, status codes, side effects.
  • Approval gate – Before a destructive action runs (a write, delete, or send), it goes through the policy and approval gate. Depending on the risk and the organization’s policy, that is an automated check, a human sign-off, or both.

The feedback loop

When a tool returns success, an error, or partial data, the result flows back into Understand and becomes part of the context for the next pass. Each pass through the loop uses this new context to move closer to the right answer. What flows back includes:

  • Tool results: Structured data, API responses, and computation outputs.
  • Errors: Error messages, timeouts, and permission denials that inform replanning.
  • New evidence: Information discovered during tool execution that changes the understanding of the task.

Tool gateway and policy enforcement

posts.title: How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions
posts.summary: Zillow sends more than 100 million personalized notifications a day, each as a short-lived AWS Step Functions Express workflow. See how the Comms Experience team replaced more than 10 campaign generators with one…
posts.content:
Every day, Zillow sends home shoppers more than 100 million personalized email and push notifications: saved search alerts, home recommendations, property updates, seller reports, and reminders. These messages are one of Zillow’s core ways to engage home shoppers, and Zillow delivers them on time with consistent behavior across every campaign. Today, each of those notifications runs as its own short-lived workflow execution on AWS Step Functions Express Workflows.

The underlying shape of this work isn’t unique to real estate. Many systems run the same kind of workflow at high volume: take an event, enrich it from several services, apply rules, assemble an output, and send it. This post shows how Zillow built one configuration-driven orchestration system to run that pattern at scale, and what teams across many domains can reuse from it.

Historically at Zillow a separate generator service produced each of these campaigns, and each service carried its own workflow, data models, and business rules. As the number of notification campaigns grew, so did duplicated engineering work, inconsistent behavior, and operational cost. Product teams needed to launch campaigns faster, reuse shared capabilities, and run consistent experiments without system-specific work.

To meet that need, the Zillow Comms Experience team, working with AWS, built two things. The first is the Campaign Orchestrator, which is a configuration-driven orchestration layer that runs each notification as a short-lived workflow execution on Step Functions Express Workflows. The second is the Universal Content Generator (UCG), a library of reusable, schema-driven content modules that those workflows call. Together they make campaign creation faster and more consistent, and they give AI-assisted tooling a declarative format to work with.

The challenge: why the original system needed replacing

The previous content generation model slowed product delivery. Zillow’s Comms Experience supported more than 20 email and push campaigns generated by more than 10 microservices. Each microservice owned its own workflow, models, business rules, and assembly logic.

Most campaigns followed the same pattern: receive a trigger, hydrate data, apply rules, assemble content, and send the message. Each campaign service implemented that pattern separately, creating duplicate engineering work and inconsistent behavior. It also added operational overhead across releases, monitoring, logs, dashboards, and on-call support.

Each campaign was built as its own service because, when these systems were first built, scale was the main challenge. As Zillow added more products, the tradeoff changed. Similar features ended up implemented differently across campaigns, so every new capability had to be rebuilt and retested in each service. That made it hard to roll out features across products and slowed development. The push to centralize came from that cost: we needed to move faster and stay consistent across every customer experience. With one shared implementation, a feature could be built once and reused everywhere, while each campaign kept the flexibility to tailor its experience. Before evaluating workflow engines, we first had to extract shared logic into reusable modules and move campaign decisions into configuration.

The following diagram shows the original architecture, where each campaign generator carries its own copy of the workflow, data models, and business rules.

Figure 1: Original system

Competitive evaluation

We evaluated Temporal, Flowable, an in-house engine, and Step Functions Standard and Express Workflows against four criteria. Those criteria were reliability, total cost of ownership, development speed, and how well the service would scale across teams. The engine had to be managed, configuration-driven, and able to orchestrate both newer and older services. Pricing also had to fit our volume.

Temporal and Flowable would have added another infrastructure component to operate. That worked against two of our core goals: cutting the release, monitoring, and on-call overhead that the original system created, and getting pilot projects running quickly. Neither is available as a managed AWS service, so we would have had to run and scale them ourselves. Step Functions is serverless, so we had no servers or worker fleets to run, and a team could start a pilot without first setting up infrastructure. An in-house engine offered control but required custom lifecycle management, worker pools, queue integration, and monitoring. Step Functions met the core orchestration needs at roughly a quarter of the estimated build effort and a quarter of the ongoing maintenance effort. It was the clear choice for the minimum viable product (MVP).

Express mode compared with Standard mode

Our planning model assumed high-throughput, low-latency workflows. The MVP plan ramped from 14 million workflows per day to more than 100 million across all campaigns. At full scale that means several thousand executions per second at peak. Each workflow runs for only a few seconds, and a notification has to arrive while it’s still relevant. We evaluated both Step Functions execution modes, and for our use case Express Workflows were the better fit.

The following table shows how Standard and Express Workflows compared against our requirements for each key characteristic:

Zillow needStandard WorkflowsExpress WorkflowsHigh workflow volumeLower default start quota.Higher default start quota.Low latencyOptimized for durable, long-running workflows.Optimized for short-running workflows.Execution guaranteesExactly once, which is stronger than needed.At least once, sufficient with idempotent modules.

Our workflows are high volume, short-lived, finish well within the five-minute Express limit, and are designed around idempotent module calls. We validated quota, latency, and operational behavior during the traffic ramp-up.

The architecture

Campaign Orchestrator is a configuration-driven workflow platform. Each message is input data combined with persisted campaign configuration. The configuration is relatively static for each workflow, while the input data stays flexible based on how the configured steps are assembled.

A shared orchestration layer reads queued campaign events, groups work where appropriate, and invokes the corresponding Step Functions Express Workflow for each campaign. Campaign metadata describes product constants, ownership, and Zillow environment features. Workflow configuration describes step topology, step-level configuration, mappings, branching, delay behavior, and send behavior.

The following JSON shows a simplified workflow input, combining the message payload with the platform, campaign, and configuration metadata that drive the workflow:

{
  "payload": {
    "trackingId123": {
      "recipientId": "user123",
      "homeIds": ["home1", "home2"]
    }
  },
  "platformMetadata": {
    "messageType": "email",
    "source": "savedSearch"
  },
  "campaignMetadata": {
    "campaignName": "saved_search_alert",
    "owner": "comms_experience"
  },
  "config": {
    "modules": ["user_profile", "property_data", "email_transformation"],
    "experiment": "cta_test"
  }
}

The following diagram shows the new architecture, where a single shared orchestration layer and one library of reusable modules serve every campaign. A message moves through the diagram from left to right. The ingress service queues it, and the router applies campaign controls and starts the workflow. Campaign Orchestrator runs the Step Functions steps, each step calls a UCG module, and the delivery service sends the result.

Figure 2: The new system

Router

Our campaigns need a set of controls applied before a workflow starts: queue polling, batching, idempotency checks, pause and resume behavior, replay coordination, speed control, and campaign routing decisions. Some of these controls are specific to how we order and throttle campaign sends, so they live outside Step Functions.

We centralized these controls in an in-house router service that reads from Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) and starts the right Step Functions workflow. Keeping them in one place gives us a single point to pause a campaign, replay a batch, or adjust send speed without changing any workflow definition.

Shared modules (UCG)

The Universal Content Generator is the modular content generation layer behind Campaign Orchestrator. Instead of each campaign owning a separate generator, UCG organizes shared capabilities into reusable modules. Before UCG, this logic was spread across more than 10 separate generators. Centralizing it in one service also smoothed its traffic. Some daily campaigns used to run for about four hours and leave their generator idle for the other 20. Now all campaigns share one fleet, so the load spreads across the day.

Modules handle capabilities such as property hydration (loading listing details such as price, photos, and address for each home in a message), hidden homes (listings a user has chosen to hide, which we filter out of notifications), common data (the subscriptions, saved homes, eligibility flags, and propensity scores every campaign loads for a recipient), recommendations, A/B testing, and content assembly. They are stateless and schema-driven.

Direct service invocation with HTTP Invoke

A key design choice was to call UCG directly through Step Functions HTTP Invoke. This fits the workload for two reasons. First, our content generation logic already ran as long-lived containerized services inside our private service environment, with network access, service discovery, and authentication established. Second, routing workflow steps to UCG added no new compute cost.

With Step Functions HTTP Invoke, we call UCG modules for data hydration, rule checks, and content assembly as they already run. Authentication runs through an Amazon EventBridge connection. Each HTTP Invoke task points to the connection with a ConnectionArn. The connection holds an API key, and UCG checks that key on every request. Amazon EventBridge keeps the key in AWS Secrets Manager and adds it to the request at call time. The workflow definition never contains the key, and neither does our application code. When the key rotates, we rotate it once in the connection and every workflow picks it up.

To avoid repeating the same HTTP Invoke settings in every workflow, we introduced component inheritance. Components are written in a slightly modified version of the Step Functions task definition we deploy through AWS CloudFormation. A base component holds the settings that many steps share, and other components extend it. The following base component, content_module_call, defines how every workflow step calls UCG services directly through HTTP Invoke: the resource, method, headers, and the ConnectionArn for the connection described earlier.

{
  "Type": "Task",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::http:invoke",
  "Arguments": {
    "ApiEndpoint": "{% '${contentServiceEndpoint}' & '/modules/' & $moduleId %}",
    "Method": "POST",
    "Headers": {
      "Content-Type": "application/json"
    },
    "InvocationConfig": {
      "ConnectionArn": "${connectionArn}"
    }
  }
}

Business modules extend the shared HTTP component and supply only the module endpoint. Before deployment, our build script replaces each component with a standard Task state: it loads the component named in Extends, merges the step’s own fields on top, and writes the result into the Terraform we deploy. Workflow definitions stay focused on product intent rather than network plumbing:

{
  "Type": "Component",
  "Extends": "content_module_call",
  "Arguments": {
    "ApiEndpoint": "{% '${contentServiceEndpoint}/modules/profile_module' %}"
  }
}

Configuration abstraction layer

Step Functions state machine definitions, JSONata expressions, and infrastructure definitions are powerful, but they are not the right interface for every campaign owner. We added a higher-level configuration layer so campaign owners can define their own workflows without having to understand Step Functions CloudFormation configuration. Each campaign config describes a workflow: which modules run, in what order, and how data moves between them. The system translates that config into the Step Functions definition and CloudFormation template that gets deployed. Campaigns don’t share one generic workflow that picks modules at runtime. Each campaign gets its own workflow, built from the same shared modules and components. As a next step, we are considering a generic workflow that assembles modules in real time from config. Each campaign would still run its own copy of that workflow, so ownership stays isolated per campaign.

Campaign owners specify the modules needed for an email template or push notification. Each module exposes input, output, and configuration schemas. Campaign owners define module outputs to satisfy the template input schema. Module inputs define what triggers need to provide.

With this structure, campaign owners onboard through a declarative process. They work with configuration instead of raw workflow code or JSONata expressions. They can also run controlled experiments and give AI tools a format they can inspect, generate, and modify with appropriate validation.

The following simplified A/B test config is adapted from a real Campaign Orchestrator config. It injects an A/B test module before email transformation and maps the experiment result into the next step without directly touching Step Functions or CloudFormation definition.

{
  "steps": [
    { "module": "profile" },
    { "module": "property_data" },
    { "module": "experiment", "experiment": "cta_variant_test", "before": "assemble_email" },
    { "module": "assemble_email", "inputs": { "variant": "experiment.result" } }
  ]
}

Because a campaign is declared as schema-validated configuration, the same contracts that protect human changes also apply to AI-assisted tooling. Our internal assistants already draft module selections and mappings from a product brief, and the output must pass the same schema checks, JSONata tests, and Step Functions validation before it can be deployed.

Batch mode optimization

Campaign Orchestrator supports batching, which improves overall throughput while reducing cost. Instead of launching one workflow per message, the router can group messages and invoke one workflow for the batch.

For example, processing 100 messages individually could produce 100 workflow executions and 400 HTTP requests to UCG services. With batching, the same messages can be processed in one workflow with four HTTP requests, assuming each step supports bulk input and output. That matters at our volume for two reasons. Express Workflows charge for each request and for run time. Batching cuts the number of requests, but each batch runs longer. A rule of thumb: a batch of 10 messages costs less than 10 separate runs as long as it takes no more than 10 times as long as one run. In the preceding four-step example, one message takes about 1.2 seconds, so a batch of 10 saves money if it finishes within 12 seconds. In practice, a batch runs only 10 to 20 percent longer than a single message, about 1.4 seconds instead of 12. That makes a batch of 10 about 90 percent cheaper than 10 separate runs. The batched payload stays under the 256 KiB limit, so memory is still billed at the 64 MB minimum. Fewer executions and HTTP requests also use less of the StartExecution rate, HTTP Invoke concurrency, and logging throughput we size for. That leaves headroom to send more notifications on the same quotas.

The batching model appears in the Step Functions definition and JSONata expressions. This simplified example shapes a batched payload into a bulk UCG request while preserving each tracking ID:

{
  "campaignName": $campaignMetadata.campaignName,
  "messages": $map($keys($states.input.payload), function($trackingId) { (
    $message := $lookup($states.input.payload, $trackingId);
    {
      "trackingId": $trackingId,
      "recipientId": $message.recipientId,
      "homeIds": $message.homeIds,
      "config": $config.propertyHydration
    }
  ) })
}

Batching works only if every step in the workflow can handle a batch rather than a single message. For UCG, that requirement is built into the module API. Each module’s schemas define its input, output, and config models, and the module API accepts those models as a batch keyed by tracking ID. A module that doesn’t follow that API won’t build. Our JSONata mappings and upstream and downstream service contracts already accepted bulk input internally, so adding batching didn’t require reworking them.

Batching also can’t cost us visibility into individual messages. Because each batch is keyed by tracking ID, as the preceding example shows, UCG returns a result from each module for each tracking ID. The router uses those per-message results to deliver, retry, or drop each message individually, so one failed message doesn’t fail the whole batch.

The following diagram shows how the router groups messages into a single batched workflow execution.

Figure 3: Batching mode

Scaling: Performance and organizational

At our target throughput, service quotas are part of the architecture. We reviewed Step Functions StartExecution rate limits, HTTP Invoke concurrency, and Amazon CloudWatch logging throughput before traffic ramped. HTTP Invoke concurrency needed attention first, because its default quota is lower than the rate at which Express Workflows can start. We sized the required concurrency from our capacity model and worked with AWS to raise the quota before each rollout phase, so throughput limits never gated the traffic ramp.

We planned the rollout in phases, from early traffic to more than 100 million daily executions. With this approach, we could validate cost, quotas, latency, and operations before full scale.

The architecture also supports organizational scaling. Product teams own campaign modules, steps, configuration, and the Step Functions cost tied to their traffic, so they can launch and change campaigns without waiting on the central team. Central teams own shared infrastructure such as the router service, Step Functions patterns, Amazon SQS integration, and deployment tooling, so one improvement reaches every campaign.

posts.title: Intelligent Delivery: Making Every Unit of Compute Serve Better Ads
posts.summary: Ads ranking models are growing toward LLM scale faster than the hardware to run them can keep up. An extra unit of compute has more impact on some ad requests, models, and chips than on others. The challenge is deciding…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Zhaojun Zhang, Qinwei Zhu, Gang Li, Jianwei Xiao, Yanan Wang, Hongmei Li, Deepak Vijaywargi, Ke Pan, Li Yu
  • Ads ranking models are growing toward LLM scale faster than the hardware to run them can keep up. An extra unit of compute has more impact on some ad requests, models, and chips than on others. The challenge is deciding where to allocate it to get the best outcome for the entire system.
  • We built Intelligent Delivery, an ML-driven system that allocates resources across the serving stack toward the system-wide optimum. It has delivered ~10% incremental ranking performance on top of model and system advancements since 2017.
  • We’re sharing a few of Intelligent Delivery’s capabilities: how we build ML models to predict the marginal utility of compute, multi-layered mechanisms to move resources across the system, and how we increasingly leverage agentic AI to continuously detect and respond to system shifts. 

As frontier ads ranking systems advance toward larger models, broader candidate sets, and richer delivery architectures, they also place greater demands on serving efficiency. Compute resources do not scale at the rate that models and system complexity do. The challenge is not just how to build more powerful models, but how to operate them efficiently across a heterogeneous system, with finite serving capacity, and under a tight latency budget. We recently shared how we put idle inference capacity to work. This post covers how we decide where each unit of compute goes to achieve globally optimal system efficiency.

Intelligent Delivery is our approach to the problem, and it has contributed an additional ~10% improvement in ads ranking performance on top of model and system advancements across major surfaces, from 2017 through the first half of 2026. It introduces an ML-driven, increasingly AI-operated adaptive optimization layer that continuously directs resources toward the requests, models, hardware fleets, and ranking stages with the highest marginal utility. This helps us run advanced ads ranking models efficiently in production, getting more out of every unit of compute to serve better ads for people who use our apps and services.

The Goal and What Makes It Difficult

One of our goals is to create a delivery system that continuously converges on its global optimum, regardless of how user behavior changes, models evolve, and the serving stack grows more complex. 

Three fundamental properties of ads delivery systems make this challenging:

The marginal impact of compute is highly heterogeneous and context-dependent: The same additional unit of compute can generate very different returns depending on the product surface, user intent, candidate quality, and system state. Request-aware signals alone are not sufficient; allocating well means estimating, for every request, the return on every available tunable system parameter, where each knob behaves differently at each stage of the funnel. We need to produce a per-request result calculation across a vast decision space within milliseconds.

Local optimality does not translate to global optimality: Result estimation is just the start; the serving stack must also be dynamically controllable. Ads delivery spans multi-stage ranking, hundreds of models, generations of hardware, and many data centers. Resources cannot be shifted freely and reliably across these boundaries without adaptive controls that account for complex dependencies throughout the stack. 

The global optimum is a moving target: The optimization landscape is continuously shifting. Every new model, hardware generation, or new architecture changes the landscape and can invalidate previously optimal allocation decisions. The system needs to adapt quickly enough to retain its optimality. 

Intelligent Delivery includes three capabilities, each designed to address one of these fundamental system challenges.

Capabilities of Intelligent Delivery

1. Request Understanding: A Shared ML Intelligence Layer for Compute

Some ad requests benefit more from additional computation than others. Initially, we captured these differences through coarse segments: Requests were grouped by attributes such as surface, context, and ad creative representation, with engineers creating policies to allocate resources for each group. This approach delivered improvements but did not scale. Every new signal multiplied the rules, making the effort unsustainable, and independent segments could not capture the nonlinear interactions among thousands of signals, which limited accuracy.

We achieved about a 20% improvement in identifying the highest-impact ad requests in offline benchmarks on major surfaces, relative to our previous production model, after reframing this into two ML problems: Which ad requests are most likely to benefit from additional compute? And how will different resource settings affect their outcomes and serving performance?

To answer the first question, we built the Resource Core Model, deep learning models with 6B sparse parameters and 20M dense parameters that run once before candidate retrieval and are shared across the delivery funnel. Learned embeddings and deep feature interactions capture nuanced request patterns that manually defined segments cannot.

We then fine-tune the Resource Core Model into a set of specialized models, each generating incremental signals about outcome, compute consumption, and latency impact. Together this forms a shared ML intelligence layer for resource allocation: The Resource Core Model understands each request and its serving behavior, while individual mechanisms determine how to translate those predictions into actions.

2. Allocation Mechanisms: A Hierarchy of Decision Engines

Ads serving runs on a globally distributed, heterogeneous fleet with many data center regions, several hardware generations, and millions of hosts, all shared by a multi-tier serving stack. A single allocation mechanism cannot control the complex resource distribution end to end. So we decomposed the problem into a hierarchy of layers and built a dedicated decision engine for each. The easiest way to see the hierarchy is to follow a single request through it.

Someone opens their feed. An ad request is created, and over the next few hundred milliseconds it passes through a chain of resource allocation decisions. This leads us to three important questions and answers.

Which region serves it? Traffic and capacity are not colocated, and each region carries a different hardware mix and a different amount of headroom — so the same unit of compute is more efficient in some places than in others. We built real-time infrastructure to dynamically shift traffic between regions in a cycle of minutes, driving toward the point where every region achieves the same level of efficiency on its marginal unit of capacity.

What hardware does it land on? Our fleet spans CPUs from Intel, AMD, and Arm and accelerators from NVIDIA, AMD, and our own Meta Training and Inference Accelerator (MTIA), across several generations of each. The hard part isn’t the variety; it’s that capacity isn’t interchangeable. Our stages are bound by different resources — retrieval by memory capacity, ranking by compute, and model inference by accelerator throughput — so there is no single fastest SKU, only a best match per workload. We benchmark measured efficiency for every workload-SKU pair, then solve the assignment so that scarce hardware goes to the workloads that convert it into the most useful work. 

Inside the host, how much of this machine does the request get? Concurrent requests differ in latency budget and impact, under a hard tail-latency SLO. We predict each request’s expected outcome and its compute and latency cost in real time using our advanced deep learning models, and solve a constrained optimization that maximizes impact delivered within the host’s latency budget — as the host load increases, the performance trade-off rises and resource-intensive low-impact work is trimmed first. Enforcing those decisions takes control across the whole stack, so the framework spans from kernel-level scheduler up to application-level thread pools.

These three steps are just a subset of the allocation decisions we make during a request’s lifecycle. Following this, we optimize the number of ads to rank for each request in each ranking stage, what ad candidates enter the pool, and much more.

These allocation decisions are tightly coupled, so a resource change in any one of them ripples across the whole system. Shifting traffic between regions changes per-host load, which drives the feedback controller that sets how much work each request gets. We validate these changes in an end-to-end, closed-loop hardware testing environment to make sure we are optimizing for the global optimum instead of a local optimum.

3. Optimization Loop: Self-Optimizing Serving with Agentic AI

As our ad system advances, productionizing a new model, a new mechanism, or new hardware into the system requires a lot of effort to achieve seamless integration. We can’t brute-force every single configuration across millions of tunable dimensions built in our system for a new change. That would require too much time and far more hardware resources than we have. 

We relied heavily on human expertise and engineers’ prior knowledge to identify promising configurations. But this approach didn’t scale, because every new model, mechanism, and hardware generation expanded the search space faster than engineers could explore it.

We tried automating this with a constrained optimization approach, which delivered improvements but remained inflexible and slow. We found that it lacked the ability to generalize (it could only cover a few key knobs) and couldn’t effectively incorporate human intuition from prior experience.

Instead of doing a blind search, AI agents continuously monitor the entire system landscape, identifying changes and inefficiencies to address. In a long context window, an agent reads mechanism source code, design documents, and a decade of experiment logs and narrows that to a handful of changes worth testing. Engineers review and approve the final change before it ships.

Today, agents can already propose well-reasoned changes and design and run rigorous experiments. In the first half of 2026, agents contributed to about 20% of Intelligent Delivery optimizations. On our most automated mechanism, they now contribute to about 80% of the engineering effort, from understanding the system landscape and forming hypotheses to running experiments and converging on the final change. This shortens the optimization loop from months to weeks while keeping people firmly in control. And it steadily captures the expertise engineers have built over the years.

The Next Frontiers for Intelligent Delivery

End-to-end real-time optimization: Today, understanding a request and deciding how to serve it are still two separate steps. We’re building toward fusing them into a single model that reads a request and serves it in real time, without months of experiments. There’s established work in varying compute per request with learning-based methods. However, doing it jointly across every serving stage at once — under shifting traffic, hard capacity limits, and tight inter-stage dependencies — is the part that’s still open, and it’s what we’re pushing on.

Serving state-of-the-art models on GPUs: Large ranking models, like Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM), are growing toward LLM scale and increasingly run on GPUs, which opens a different optimization space. GPU capacity doesn’t divide the way CPU time does — it comes in whole, fixed blocks, and throughput, batching, and memory all behave differently. The levers we built for a CPU world have to be reimagined, and much of our work now goes into understanding those mechanisms and turning them into new levers. The more useful work we get out of each accelerator, the more people we can serve with strong models under the same capacity.

Acknowledgements

Sowji Adavi, Karthik Alle, Tao Cai, Olivier Chaine, Jianhao Du, Antonio Frigo, Gayatree Ganu, Chao Li, Chao Ma, Bennet Matazzoni, Riddhi Mehta, Saurabh Pohnerkar, Sudhir Pokhrel, Yuehui Qian, Liang Qiao, Yitao Qiu, Rob Schwartzberg, Sanketh Shetty, Ganlin Song, Samuel Tatipamula, Xueqi Wang, Ye Wang, Wei Wei, Jing Xu, Haomin Yu, Jiayi Yu, Jay Zang, Caijie Zhang, Shengjie Zhang, Tong Zhang, and Wei Zheng.

posts.title: Self-service regional failover with Amazon Application Recovery Controller Region Switch and centralized ingress controls
posts.summary: Application teams in regulated enterprises can execute self-service regional failover with Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) Region Switch, even behind centrally managed ingress proxy fleets. Learn how…
posts.content:
In highly regulated industries such as financial services, healthcare, and government, security isn’t negotiable. Compliance frameworks require defense in depth strategies where incoming requests are inspected against security policy to confirm they are safe before reaching applications.

Organizations typically solve this challenge by implementing centralized ingress proxy fleets: hardened entry points that enforce consistent authentication, authorization, threat detection, and audit logging across hundreds of applications.

For critical applications that use regional services and need to operate multi-Region disaster recovery (DR) strategies, this creates a challenge. These applications must regularly demonstrate failover capability, not only to prove DR works, but to satisfy auditor expectations for tested, repeatable recovery procedures. Yet with centralized ingress controls in place, the teams accountable for recovery time objective (RTO) commitments often cannot independently execute failover. They depend on centralized infrastructure teams who might be handling many similar requests simultaneously. This introduces coordination overhead, extends recovery times, and conflicts with the DevOps principle of “you build it, you run it.” Scale this to dozens of interdependent applications and the problem compounds. Individual team recovery is necessary, but without coordinated portfolio-level failover, the enterprise remains exposed.

The challenge isn’t whether to implement defense in depth, which is non-negotiable, but how to preserve application team autonomy, support self-service failover within the constraints of centralized enterprise ingress controls, and ultimately orchestrate coordinated recovery across the portfolio.

In this post, we show how application teams in regulated enterprises can execute self-service regional failover using Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) Region Switch, even when operating behind centrally managed ingress proxy fleets. The pattern uses AWS Transit Gateway peering, Amazon Route 53 Private Hosted Zones, and (optionally) Amazon VPC Lattice to maintain security controls while removing cross-team coordination during DR events. We then demonstrate how a central parent plan can run each application team’s child plan, shared through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM), to support coordinated portfolio-level failover. A single central action runs dependent plans across the enterprise in dependency order, delivering deterministic, fully automated recovery orchestration that replaces the manual coordination of today’s DR playbooks.

Why ARC Region Switch?

Launched in August 2025, Amazon Application Recovery Controller Region Switch is purpose-built for disaster recovery orchestration. Custom scripts and home-grown automation must be built, tested, and maintained independently, often across multiple AWS Regions with no guarantee of synchronization. Region Switch is a fully managed, highly available failover orchestrator that removes the undifferentiated heavy lifting of DR operations.

Effective disaster recovery orchestration for enterprise applications has to overcome three common challenges. The following table describes each one and how Region Switch addresses it.

DR challengeHow ARC Region Switch addresses itConfiguration drift. A recovery plan written months ago might no longer match the environment it protects. Permissions change, resources are renamed, and standby capacity shrinks, and teams often only find out mid-failover.Plan evaluation. Region Switch automatically evaluates your plan’s configuration, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions, and resource readiness multiple times per hour, surfacing issues before they block a recovery. Warnings are visible on the console and available through Amazon EventBridge or the API.Slow detection and decision-making. In a real incident, time is lost noticing the problem, assembling the right people, and agreeing to fail over. All of it adds to your RTO.Automatic triggering. Plans can be initiated automatically from Amazon CloudWatch alarms, removing the time to detect and time to decide from your effective RTO. Teams that want a human checkpoint can add a manual approval step.Recovery logic that drifts across Regions. Multi-step recovery is often scripted separately for each Region. The scripts diverge, are hard to review, and fail silently when they’re finally needed.Codified recovery workflows. Plans are fully codifiable with AWS CloudFormation, the CLI, and the API, so they’re version-controlled and deployed through your existing continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines alongside the application. The visual Workflow Builder helps teams design and modify recovery steps, with the ability to export the configuration back into your infrastructure as code (IaC) pipeline.

A Region Switch plan isn’t bound to a single Region. Its execution engine operates independently in each Region, keeping the failover orchestrator outside the blast radius of the very impairment it’s responding to.

The solution: Self-service regional failover with ARC Region Switch

Application teams create a plan in the ARC Region Switch Workflow Builder that includes task-specific execution blocks: automated steps that handle different aspects of the failover activity. A typical plan might include execution blocks to promote database read replicas, scale compute resources (Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) Auto Scaling groups, EKS pods, or ECS tasks), manipulate Route 53 health checks to redirect traffic, and invoke custom AWS Lambda functions for application-specific logic.

When the team runs a Region Switch plan, whether for a DR test or during an actual incident, ARC runs this workflow from the recovery Region automatically, orchestrating the entire failover sequence without requiring manual intervention from application teams.

Figure 1: ARC Region Switch runs a plan’s execution blocks from the recovery Region to orchestrate failover

To understand how ARC Region Switch supports this self-service capability within the constraints of centralized ingress controls, we need to examine the underlying infrastructure. The architecture relies on a shared responsibility model where infrastructure and application teams each control distinct layers of the stack, creating clear boundaries that preserve security while supporting operational independence.

Building the foundation: Centralized networking with decentralized control

The architecture rests on two foundational elements: centrally managed AWS Transit Gateways and an application-team-owned Amazon Route 53 Private Hosted Zone (PHZ).

Figure 2: Centrally managed Transit Gateways with an application-team-owned Route 53 Private Hosted Zone

A central infrastructure team owns and manages the peered Transit Gateway infrastructure in both AWS Regions, providing VPC attachments to each application team account so traffic can flow from their secure ingress proxy solution. The application team owns and manages a Route 53 PHZ, associated with all four VPCs: both the infrastructure team’s centralized ingress proxy fleet VPCs and the application team’s own VPCs in each Region. This PHZ contains a failover recordset that the ingress proxy fleet uses to resolve the active application endpoint.

This establishes a clear technical boundary. The infrastructure team provides the secure networking foundation and VPC attachments. The application team controls the Domain Name System (DNS) records that determine where traffic flows. Neither team needs to coordinate changes with the other during failover events.

Understanding the multi-Region architecture

To understand how these components work together, let’s examine the complete architecture. The following diagram illustrates the multi-Region design, showing how AWS Global Accelerator, cross-Region AWS Transit Gateway peering, Amazon VPC Lattice, and Amazon Route 53 Private Hosted Zones combine to support self-service failover through Amazon ARC Region Switch while maintaining centralized security controls.

Figure 3: Multi-Region architecture combining Global Accelerator, Transit Gateway peering, VPC Lattice, and Route 53 to support self-service failover

AWS Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs for the ingress proxy fleet. The 50/50 traffic weighting reflects the platform’s multi-tenant design. Because the centralized ingress proxy fleet serves multiple application teams simultaneously, it must be able to route traffic to applications running in either Region, or active-active across both.

The goal of AWS Global Accelerator is to route traffic to the closest point of presence. If your application is active in Region 1 but a consumer is closer to Region 2, traffic routes to the Region 2 endpoint first, then traverses the cross-Region Transit Gateway peering connection to reach the active application.

The architectural trade-off

This represents an intentional trade-off: accepting an additional network hop through Transit Gateway peering in exchange for true self-service failover. Without this cross-Region connectivity, application teams would need to coordinate with infrastructure teams during failover, reintroducing the exact coordination dependency this architecture seeks to remove.

Fine-grained failover control with Amazon VPC Lattice service network endpoints

While the architecture we’ve described supports independent regional failover, Amazon VPC Lattice service network endpoints add another layer of flexibility worth highlighting: fine-grained control over which services fail over.

Each service network endpoint acts as a consolidated endpoint that can host multiple VPC Lattice services behind it. When you associate a Lattice service with a service network endpoint, it receives its own unique Regional DNS name. For example, an authentication service and a payments service hosted behind the same endpoint each receive distinct DNS names. These per-service DNS names each map to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone failover record set, giving each service its own independent failover control.

Figure 4: Each VPC Lattice service behind a service network endpoint maps to its own Route 53 failover record set

The key benefit is fine-grained control: application teams can fail over individual Lattice services one at a time, rather than being forced to flip every service behind the same service network endpoint at once. You can validate your authentication service this week, your payment processing service next week, and your inventory service the week after. Each has its own dedicated failover record set in your PHZ, and each is tested without affecting services still running in the primary Region.

This component-level approach requires the least operational overhead, but it carries a risk of bi-modal behavior, where a workload performs differently, with different response times or processes, under normal conditions versus failure modes. Each independent failover adds another active/standby combination, and each must tolerate the cross-Region latency when a service calls a dependency now in the other Region. Design your components to be resilient to this latency and test the realistic combinations. Component-level failover is best suited to teams who have that confidence, so where you don’t, a coarser-grained approach might be the safer choice.

Operationally, the boundary stays clean. The infrastructure team’s ingress proxy fleet continues resolving through the service network endpoint, while the application team controls which services are active in which Region by managing the health check on each service’s DNS record in their PHZ. As your application grows, you associate new microservices with the existing service network endpoint and add their failover record sets, with no changes required to the infrastructure team’s proxy configuration or VPC attachments.

Note: While this post demonstrates a pattern using Amazon VPC Lattice as the application endpoint target, the same shared responsibility approach works regardless of your application stack. Whether you’re running containers on EKS, serverless functions, or traditional EC2 workloads behind Application Load Balancers or Network Load Balancers, the foundational pattern of centralized networking with decentralized DNS control applies equally.

How an application team fails over independently

When the application team runs their ARC Region Switch plan, traffic shifts between Regions without any involvement from the central infrastructure team.

Each application team can independently test their failover capability at their own cadence, as frequently as they choose. These tests are completely independent: one team’s DR exercise has no impact on any other team’s services. As noted in the preceding section, teams should validate the realistic combinations of failed-over and in-place services rather than only the all-in-one-Region baseline.

The failover sequence

What makes this powerful is that it’s a single orchestrated flow, not a set of manual steps. ARC Region Switch runs each block, verifies it has completed successfully, and only then manages the transition to the next, so the sequence advances deterministically, with no human stitching steps together under pressure.

1. Plan initiation. The application team runs their Region Switch plan through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or API, whether for a scheduled DR test or in response to a real incident. The application team can also set up CloudWatch alarms to trigger plans automatically, then run either fully automatically, with no human intervention required, or with a manual approval step built into the workflow that gives teams control to gate execution at critical points.

Figure 5: Plan initiation through the AWS CLI or API, with optional CloudWatch alarm triggers and a manual approval step

Note: While plans can be built and run through the AWS console (useful during initial testing), the best practice for real DR invocations is to use the Region Switch API or AWS CLI directly. This reduces cross-service dependencies in your critical path and makes sure your recovery execution doesn’t rely on console availability.

2. Database failover. The first execution block initiates the database transition, promoting the secondary Region’s database to become the primary writer. ARC Region Switch supports both switchover and failover for Amazon Aurora Global Database, RDS instances with cross-Region read replicas, and Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) clusters. For databases beyond these, such as Amazon DynamoDB global tables, execution blocks can invoke custom Lambda functions to handle service-specific failover logic.

3. Application stack scales up. Subsequent execution blocks handle application infrastructure: scaling compute resources in the standby Region (EKS pods, ECS tasks, or EC2 Auto Scaling groups) and invoking Lambda functions for application-specific logic, such as warming application-level caches so the standby Region doesn’t serve its first requests from a cold cache. This makes sure the standby Region is fully prepared to handle production traffic before any DNS changes occur.

4. Route 53 health check manipulation. After the application stack is ready, ARC Region Switch marks the primary Region’s health check as unhealthy through the native Route 53 health check block, or flips state through an ARC routing control block, triggering Route 53’s failover record logic and redirecting traffic to the now-ready standby Region. You can monitor the current status on the Region Switch plan’s monitoring tab.

Completing the failover: With the health check marked unhealthy, Route 53’s failover mechanism activates. After DNS time-to-live (TTL) values expire, the ingress proxy fleet’s queries resolve to the standby Region’s endpoint. The infrastructure team never needs to reconfigure proxies, update routing rules, or modify DNS records. The application team controls traffic flow through the PHZ record’s health check state by using ARC.

Failback: Returning traffic to the original primary Region works exactly the same way: you trigger your failback plan. Because the design is symmetric, the plan scales the original Region, transitions databases back, and redirects traffic through the same orchestrated flow, in the opposite direction. Failback is as automated, tested, and repeatable as the failover itself.

For more information about creating your own ARC Region Switch plan, refer to the service documentation and the introductory blog post.

From independent to coordinated recovery across the portfolio

The pattern described in the preceding section gives each application team independent failover capability. In practice, however, applications rarely exist in isolation. A payments service depends on an authentication service, and a customer portal depends on an API gateway. When interdependent applications need to recover, they must do so in dependency order. Without a mechanism to coordinate this sequence, the answer today is humans in a war room making phone calls.

posts.title: Skipper, Airbnb’s embedded workflow engine, is now open source
posts.summary: Durable workflows, running inside your service with no separate orchestration cluster. By : Ricardo Gamba , Andriy Sergiyenko Skipper , an embedded workflow engine used in production by teams all across Airbnb, is now…
posts.content:
Open SourceTechnologyEngineeringWorkflowSoftware Architecture

Durable workflows, running inside your service with no separate orchestration cluster.

Andriy Sergiyenko6 min read·Just now

--

By: Ricardo Gamba, Andriy Sergiyenko

Skipper, an embedded workflow engine used in production by teams all across Airbnb, is now available to the open source community. Skipper lets you express multi-step business processes as Java or Kotlin classes, persist their progress, and recover from crashes and transient failures. It runs inside your service and reuses its existing dependencies.

Skipper is available under the Apache 2.0 license. The code is on GitHub, alongside documentation and runnable examples. Our earlier engineering deep dive explains how we built it. Here, we’ll focus on the architecture of Skipper and where it fits in the ecosystem of options for development around workflows.

Why we developed Skipper

A process that spans multiple services, waits for human input, or involves a mix of synchronous and asynchronous steps, needs persistent storage for recording its progress. When a server restarts, it must know what has already happened, what (if anything) should be retried, and what is still awaiting processing. Implementing this separately for each process would mean repeatedly solving the same problems around partial failure, timers, and recovery, with associated testing and debugging; using a proven library is likely to improve quality and reduce toil.

Existing workflow engines meet these challenges. A common approach relies on a central orchestration service, whether self-hosted or fully managed, to handle durable execution. This setup provides a unified platform for multiple teams, streamlining central operations and monitoring.

For Airbnb, we wanted a new approach, one in which each service owned its workflows within its existing deployment and database. For critical services, that meant avoiding an additional shared orchestration dependency. It also let workflow execution stay in-process, without a separate coordinator between steps.

That requirement shaped Skipper’s architecture, as shown in the figure.

With Skipper, the service’s replicas also run the workflow runtime and scheduler. In a typical production deployment, they share a database that holds workflow state and scheduled work. The scheduler polls for runnable tasks and uses leases to coordinate ownership. If a replica fails, another can recover the work; takeover timing depends on scheduling and lease settings.

This reduces the number of separately deployed systems. It also puts responsibility for workflow execution, database capacity, and recovery with the service’s team. The duty of assuming those responsibilities is part of the tradeoff.

We believe that Skipper will appeal to teams that have a robust operational environment and need a workflow engine that adapts to their existing ways of working.

A workflow is a class

Skipper has two main abstractions. A workflow describes the orchestration: decisions, ordering, and waits. Actions perform work with potential side effects, such as calling an API or updating a database. Skipper records action results so they can be reused during recovery.

Consider a hypothetical listing-publication process. Some listings require a human review before publication; afterward, the host receives a notification:

class PublishListing : Workflow() {
  private val listing = actions<ListingActions>()

  @StateField var reviewApproved: Boolean? = null

  @WorkflowMethod
  suspend fun publish(request: PublicationRequest): Boolean {
    if (request.requiresReview) {
      val reviewed = waitUntil(
        { reviewApproved != null },
        Duration.ofDays(1)
      )
      if (!reviewed || reviewApproved != true) return false
    }

    listing.publish(request.listingId, request.requestId)
    listing.notifyHost(request.listingId, request.requestId)
    return true
  }

  @SignalMethod
  fun recordReview(approved: Boolean) {
    reviewApproved = approved
  }
}

waitUntil hibernates the workflow without holding a thread. The recordReview signal lets an API handler or queue consumer supply the review decision. A redeploy during the wait does not discard the persisted workflow. If approval never arrives, the timer allows the workflow to complete and deliver a negative result.

The action implementations and request type are omitted here. Each action must make its own side effects idempotent, for example, by deduplicating publication and notification separately using the stable request ID. Skipper does not make calls to downstream systems transactionally.

Java workflows use the same model, with methods that can return CompletableFuture. The examples include Java, Kotlin, Spring Boot, and Dropwizard projects. For tests, WorkflowTest provides an isolated in-memory runtime with controllable time, so you can exercise waits, signals, retries, and completion while supplying fakes for downstream collaborators.

Recovery through checkpoints and replay

When Skipper resumes an interrupted workflow, it re-executes the workflow method from the top. Actions with durably persisted checkpoints return their saved results. Execution continues through the remaining work.

This requires deterministic workflow code: orchestration must remain compatible with replay. Clock reads, randomness, and I/O belong in actions or explicit checkpoints rather than directly in the workflow body.

By default, Skipper batches action checkpoints until execution completes or pauses for a wait or retry. This reduces database writes, but a crash before that batch is persisted can require several previously completed actions to execute again. Actions can request immediate checkpointing to narrow that window. Even then, a downstream effect and its checkpoint are not one atomic operation, so side effects remain at least once.

On the normal execution path, a workflow can run directly in the service process, backed by persisted state and scheduled recovery work. It does not need a round-trip to an external orchestration service between actions. Database access and downstream calls still contribute to latency; the benefit is removing the separate orchestration tier from that path.

Durability does not mean every business operation succeeds. Developers define which errors are retryable and choose retry policies. Permanent failures and exhausted retries are surfaced for handling; scheduler tasks that exhaust recovery attempts can require manual intervention. Skipper also supports Saga-style compensation when a process needs explicit recovery actions for previously completed steps.

Where Skipper fits

Skipper’s production use already spans multiple teams at Airbnb. It is a good fit for a Java or Kotlin service that owns a multi-step process, and wants durable execution within its existing deployment. It is especially useful when the alternative is maintaining custom retry jobs, state tables, and polling loops for each new process.

What’s in the release, and what’s next

The open-source release includes the core engine, MySQL and SQLite adapters, test utilities, and the admin UI. Signals, queries, retries, compensation, and workflow evolution primitives are part of the programming model. It also includes Skipper State Machine, a Kotlin DSL for processes that are easier to describe as states, events, and transitions. The documentation covers these capabilities and JVM compatibility.

Next, we plan to explore adding more storage plugins, such as Postgres, DynamoDB, etc., and improve tooling for workflow evolution and replay debugging. Open source project contributions around automated compatibility checks, migration assistance, and clearer replay visualization could also help developers work through problems common to replay-based engines.

If this type of work interests you, check out some of our open positions!

Acknowledgements

A huge thank you to everyone who contributed code, adopted Skipper, shared feedback, and helped get this release over the finish line. This work reflects contributions from teams across Airbnb.

Special thanks to:

Our engineering leadership sponsors Navjot Sidhu, Musaab At-Taras, Mini Atwal. Jon Parise for guiding the team through the open source process, and Gary Leung and Harshit Gupta for helping us shape Skipper with its first use-case.
