posts.title: Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
posts.summary: By Shreya S Ramanujam , Yongce Li , Afshine Amidi , Sina Ghiassian , Benjamin Klein . Introduction Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix…
posts.content:
Netflix Technology Blog11 min read·20 hours ago

--

By Shreya S Ramanujam, Yongce Li, Afshine Amidi, Sina Ghiassian, Benjamin Klein.

Introduction

Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen:

If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode.

A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything.

“In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.”

Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton. Which leads us to the first (and most important) rule of writing a good synopsis: it must be factual. At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale. This is where our factuality service comes in: an automated way to judge whether a synopsis is factual or not.

Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric. There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize:

  1. High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants.
  2. Misaligned rationales: The model’s explanations often diverge from our annotators’ reasoning, which makes its factuality verdicts less reliable. We want these rationales to be better aligned so that (1) the model can consistently flag nuanced errors, and (2) its explanations can be used downstream to automatically correct issues in the synopsis.

Our new approach tackles both problems at once. On the cost side, it delivers a 52.4% reduction per synopsis. On the quality side, it significantly improves both verdict accuracy and reasoning alignment: Recall–Fail (“Of all truly non-factual synopses, how many does the system correctly reject?”) rises from 0.77 to 0.86, and the new factuality service’s explanations now show ~82% overlap with human rationales (up from ~69%). In other words, it’s not just cheaper and more accurate — it’s also much better aligned with how our expert annotators actually judge synopses.

So, what exactly does factuality mean?

Let’s go back to the Bridgerton example. Say you see this synopsis about Bridgerton Season 1:

Synopsis A: “Bridgerton follows Daphne Bridgerton, the eldest daughter of the powerful Bridgerton family as she makes her debut onto Regency London’s competitive marriage market.”

It’s easy to judge that this synopsis is factually correct — no wrong facts, and it gives the reader a clear, accurate glimpse of what to expect from the show.

Let’s take another example:

Synopsis B: “Set in modern-day London, this gritty crime drama follows Detective Daphne Bridgerton as she hunts a serial killer while hiding her own criminal past.”

Another easy one — the plot is so blatantly off the mark that it is definitely not factual.

But what about this?

Synopsis C: “Bridgerton follows the mysterious, sharp-tongued Lady Whistledown as she exposes the secrets of London’s high society through her scandalous gossip sheet.”

Technically, every statement here is true — Lady Whistledown does indeed publish a gossip sheet, and if there’s one thing she is known for, it’s her scathing exposés. So then, is this a factual synopsis?

Not quite! While technically true, it paints a misleading picture of the show. A new viewer might reasonably expect it to revolve around Lady Whistledown, rather than Daphne navigating the marriage market. This, too, is a type of non-factuality we want to catch.

Lastly, here’s the trickiest of all:

Synopsis D: “When Daphne Bridgerton makes her society debut, she catches the eye of the aloof Duke of Hastings, and the two begin a passionate love affair that sets the whole ton abuzz.”

Again, every statement is true, but the phrasing is misleading. A new viewer might assume they fall in love immediately, missing the fact that their relationship begins as a fake, mutually beneficial arrangement. This is another type of nuanced error our system should flag.

So now that we have an idea of the kinds of errors we care about, the real question is: how do we build a system that is able to catch both glaring as well as subtle factuality violations?

Current Service and Its Limitations

Our current factuality pipeline is a straightforward, holistic LLM call. We feed a reasoning model everything we know about a title (text assets, metadata, and a detailed factuality rubric) and ask it to judge the factuality of a synopsis. We repeat the call several times to reduce output randomness, and if any run flags the synopsis as non-factual, it fails. This approach has two main limitations:

  1. High cost: Each judgment requires multiple (five, to be exact) calls to a large reasoning model over extremely long contexts (100k+ tokens), which does not scale well.
  2. Misaligned reasoning: The model can fail synopses for nitpicky reasons (e.g., “This is a show about wonderful magic” gets failed because the characters never literally call the magic “wonderful”) while overlooking nuanced errors by convincing itself they “don’t really make the synopsis false.” This misalignment makes verdicts less reliable and rationales less useful for downstream correction.

Optimizing the Holistic Pipeline

To understand exactly where we should optimize the current holistic pipeline, we study the current pipeline both qualitatively and quantitatively on a custom factuality benchmark that we built. This benchmark comprises synopses hand-labeled by human annotators as factual or non-factual, along with their rationales. This analysis reveals several key insights:

Insight 1: Do we really need five holistic calls?

Let’s think back to why we added multiple holistic calls in the first place: to reduce sampling noise. In practice, though, we see an interesting dichotomy:

  • Blatantly true / false synopses (Bridgerton A, B): All runs agree on the verdict with near-identical reasoning.
  • Nuanced errors (Bridgerton C, D): The model is much more likely to disagree with itself — some runs catch the error, some don’t. This is exactly where additional sampling helps.

This suggests a simple optimization: A and B don’t really need all 5 calls. If we can somehow identify these “easy” synopses upfront, we can cut down on the number of calls for them, while still giving harder cases like C and D the extra calls they need.

The easiest way to do this is to ask the model to output its confidence alongside its verdict and rationale. We can then separate “easy” (high confidence) synopses from “hard” (low confidence) ones and only send the hard cases through additional checks. Think of it like airport security: most bags go straight through, but those that trigger the alarm (low confidence) get extra screening.

Implementing this easy fix makes our pipeline go from the current holistic model to a new “confidence gated” holistic model:

Insight 2: Five identical judges calls give us no new information

With confidence gating, our pipeline only escalates harder synopses to the full five holistic calls. But extra calls only help with sampling noise, not systematic reasoning errors: if every run follows the same flawed rationale, they’ll all reach the same wrong verdict, rendering the extra calls useless. How can we ensure that each call counts?

Idea: Diversify the judges and make them specialized

Get Netflix Technology Blog’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Remember me for faster sign in

Instead of running five holistic judges with the same generic factuality prompt, we introduce two specialized judges that individually target the two aspects of factuality we care about:

  • Literal Judge: Is the synopsis literally true?
  • Implicature Judge: Does this synopsis give a false picture to a new reader who has not watched this show?

Explicitly searching for specific types of errors helps us better flag both literal and subtler implicature errors. In practice, we observe that this works better than repeatedly querying a single holistic judge, hoping that sampling stochasticity will surface nuanced errors.

Insight 3: The rationale reveals mistakes the verdict hid

At this point, we have a pretty good pipeline, but we’re still underusing one of the richest signals available to us: the model’s rationale behind its verdict. For nuanced errors, we often see the model identify a point of contention, then brush it aside based on a faulty assumption or because it deems the issue too minor to affect the verdict. Can we use these shaky spots in the rationale to catch (and correct) errors the verdict misses?

Idea: Secondary atomic-claim checking via a router:

Since our literal and implicature judges are already strong reasoning models, we ask them to additionally critically analyse their own reasoning and surface shaky spots — any doubts, concessions, or assumptions that might need rechecking. These include cases where the model:

  • Makes an assumption.
  • Raises a doubt that the available evidence can’t resolve (e.g., an external critic quote).
  • Notices a contradiction but dismisses it as insufficient to change the verdict.

We pass all concessions from both judges to a router model, which:

  1. Reframes them as self-contained, verifiable atomic claims, each with a materiality field specifying the evidence needed to support or refute it.
  2. Routes each claim to the appropriate secondary Stage-2 judge: a web judge for external facts (e.g., citations, media quotes, or prior work), or a source-material recheck focused on the reframed atomic claim. By pinpointing the exact point of contention, the recheck is more targeted, making it easier to mark the claim as true or false.

Putting It All Together: Proposed Cascade Factuality Service

Our findings lead to three key improvements: specialized judges, confidence-gated escalation, and targeted rechecking of shaky reasoning using a secondary stage when escalated.

We implement these improvements as a tiered system shown in the figure below: every synopsis first passes through both the literal and the implicature judges. High-confidence verdicts are retained, while low-confidence cases escalate to the router and Stage-2 judges for further checking. Stage 2 can overturn the initial verdict in two cases:

  • FAIL → PASS: All concessions, including the original failure reasons, are supported by the secondary check.
  • PASS → FAIL: At least one concession is contradicted.

Results

Based on our discussions from above, we evaluate three different pipelines:

Evaluation: Datasets and Metrics

We evaluate these systems on two datasets: show-level and episode-level synopses. Each datapoint includes a synopsis, a human gold label (factual / not factual), and the annotator’s rationale. For episode-level synopses, we additionally require that the synopsis be specific to that particular episode, not just a generic synopsis of the overall show.

We focus on two main axes: Quality and Cost. The quality metrics are listed below:

Recall-FAIL is our primary metric: higher recall means fewer Gold FAILs are missed. We also track Precision-PASS, which measures how reliably PASS verdicts identify Gold PASSes, and alignment with human rationales.

On the cost side, we want to reduce both the average number of LLM calls per synopsis and the end-to-end cost of producing a final verdict. Latency is not our primary optimization target, but we do want to ensure the median (P50) latency does not blow up to impractical judgement times.

Evaluation Results

The best numbers per metric per dataset are shown in bold.

Note: We compared the cascade against two holistic ablations — increased reasoning effort and a smaller, cheaper model — to test if simple ablations could achieve better performance. For episode-level synopses, we also added a full-show summary to the prompt to provide context from previous episodes; we observe summaries substantially improve performance when compared to non-summary context variants, so we report only summary-based variants.

Our takeaways from this experiment are:

  • Cascade improves quality. Our primary metric, Recall-FAIL improves on both show and episode level synopses, with a limited impact on Recall-PASS. In other words, we now catch more Gold FAIL synopses without sacrificing the reliability of our PASS verdicts.
  • Cascade is cheaper. Cascade cuts total cost by 52.4% on the show-level dataset. Cascade (with summary) is also 15% cheaper than the current (no summary) holistic pipeline on episodic dataset.
  • Cascade’s P50 latency increases with respect to the holistic baseline. Even so, this remains within what we consider a reasonable range for factuality judgment.
  • Simple tweaks aren’t enough. Increasing reasoning effort makes the factuality checker too lenient, while using a smaller model makes it too strict — neither addresses the underlying problems of the holistic baseline.
  • Summary context matters for episodic tasks. Without a full-show summary, the model tends to over-fail because it lacks the context to determine whether a detail from the episode summary fits the broader storyline.

Alignment with Human Rationale

So far, we’ve established that the cascade produces better verdicts: it catches more non-factual synopses and produces more reliable PASS decisions. But are these verdicts correct for the right reasons?

To measure this, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge to compare each pipeline’s reasoning against the human rationale on Gold-FAIL (GF) synopses. The judge assigns a Reasoning Similarity Score (RSS) of 0 (dissimilar), 0.5 (partially similar), or 1 (very similar) based on rationale overlap.

We observe that cascade is significantly better aligned with human rationale in all cases. This is a big gain — not only is the cascade giving us more accurate factuality verdicts, but it also identifies the same points of contention in the synopsis as a specialized human annotator.

Conclusion + Future Work

Overall, our proposed cascade pipeline improves both cost and quality of the existing factuality service:

  • On the cost side, confidence gating lets us avoid unnecessary calls, reducing the average cost of factuality evaluation.
  • On the quality side, two diverse judges allow us to collect complementary informative verdicts, while the Stage-2 judges recheck and correct the assumptions behind uncertain decisions. This results in higher verdict accuracy and substantially better alignment between model and expert annotator reasoning.

The cascade gives us a path toward a factuality system that is not just more accurate, but also more interpretable and self-correcting. Some future directions to consider would be:

  • Adding multimodal inputs to help verify claims that text assets alone cannot confirm.

posts.title: Extending LLDB to Debug Applications That Span CPUs and GPUs
posts.summary: We built a vendor-neutral accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server for debugging applications that span CPUs and GPUs. It separates shared debugger infrastructure from hardware-specific device control. The design…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Greg Clayton, Satyanarayana Janga, Jeffrey Tan, Janet Yang, Bar Soloveychik, Chen Li, Vipul Bansal
  • We built a vendor-neutral accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server for debugging applications that span CPUs and GPUs. It separates shared debugger infrastructure from hardware-specific device control.
  • The design represents the CPU and GPU as separate debugger processes while presenting them in one debugging session.

Modern AI applications rarely execute in one place. A workload can begin in a high-level framework and move back and forth between native CPU code and kernels running on a GPU. When a bug crosses those boundaries, developers need to understand the host application and the device together.

That is harder than attaching a conventional debugger to another process. The CPU and GPU may use different instruction sets, registers, memory spaces, and execution models. The GPU is also controlled through a runtime and driver inside the host process, so debugging the device often requires careful coordination with the CPU.

Historically, GPU vendors built device-specific debuggers, including AMD’s ROCgdb and NVIDIA’s CUDA-GDB. These tools provide deep support for their respective platforms, but common debugger capabilities must often be implemented and maintained separately.

At Meta, we have been developing a different approach for LLDB: a common accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server. In this post, “GPU” refers to the concrete devices and examples, while “accelerator” refers to LLDB’s broader, vendor-neutral plugin abstraction. The architecture has evolved through contributions from engineers at Meta and across the accelerator ecosystem. It keeps the shared debugger independent of any one GPU while giving hardware vendors a focused place to implement device-specific behavior.

Why GPU Debugging Challenges Traditional Debugger Models

A traditional debugger generally assumes that one process has one architecture and a consistent view of threads, registers, and memory. GPU programs challenge each of those assumptions.

A host process might run on x86-64 while its kernels use a completely different instruction set. A CPU thread has a familiar register context, while a GPU may execute groups of lanes in lockstep. Host and device pointers can refer to different address spaces. A GPU can expose thousands of execution lanes, which do not map cleanly onto the thread model that most command-line and graphical debuggers present.

Combining all of this state into one artificial process model makes the debugger more complicated. Every operation must first determine whether it applies to the CPU or the GPU. Register handling, memory reads, breakpoints, stepping, and stop events all become conditional on the selected hardware. A single process model also forces the CPU and GPU into one unified memory map, even though their address spaces can be independent: The same address, such as 0x1000, can refer to different locations in the CPU and GPU processes.

Instead of hiding those differences, the LLDB accelerator architecture gives them a clear boundary.

Plugin Support in lldb-server for GPU Debugging

LLDB uses a companion process called lldb-server to launch or attach to a program and perform low-level debugging operations. The LLDB client communicates with the server through the GDB remote protocol, a command protocol for operations such as reading memory, inspecting registers, controlling execution, and setting breakpoints.

Because lldb-server already controls the native process, it is also the right place to coordinate with an accelerator runtime. The new plugin interface lets a hardware-specific backend work alongside the normal CPU debugger. The backend translates a vendor’s device debugging API into concepts LLDB already understands, such as processes, threads, registers, memory, modules, and stop reasons.

This separation keeps the LLDB client vendor-neutral. Common improvements to the command line, remote protocol, symbol handling, and IDE integration can benefit every accelerator. At the same time, each vendor remains responsible for the details that are unique to its hardware and driver stack.

GPU debugging support is activated only when the debugged application uses a supported GPU runtime. For CPU-only applications, LLDB and lldb-server continue through the existing native debugging path without incurring runtime computational overhead.

Two Targets, One Debugging Experience

The architecture represents the CPU and accelerator as separate LLDB targets.
Each target has its own architecture and is associated with a debugger process that maintains its threads, registers, address space, and execution state. The CPU continues to use LLDB’s established native debugging path. When the accelerator becomes available, the plugin provides a second connection that LLDB uses to create the device target.

To the debugger, the two targets remain technically independent. To the developer, they can appear in one LLDB or IDE session. This avoids forcing incompatible CPU and GPU concepts into a single process while still supporting a unified workflow.

Coordinating the Host and Device

A typical debugging session follows a small set of steps:

  1. LLDB connects to lldb-server and discovers which accelerator plugins are available.
  2. A plugin can ask LLDB to set internal breakpoints in the host process. These breakpoints identify important runtime events, such as the point at which a GPU debugging session can begin.
  3. When the host reaches one of those points, lldb-server notifies the plugin. The plugin initializes the vendor debugging API and prepares an accelerator debugging endpoint.
  4. LLDB creates a second target for the accelerator and connects to it. Device threads, registers, memory, modules, and breakpoints can then use LLDB’s existing abstractions.

Structured actions coordinate the two sides. A plugin can request CPU breakpoints, provide connection information, report device modules, and synchronize host and device execution. The common protocol describes what the debugger needs to do without exposing vendor-specific API details to the LLDB client.

We also built a mock accelerator plugin that exercises this flow without specialized hardware. It lets the LLVM test suite verify discovery, breakpoint coordination, connection creation, and basic device state. This has been important for developing shared infrastructure that can be reviewed and tested independently of any particular GPU.

A Typical GPU Workflow

The vector dot-product HIP sample produced this abridged session:

(lldb) target list
Current targets:
  target #0: gpu_demo (x86_64, stopped)
* target #1: amd_memory_kernel[...] (amdgcn, stopped)
(lldb) b compute_element
Breakpoint 1: no locations (pending).
(lldb) c
(lldb) target select 0
(lldb) c
Launching kernel: 2 blocks x 32 threads
1 location added to breakpoint 1
Target 1 stopped.
(lldb) target select 1
(lldb) bt
* frame #0: compute_element(..., idx=32) at gpu_demo.hip:26
  frame #1: vector_dot_kernel(..., n=64) at gpu_demo.hip:35
The pending breakpoint resolves when the GPU module loads, and the backtrace
comes from the GPU target.

A Common Plugin Framework Across Hardware Vendors

The plugin boundary is intentionally based on debugger operations rather than concepts from a specific GPU platform. That makes it useful across devices with very different instruction sets, runtime APIs, and execution models.

The framework supports postmortem GPU debugging as well as live sessions. GPU core-dump plugins use a common base class for their LLDB integration, while vendor implementations provide the device-specific thread, register, memory, and module state.

GPU debugging efforts at Meta are already leveraging the architecture. Because we operate a heterogeneous fleet of GPUs with different hardware and software stacks, the fact that these efforts use the same model is an important validation of the design: the common LLDB layer can remain stable while each backend represents its own device accurately.

At the time of writing, we have upstreamed most of the common framework to LLVM. This includes the lldb-server plugin interface; GDB-remote packets for plugin discovery, initialization, runtime-event coordination, and GPU connection creation; support for associating CPU and GPU debugger processes while preserving their independent architecture; support for multiple address spaces, and hardware-independent mock tests. We expect to upstream the remaining pieces soon.

Looking Ahead

Next, we plan to finish upstreaming the remaining common infrastructure and expand the vendor integrations built on it. Our goal is that integrating new hardware with LLDB should require only a vendor-specific plugin, not a separate debugger to build and maintain. 

Acknowledgements 

We are grateful to Meta’s Developer Infrastructure leadership team, especially Shane Nay, Todd Fiala, and Ale Contenti, whose direct support made this work possible.

We also thank our Debugging & Tooling teammates Jacob Lalonde, David Young, Alexandre Perez, Zhiyuan Li, Piyush Jaiswal, and Philip DePetro for their collaboration and support.

Finally, we thank the open source community, especially Jonas Devlieghere, Jim Ingham, David Spickett, and Jason Molenda, for reviewing the RFCs and upstream pull requests.

posts.title: AI Product Management at Spotify: A View From Three Angles
posts.summary: Almost every article or podcast about product management and AI refers to "the AI PM" as one job. But what... The post AI Product Management at Spotify: A View From Three Angles appeared first on Spotify Engineering .
posts.content:
Almost every article or podcast about product management and AI refers to "the AI PM" as one job. But what that job looks like depends on what you’re building.

The three of us work at the same company, on the same technology stack, and in the same part of the organization. We talk constantly, but our day-to-day work, and what success looks like, is quite different.

Henok leads product in Tech Research, where success might be a team making the right technology choice, a methodology that helps several teams work with greater confidence, or a result that shows the organization what is possible. Divita leads product for a recommendation foundation model, shaping what it learns and how its capabilities help teams build better experiences for listeners. Humberto builds the experience users actually interact with, bringing model capabilities, interaction design, and user feedback together into something users find valuable and trustworthy

We share more than the technology. We’re working toward the same company priorities, and ultimately, serving the same external users. Our work is deeply connected: an idea from research can become a reusable model capability that opens up a new possibility in the user experience. Getting it to ship takes collaboration across all three. 

That closeness can make the differences between our roles easy to miss, especially when we use the same PM vocabulary. We all talk about “quality”, “evals”, and “shipping”, but their meaning shifts with the problem space each of us owns. Even impact looks different. A shift in what the organization believes or where it invests can be a major research win; for a model PM, the payoff comes when a model improvement translates into better recommendations across multiple user experiences. And for an experience PM, it comes down to whether users love the product and come back. 

The fundamentals of product management still apply. But building AI products requires different kinds of specialization depending on what you own. Below, each of us shares what that looks like in practice.

The research layer: where the product is technical leverage

Henok, Principal Product Manager, Tech Research, Personalization

As the product lead for Tech Research, I work with product teams on today's needs while looking at what might matter next as AI changes what’s possible. I think of our product as technical leverage: applying scientific expertise where it can change what Spotify builds or how confidently we build it.

1. AI is changing which problems need research

Better models and tools mean product teams can increasingly do work that previously required deep involvement from research. This allows research to focus more on shared methods, system design, and emerging capabilities where the right approach remains unclear.

The questions that matter tend to span several teams, further changing the research-product team dynamic. Two examples are how to evaluate open-ended model behavior, and how to represent users and content in ways that several products can use.

AI makes it easy to build an exciting prototype quickly. However, the gap between that prototype and a product that works reliably for hundreds of millions of users can be significant. Similarly, a more complex model might look great in a demo, without any meaningful difference on the production tasks that matter. With this in mind, evaluation, latency, cost, data, and integration all become part of the research question. This is what helps us make informed investment decisions.

2. A promising model architecture is not a roadmap

One project has made this particularly clear to me. We have been exploring an architecture that brings together capabilities currently spread across different systems. At first, the question was whether it could work. As the evidence grew, a harder product question emerged: what should the organization do with it? A new architecture may affect infrastructure, evaluation, interfaces, and several teams' plans, and it sits alongside systems that already work. 

My job is to turn the bigger idea into decisions the organization can reasonably make: start with a concrete problem, find a useful test, and agree on what evidence would justify the next step. It isn’t all or nothing. The methods and components we develop along the way can already improve existing systems, even while the larger questions stay open.

What began as exploration now informs model and experience teams, and its methods and components can improve existing systems even while the larger architecture question remains open. The harder work is finding a credible path through product needs, technical constraints, and existing commitments.

3. Long feedback loops in a field that moves quickly

Research impact can take months to appear, often in another team's roadmap or metrics. During that time, the technology and the organization's priorities may change. This makes influence a critical part of the role. 

Within the research team, I provide product and strategic context without prescribing the answer. Outside it, I connect the work to decisions and involve the relevant teams early, while being clear about what the evidence does and does not show. If that starts only when the research is complete, the decision window may have closed.

The pace of AI also requires me to understand the technology more deeply than in many of my previous PM roles. AI tools help me work through papers and prototypes, and I stay close to one or two projects at a time to judge the choices and obstacles involved.

The role calls for technical depth and organizational judgment: seeing which questions matter across teams, testing ideas before they become commitments, and connecting evidence to decisions in time. When we get that right, the impact compounds through the methods teams use, the technology they choose, and the experiences they build.

The model layer: where the product is a capability and the customer is another team

Divita, Principal Product Manager, AI Foundation, Personalization

I lead product for a foundation model, a language model that is purpose-built for recommendations, designed to reference real items on Spotify. Like any platform team, everything we build reaches users through other product teams. What makes this platform different is the product itself. Its behavior is shaped through data, its outputs are probabilistic, and quality means something different to every team that integrates it. That combination is what shapes the job.

My customers are internal teams that build the surfaces and experiences Spotify users interact with every day. They have their own roadmaps and metrics, and the same model needs to serve different definitions of a good recommendation. My job is to understand those needs and decide where a shared capability can serve them well. A request from one team can point to something useful across several experiences; recognizing those opportunities helps shape the model’s direction. 

This is where the product fundamentals become concrete. Product-market fit means understanding which problems teams can solve with the model. A clear value proposition means explaining what it offers for their particular experience. And business impact comes through what they ship with it. Understanding those needs gives us direction. Translating them into model behavior is where the work changes.

1. You cannot spec model behavior. You shape it, and then you prove it matters.

In a traditional product role, I would define what the system should do and work with engineers to build it. Here, behavior is learned through training rather than specified directly in code. If we want to improve the relevance of recommendations, a spec alone won’t get us there. I work with the team to decide what the model needs to learn, which data could help it learn that, and how we’ll know whether it has. Training takes time, so those decisions shape what we prioritize for each cycle.

The two real levers are what you teach the model and how you check what it learned. Data and evals. A large part of my job is deciding what those evals should measure. What makes a recommendation good for a particular listener, in a particular moment? A plausible recommendation is only the starting point. We need to understand how well it fits the listener’s context, balances familiarity with discovery, and stays relevant over time. Designing evals means turning those expectations into criteria we can consistently assess. 

Then we need to connect what we measure in the model to what listeners experience. Offline evals help us understand model behavior, while online metrics show how that translates into the user experience. I work with partner teams to understand which model improvements make a difference in their products. What we learn together helps us prioritize the next training cycle.

2. Show what a shared model makes possible

The promise of a shared recommendation model is that an improvement can benefit multiple experiences. But each team already has a system optimized for its own needs. Our first task is to show that the shared model can meet that experience’s requirements for quality, latency, and cost. I work with partner teams to define those criteria and agree on how we’ll assess them.

Meeting those requirements establishes a starting point. The longer-term question is what teams gain by building on the same model. Can something we learn in one experience improve recommendations in another? Can a team build on an existing capability to try something new? Part of my job is turning that promise into specific questions we can test.

A single evaluation can’t answer all of them. We need to track how the model develops across training cycles and how those changes translate across experiences. That gives us a way to distinguish a promising result from a pattern we can plan around.

A foundation model takes time and resources, and the benefits build as more teams use it. Being clear about where those benefits are showing up, and what we still need to establish, helps us decide what to prioritize next. That is how we make the case for the model over time: through evidence teams can use in their own product decisions.

3. Good is not enough if nobody ships with it

Success means getting teams to ship with your model. A good model is essential, but its value depends on whether another team can use it to solve a problem that matters to them.

Much of the work that makes that happen looks nothing like model work. It means finding a team whose current system has hit a ceiling on a metric they care about, then making the model a compelling, practical path forward. That requires agreeing on what the capability needs to deliver, defining the integration contract, and taking responsibility for testing the riskiest assumptions before asking the partner team to commit.

My team’s best result this year came from a surface team that wanted an outcome we were positioned to deliver. The collaboration worked because we agreed on how we would measure success before we agreed on the architecture. That gave us a shared basis for deciding what to build and whether it was working.

That is the version of the job I would describe to someone considering it. You own the model, but you also own the work of turning its capabilities into something another team can confidently ship, and users can benefit from.

The experience layer: where the customer is the user and the model is one ingredient among many

Humberto, Principal Product Manager, Sessions, Personalization

If the research layer creates technical leverage and the model layer creates a reusable capability, the experience layer is where all of it has to work for Spotify's hundreds of million of users. I build the product users actually interact with: the surface where a vague mood becomes a set of songs and where the system has to do something useful even when the request is ambiguous.

My customers are Spotify's users, directly. That is the simplest difference from the other two roles, and it changes almost everything about the job. The research and model layers are my base technology, and my job is to turn that technology into something delightful. Because the experience team is closest to the user, we have the most direct view of which model gaps and unanswered research questions matter most right now. That makes the dependency on the other layers less of a bottleneck and more of a shared prioritization signal across the stack.

1. Designing for infinite input

The biggest shift from previous product work is the nature of the input. In a traditional product, the user's action is constrained: they tap a button, select from a menu, type a search keyword. The system's response is predictable, and so is the test. You know what the user did, you know what the system should do, and you can verify it.

In an AI experience, the input is open-ended. Users make vague, underspecified, or complex requests that do not map to any single entity in the catalog. Agents interpret what the user likely meant and construct a response.

That reshapes constraints you thought were fixed. Latency that’s unacceptable in a keyword search turns out to be perfectly tolerable in a conversational interaction, because users understand they are asking for something harder. But questions like how the system should respond when it is not confident, and how you recover when something goes wrong, do not have stable answers - and they belong to the product, not the model.

2. Evaluation is a product, not just a process

A/B testing and offline evaluation still matter, but they are not sufficient on their own. When the input space is open-ended, you cannot predefine every scenario worth testing.

So we build new instruments. We build datasets from real usage patterns and design feedback loops that show where the system misunderstood a request or fell short. We build LLM-based judges and custom evaluators tuned to the specific interactions our product supports, then use them to measure whether changes are actually improvements or just different.

Evaluation is not a phase that happens before launch; it is a continuous product in itself. A general-purpose eval that works across the foundation model's many use cases is a starting point, not the finish line. The experience team has to close the gap between "the model is generally good" and "this specific interaction was good for this specific user."

3. Conversation makes feedback natural

In a conversational product, users do not just interact with the system. They talk to it. When things go wrong, they say so, in their own words, in real time. That directness did not exist in previous product surfaces, and it changes what is possible.

User frustration with a specific interaction is feedback on the experience, the model, and potentially the training data all at once. A user telling the system "that is not what I meant" is not just a product issue to fix locally. The job is to build mechanisms that detect that signal at scale, interpret it, and pass it back through the collaboration chain so that every layer improves.

This is the version of the role I would describe to someone considering it. You have the most direct line to the user and the most tangible ownership of the outcome. But you are building on top of systems you influence rather than control, for users whose expectations are being shaped in real time by every other AI product they touch. The craft is in making something trustworthy out of ingredients that are, by nature, probabilistic.

Overall reflections

The longer we work across this stack, the more we understand that there isn’t one simple new “AI PM” skillset. Product Management is the same craft it has always been: defining the problem clearly, knowing your customer deeply, measuring what matters, and building conviction through evidence rather than enthusiasm. But what the AI stack adds is not a different job. It is a layer of specialization on top of the fundamentals and those layers come in more flavors than people realize, and vary from product to product. AI Product Management is a varied and complex role which only gets more exciting with the rate of change.

posts.title: How OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS
posts.summary: See how Cognizant and AWS Professional Services transformed the OrderServ food-ordering platform into a multi-tenant SaaS offering on shared Amazon ECS, cutting compute costs up to 64%, reducing scaling time from…
posts.content:
When your food-ordering platform doubles its brand count, dedicated clusters become your biggest cost problem, and every failed request during a traffic surge is a lost sale.

Here is how Cognizant and AWS Professional Services solved it.

Cognizant is a global services company that helps organizations modernize technology, reimagine processes, and transform customer experiences. Its OrderServ service is an omnichannel ordering solution for the food services industry that supports ordering across devices and integrates with point-of-sale, kitchen display, payment, loyalty, and other enterprise systems. Cognizant is an AWS Premier Tier Services Partner with multiple AWS Competencies and a member of the AWS Managed Service Provider (MSP) and AWS Well-Architected Partner Programs.

In 2022, Cognizant published how OrderServ 2.0 reimagined digital food ordering by migrating from a monolith to microservices on AWS Fargate, achieving 30 percent cost savings over traditional hosted architectures.

Since then, the service grew from serving a single quick-service restaurant (QSR) brand to powering multiple brands across markets. Each brand ran as a dedicated Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster with 21 microservices. This provided hard isolation, but cost scaled linearly with every brand onboarded, and scaling speed could not keep up with promotional traffic surges that spike 5–10× within minutes.

In this post, we describe how AWS Professional Services partnered with Cognizant to transform OrderServ into a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) offering, achieving 47–64 percent compute cost reduction, scaling time reduced from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds, and authentication costs cut by 80 percent.

The problem: Dedicated clusters don’t scale with brands

OrderServ 2.0 ran 21 microservices per brand on dedicated AWS Fargate clusters. For five brands, this meant:

  • 105 ECS services (21 × 5), each with idle capacity during off-peak hours.
  • 315 sidecar containers for observability, configuration, and log routing, duplicated per brand.
  • Linear cost growth, because onboarding a new brand required provisioning an entire cluster.
  • 5-minute scaling gap, because large container images increased image-pull and task startup times on AWS Fargate, delaying the addition of capacity during promotional traffic surges.

In QSR, every failed request during a surge is a lost sale and users may switch to competitor services immediately. The service needed to serve over 10 brands cost-effectively while handling unpredictable traffic patterns: lunch rushes, promotional events, and festival surges.

Solution overview

We addressed these challenges through four architectural changes:

  • Shared ECS cluster with a tenancy library: Application-level isolation replaces per-brand infrastructure.
  • EC2 warm pools with Bottlerocket: Sub-minute scaling replaces AWS Fargate cold starts.
  • Crash observability pipeline: Zero-loss logging and 90-day forensics at $10/month per service.
  • Passkeys for multi-tenant authentication: Biometric login reduces recurring SMS costs.

Solution 1: Shared cluster with application-level isolation

As OrderServ scaled from one to five brands, the cost of replicating 21 microservices per tenant made the economics unsustainable. We needed to consolidate infrastructure while preserving the data isolation guarantees each brand required.

Why we moved away from dedicated clusters

The dedicated-cluster model provided strong isolation but no economy of scale. With the platform growing from five brands, onboarding a new brand needed to become a configuration change, not an infrastructure provisioning exercise.

ModelProsConsDedicated cluster per brand (status quo)Hard isolation, simple AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)Linear cost, idle capacity, slow onboardingShared cluster with opt-outAggregate scaling, config-only onboardingRequires application-level isolation, wider IAM scope

We chose the shared cluster as the default, with the ability to place high-volume brands on dedicated clusters when needed.

Figure 1 illustrates this transformation, from five dedicated ECS clusters (105 services, 315 sidecar containers) to a single shared cluster with 21 services and an opt-out path for high-volume brands. The tenancy library handles tenant resolution, resource routing, and context propagation, while per-tenant data stores (Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon Aurora, Valkey) maintain strict data isolation.

Figure 1: Evolution from dedicated clusters per brand to a shared cluster model with opt-out for high-volume brands

The service uses AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys to encrypt every data store at rest, and the architecture implements Transport Layer Security (TLS) to protect all service-to-service and client-to-service communication. Amazon DynamoDB automatically encrypts tables by default. Customers enable encryption when creating Amazon Aurora Clusters and the Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system, and customers configure both at-rest and in-transit encryption for the Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey cluster.

The tenancy library as primary isolation

Most multi-tenant architectures enforce isolation at the infrastructure level: separate accounts, separate IAM roles, or separate compute. We took a different approach: a shared .NET Core library as the primary enforcement point for tenant isolation. IAM and resource policies are the backstop that contains the blast radius when the library has a defect.

Every request carries an X-Tenant-Id header injected by the Amazon API Gateway authorizer. The tenancy library:

  • Resolves tenant context per request using request-scoped storage (AsyncLocal<T>), never static or singleton state.
  • Routes all data access: Amazon DynamoDB table names, Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey key prefixes, Amazon Aurora schema selection, and S3 paths.
  • Refuses to construct resource IDs without a tenant prefix, so a missing tenant context fails closed instead of reading another tenant’s data.
  • Propagates tenant context on service-to-service calls and asynchronous messages (SQS/SNS attributes).
  • Enriches every log line and distributed trace with the tenant ID.

This design means the same service binary runs identically in a shared cluster or a dedicated cluster. The compute model becomes a deployment decision, not an architectural constraint.

Application-level isolation moves the isolation boundary into code, and code could potentially have defects. Because an Amazon ECS task role is granted per task rather than per request, a task in the shared cluster necessarily holds permissions spanning every brand it serves. To narrow that scope, the tenancy library acquires tenant-scoped credentials at run time: it calls sts:AssumeRole with the tenant ID as a session tag, and the role’s policies reference that tag so the credentials reach only that tenant’s DynamoDB tables, S3 prefixes, and Aurora schema. Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey enforces its own layer, with per-tenant role-based access control (RBAC) users restricted to the tenant’s key pattern, so the cache engine itself refuses a cross-tenant key access rather than trusting the library to have built the key correctly.

Impact

The following table compares key operational metrics (service count, sidecar overhead, onboarding time, and capacity utilization) before and after the migration to a shared cluster model.

MetricBefore (dedicated)After (shared + library)ECS services to deploy21 × N brands21 totalSidecar containers315 (for 5 brands)63 totalOnboarding a new brandProvision full cluster (days)Configuration change (minutes)Idle capacityPer-brand (wasted)Aggregate (efficient)

Solution 2: EC2 warm pools with Bottlerocket for sub-minute scaling

With all brands now sharing a single cluster, traffic spikes from any one brand could impact the others. We needed a scaling strategy that could absorb sudden surges in seconds, not minutes.

Why we moved away from AWS Fargate

AWS Fargate removes infrastructure management, but OrderServ required additional capacity in under a minute during unpredictable demand surges. New tasks took 5–7 minutes to become healthy, primarily because Fargate had to download and extract the workload’s large container image before starting the application. Task provisioning, application initialization and health checks added to the delay, but image retrieval was the largest contributor. During this interval, existing ECS tasks become saturated, latency increased and some orders started failing.

The solution: EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools

We migrated to Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling groups with Bottlerocket (the AWS purpose-built container OS) and warm pools:

  • The system pre-initializes and stops warm pool instances, and you pay only for Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage (~$3/month per instance).
  • When ECS needs capacity, the Auto Scaling group (ASG) starts a stopped instance (image pre-cached, ECS agent registered) in 30–60 seconds.
  • We set capacity headroom (target utilization at 80 percent), so that the first wave absorbs instantly.
  • Bottlerocket provides atomic auto-updates, eliminating the Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) patching burden.

Five-layer scaling strategy

Rather than relying on a single scaling mechanism, we implemented five complementary layers, each targeting a specific traffic pattern to remove gaps between detection and response.

LayerMechanismTraffic pattern solvedPredictiveECS predictive scaling (machine learning, 14-day history). Scheduled scaling for specific known events (New Year, Christmas) was already handled manually via ASG scheduled actionsDaily lunch/dinner peaks, scheduled scalingReactiveTarget tracking on ALBRequestCountPerTarget (60s)Unexpected moderate spikesHeadroomEC2 ASG target capacity at 80%First wave of any spikeDownstreamECS Service Connect RequestCount metricBottleneck shiftingThrottlingAPI Gateway per-tenant rate limits via AWS Lambda authorizerExtreme surges (noisy neighbor)

Figure 2 illustrates how the five scaling layers work together with the EC2 warm pool. Pre-initialized warm pool instances launch in 30–60 seconds versus 5–7 minutes for an AWS Fargate cold start, at a cost of approximately $3/month per stopped instance.

Figure 2: Five-layer scaling strategy

Cost and performance impact

In addition to improving scaling performance, the move from AWS Fargate to Amazon EC2 reduced the projected monthly cost of running 21 services in the Asia Pacific (Mumbai) AWS Region (ap-south-1). Two instruments do different jobs here: On-Demand Capacity Reservations is designed to make sure capacity is available in the Availability Zone when a surge activates the warm pool, and Compute Savings Plan supply the discount. The reservation carries no term commitment and can be resized or released as the fleet changes, so the following one-year and three-year terms apply to the Savings Plan alone.

ApproachMonthly cost (21 services)versus AWS FargateAWS Fargate On-Demand (before)~$1,568BaselineEC2 ASG with 1-year Compute Savings Plan and warm pool~$832
  • ~47%
EC2 ASG with 3-year Compute Savings Plan with warm pool~$568
  • ~64%

The reservation covers the steady-state fleet, while you stop warm pool instances, adding approximately $30 per month in Amazon EBS storage costs. Scaling time falls from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds.

Solution 3: Crash observability pipeline

When containers crash in production, the support team needs three things: what happened, the root cause, and the container’s execution state at the time of failure. In the prior state, OrderServ used the awslogs driver to send container output to CloudWatch Logs. Although this captured normal application output, it did not provide durable task-stop metadata, cross-service request correlation or persistent crash artifacts.

  • Potential loss of final logs records during crash: When a task terminates abruptly, records still in the log driver’s delivery buffer might not reach Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
  • Short lived task metadata: Amazon ECS makes stopped-task information available through the API for a limited period of 1 hour, reducing the investigation window.
  • No cross-service correlation: Plain-text logs lacked trace IDs and consistent task, container, and service identifiers needed to follow a failed request across services.
  • No persistent crash artifacts: The ephemeral task storage of AWS Fargate disappeared when the task stopped, taking local crash dumps and diagnostic files with it.

The solution: FireLens sidecar + Amazon EventBridge persistence

Figure 3 shows the crash observability pipeline, where the application container emits structured JSON logs with X-Ray trace IDs to a FireLens (Fluent Bit) sidecar. The sidecar survives container termination and routes logs to CloudWatch Logs with Infrequent Access class and 30-day retention, as well as to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) with gzip partitioning and 365-day retention. Amazon EventBridge captures task-stop events with full metadata, while the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) collector provides auto-instrumented traces to X-Ray and EFS persists crash dumps across availability zones, all at approximately $10/month per service.

Figure 3: Crash observability pipeline. FireLens operates at the container runtime level, surviving application container crashes. Amazon EventBridge persists task metadata for 90 days

FireLens (Fluent Bit) as a sidecar is the key architectural choice. ECS redirects the application container’s stdout at the container runtime level. If the app container receives an out-of-memory (OOM) kill, Fluent Bit still has the logs.

For hard crashes where application logs are not sufficient (stack overflow, native code fault), the .NET Core runtime automatically writes a mini dump to an Amazon EFS mount at /tmp/dumps/<container-id>. Because Amazon EFS writes are immediately durable and the mount survives container death, the process state (thread call stacks, heap objects, loaded modules) helps preserve diagnostic information after a SIGKILL. An AWS Lambda function copies dumps to S3 for analysis without VPC access. Cost: ~$0.02/month.

Amazon EventBridge to Amazon CloudWatch Logs persists the complete Amazon ECS task state change event with 90-day retention. No AWS Lambda function is required.

Every log line is structured JSON with the AWS X-Ray trace ID. The support workflow: search for an error, find the trace ID, open X-Ray, and see the full request flow across all 21 services.

We also use CloudWatch Logs Infrequent Access class with FireLens dual output (CloudWatch + S3), reducing observability costs by 62 percent per service.

Cost: approximately $10/month per service for the complete pipeline.

Solution 4: Passkeys for multi-tenant authentication

QSR mobile apps need instant login. Every second of friction is a lost order. The service previously relied on SMS one-time password (OTP) for every login, which at millions of monthly active users meant significant costs and user friction.

Passkeys with per-brand cryptographic isolation

We implemented passkeys (WebAuthn) using the native support in Amazon Cognito:

  • First-time registration: Phone number + OTP verifies identity, then the device registers a passkey bound to the Secure Enclave.
  • Every subsequent login: Face ID or fingerprint, which completes in about 2 seconds with no SMS cost.
  • New device or stale profile: Because carriers reassign phone numbers, possession of a number is treated as a claim rather than proof of identity. Registering a passkey on a new device repeats the OTP verification, and a profile whose last verification predates our revalidation window is re-verified before any registered credential is honoured.
  • Per-brand isolation: Each brand operates its own Cognito User Pool with a distinct Relying Party ID that is cryptographically isolated at the OS level.

A Post-Authentication Lambda (about 60 lines) maintains a customer authentication profile in DynamoDB, keyed by a hash of the brand/tenant id and the customer’s phone number. Because the brand ID is part of the key, the same customer registering with two brands produces two unrelated records, and the system cannot locate any record without the brand context. The profile stores only authentication state, such as which devices were registered and when each was last verified. It holds no order history, loyalty balance, or other brand-specific data. Passkey credentials are isolated by the same principle: because each brand uses a distinct Relying Party ID, the authentication flow prevents presenting a credential registered for one brand to another brand, and the device enforces that boundary. The implementation required about 95 lines of custom code to integrate with Amazon Cognito’s authentication logic.

MetricBeforeAfterCost per login~$0.03 (SMS OTP)$0 (passkey)Login latency15–30 seconds~2 secondsSMS cost reduction—80%+ at steady statePhishing resistanceNoneCryptographic (device-bound)

Overall results

The architectural evolution delivered compounding savings:

DimensionBeforeAfterImprovement

posts.title: How TUI scales threat modeling for 100+ teams with Amazon Bedrock
posts.summary: Learn how TUI, the world's leading tourism group, built an AI-powered threat modeling system on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to scale security assessments across more than 100 product teams, cutting…
posts.content:
When your security team has four engineers and your organization has over 100 digital product teams, threat modeling becomes a bottleneck fast. That was the challenge TUI faced. TUI operates across the travel and tourism industry with airlines, hotels, cruise ships, and local travel experiences. Our Platform & Engineering division needs security assessments to keep pace.

At TUI, each threat modeling session took 4–6 hours of manual work: reviewing architecture diagrams, mapping threats to internal standards, researching security issues, and documenting findings in Confluence. The team could complete only 3–4 sessions per month, leaving a constant backlog.

TUI needed threat modeling to become mandatory for every new service, not a luxury TUI reserved for the highest-priority projects. TUI built an AI-powered threat modeling system using Amazon Bedrock, collaborating with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center during a 10-week proof of concept (PoC) to develop and validate the architecture. Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service for building generative AI applications, and TUI used the Claude Sonnet 4.5 foundation model from Anthropic. TUI chose Amazon Bedrock for managed access to Claude Sonnet 4.5 without operating model infrastructure, its extended thinking support that the workflow uses for deeper analysis, and its integration with the AWS services already in TUI’s stack. TUI deployed the agentic workflow on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, part of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore runtime hosts the agent in production without provisioning or scaling infrastructure. After the PoC, TUI took the system to production within 30 days.

In this post, we describe how TUI built an agentic AI workflow for threat modeling, the iteration process that shaped the architecture, and the results after deployment.

The challenge

TUI’s security engineering team followed a thorough but manual process: for each application, an engineer reviewed the architecture, identified threats using STRIDE methodology, mapped them to TUI Technology Standards, P&E-specific standards, and ISO 27001 controls, and documented findings in Confluence with Jira tickets.

With 100+ digital product teams and only 3–4 sessions possible per month, most teams waited weeks for their review. Security engineers also had varying levels of expertise across technology stacks, and there was no automated way to verify these standards were consistently applied to every assessment.

Solution overview

The solution extends AWS Threat Designer with TUI-specific capabilities through a serverless architecture deployed in the eu-central-1 (Frankfurt) AWS Region. Model availability varies by Region. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock. Together, these services replace the manual review process with an automated workflow that applies TUI Technology Standards and P&E-specific standards consistently. The system uses the following key services:

  • Amazon Bedrock for threat analysis and generation using Claude Sonnet 4.5 from Anthropic, with configurable extended thinking budgets.

  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime for hosting the agentic workflow as a managed, serverless runtime. It runs the containerized LangGraph agent without provisioning or scaling infrastructure, supports long-running sessions that exceed typical function timeouts, and provides per-session isolation for concurrent threat models.

  • AWS Lambda for serverless backend compute with LangGraph workflow orchestration.

  • Amazon DynamoDB for workflow state management with resume capability.

  • Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for architecture diagram storage, TUI knowledge base, and web search cache.

  • AWS Amplify for the React front end with Amazon Cognito authentication.

Figure 1: TUI Threat Designer system architecture. Users authenticate through Amazon Cognito and interact with the React front end hosted on AWS Amplify. Requests flow through Amazon API Gateway to AWS Lambda, which orchestrates the LangGraph workflow through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The agent uses Amazon Bedrock (Claude Sonnet 4.5 from Anthropic) for threat analysis, with Amazon DynamoDB for state management and Amazon S3 for architecture diagram storage and caching.

The core is a LangGraph-based agentic workflow that processes architecture diagrams through several specialized nodes. Engineers upload one or more diagrams (for example, a high-level architecture alongside a detailed network topology), which the workflow converts to base64 to identify components and data flows. It then loads relevant security standards and generates threats with iterative refinement. The workflow runs gap analysis, optionally compares against a subject matter expert (SME) assessment, and assembles the final threat model with export options (PDF, JSON, or Confluence).

The following screenshot shows the submission wizard. Engineers provide a title, upload architecture diagrams, add optional context and assumptions, and select a reasoning depth based on architecture complexity. The entire setup takes approximately two minutes.

Figure 2: The submission wizard guides engineers through a six-step process. The iterations slider controls the reasoning budget, from None for quick scans to High for complex architectures with 20 or more components.

Once submitted, the system processes the architecture through each workflow node with real-time progress tracking. Engineers can monitor which phase is active and return to review results when processing completes.

Figure 3: Real-time progress tracking shows the current workflow phase. The Thinking indicator on the Threats node reflects the extended thinking capability of Claude analyzing the architecture against TUI security standards.

The iteration journey: from brute force to intelligent selection

TUI’s team didn’t arrive at the final design on day one. They iterated through several approaches, and each failure pointed toward the next improvement.

Attempt 1: Load everything into the prompt. The first approach loaded all 192 TUI security standards (338 KB) directly into the foundation model context. This failed immediately. Some individual standard documents run 20+ pages, and the combined content exceeded token limits before the foundation model could begin threat analysis.

Even with a subset of standards, the foundation model struggled to follow structured instructions. When asked to recommend only TUI-approved tools for mitigations, it would ignore the approved tool list and suggest generic alternatives. Too much contradictory information from different standards confused the model.

Attempt 2: Metadata-driven selection. The breakthrough came from treating the problem as a search and selection challenge rather than a prompt-loading exercise. Instead of loading all standards, the team pre-generated lightweight metadata for each document: keywords, component types, STRIDE categories, and a relevance score.

At runtime, the foundation model reviews this metadata (about 60 KB) and selects only the 16 most relevant standards for the specific architecture being analyzed. This reduced context from 338 KB to 21 KB, a 94% reduction, while maintaining coverage. The reduction is calculated from the metadata approach versus loading all standards directly.

The metadata approach fits the structure of TUI’s knowledge base: some documents are always mandatory (security guidelines, approved tools), while others apply only to certain architectures. The team also evaluated retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but with a bounded corpus of 192 standards, some mandatory regardless of the query, metadata-driven selection proved more predictable and easier to debug. RAG may complement it as the knowledge base grows.

Agentic threat generation: a self-correcting workflow

The threat generation node is where the agentic behavior matters most. Rather than generating threats in a single pass, the system uses a Reason and Act pattern with a LangGraph subgraph. The agent has four tools at its disposal: adding threats, deleting threats, reading the current threat catalog, and running gap analysis.

The agent autonomously decides which tools to call and in what order. It generates an initial set of threats using STRIDE methodology, then reviews its own output against the loaded TUI standards. Each threat includes a title, description, affected component, and threat vector. It also assigns likelihood and impact scores using TUI’s risk matrix. Threats include recommended mitigations with TUI-approved tools and mapped ISO 27001 controls.

A tool budget system helps prevent the agent from generating indefinitely. After three threat-generation calls, the system forces a gap analysis. The agent must step back and assess what’s missing before generating more. This mimics how human security experts work: generate, review, identify gaps, fill them.

A validation node checks three conditions before the workflow can proceed: the threat catalog isn’t empty, all six STRIDE categories are covered, and gap analysis has been performed at least once. If a check fails, the agent receives specific feedback and loops back.

Based on TUI’s production data, the combination of iterative generation and gap analysis typically produces 40–60 threats per architecture, compared to the 30–40 that manual sessions identified. It also supports configurable extended thinking budgets, from 24K reasoning tokens for standard architectures up to 64K for complex systems.

Web search for current threat intelligence

Security threats evolve regularly. A threat model generated today needs to account for issues disclosed last week. The workflow integrates web search to fill gaps where TUI’s internal standards don’t cover specific technologies.

For every technology identified in the architecture (Keycloak, Kong, Redis, and so on), the system generates two search queries: one for known issues and one for hardening best practices. These queries target authoritative sources such as OWASP, NIST, and CWE databases. Before making an API call, it checks an Amazon S3-based cache with a 7-day time-to-live (TTL). Only technology component names are used for external searches. Architecture details and customer data are not included in queries.

The cache key uses a hash of the sorted component names, deliberately excluding foundation model-generated descriptions. Those descriptions vary slightly between runs even for the same diagram, which would reduce cache effectiveness.

Based on TUI’s monitoring data, the cache achieves a 70–80% hit rate because many TUI applications share core technologies. A cache hit returns results in under 100 milliseconds, compared to 2–3 seconds for a live search. TUI’s team evaluated multiple search providers during the PoC and designed the system with a pluggable provider architecture, allowing provider switching as capabilities evolve.

SME comparison: human-in-the-loop validation

TUI’s security engineers don’t just use the system. They validate it. The workflow includes an optional node where engineers upload their own manually created threat assessment as a PDF. The workflow extracts threats using Claude, normalizes risk ratings to a standard scale (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL), and matches them against the AI-generated threats using semantic similarity.

When the AI and the SME disagree on a threat’s severity, the system flags the discrepancy with both ratings and the SME’s rationale. For example, the AI might rate a credential stuffing event (automated login attempts using unintended disclosure of credential databases) as HIGH while the SME rates it MEDIUM. Over time, these comparisons calibrate the system’s risk scoring and surface areas where the AI consistently over- or under-estimates risk.

The following screenshot shows an SME Comparison Alert for a credential stuffing threat. The system matched the AI-generated threat with a similar SME threat, compared both ratings (AI: High, SME: HIGH), and provided the SME’s rationale alongside a recommendation.

Figure 4: An SME Comparison Alert for a credential stuffing threat. The system displays both the AI and SME ratings, the matched SME threat, the expert’s rationale, and a recommendation. In this case, ratings are consistent. When they disagree, the alert highlights the discrepancy for human review.

Path to production: 30 days from handover to live

After the PoC handover, TUI’s team took the system from prototype to production-ready deployment in 30 days. The following results reflect the system’s performance in production.

Results

MetricBeforeAfterTime per assessment4–6 hoursUp to 70% reduction*Sessions per month3–410–12 (300% increase)*Standards appliedVaries by engineer100% consistentThreats identified30–4040–60 per architectureMandatory for all teamsNo (backlog too large)Yes (feasible at scale)

*Based on TUI’s internal measurements comparing pre- and post-deployment performance.

The solution processes each architecture in the eu-central-1 Region, with data encrypted at rest using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) and in transit with TLS. Architecture diagrams and threat models are processed within the AWS infrastructure, helping TUI meet its data residency and security requirements.

The following screenshot shows the threat catalog, a card view of completed threat models. Each card displays the original architecture diagram, an AI-generated description, completion status, and threat counts by severity (red for high, yellow for medium, green for low).

Figure 5: The threat catalog provides an overview of completed threat models. Each card shows the architecture diagram, an AI-generated summary, and threat counts grouped by severity.

Engineers can select a threat model to view a dashboard with four analytical views: threats by likelihood, threats by STRIDE category, threats by target asset, and threat sources.

Figure 6: The insights dashboard for a completed threat model. This example shows 40 identified threats (6 high, 24 medium, and 10 low) distributed across all six STRIDE categories and mapped to specific architecture components.

“In the first four weeks after launch, 64 users registered and 19 unique creators produced 34 threat models with Threat Designer. What previously took one to two weeks per assessment is now available on demand. As of October 2026, adoption has grown to 255 registered users, 86 threat models, and 43 active creators, demonstrating that teams are embracing self-service security as part of their development workflow.”

— Marvin Jordan, Head of Technology for Security Platform and Practices, TUI

Conclusion

TUI’s experience shows that agentic AI workflows can address a real operational challenge in enterprise security: making thorough threat modeling fast enough to be mandatory. The combination of metadata-driven context selection, self-correcting threat generation, and intelligent caching allowed a four-person security team to support over 100 digital product teams. TUI achieved consistent, standards-aligned assessments at scale.

Looking ahead, TUI plans to expand the system with automated Jira ticket creation for mitigation tracking and integration with CI/CD pipelines for pre-deployment security checks.

You can get started with Amazon Bedrock to build AI-powered security workflows and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to deploy agentic applications in production. For hands-on guidance with your specific use case, connect with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center. To explore the open source foundation that this solution extends, see the Threat Designer project on GitHub and the AWS blog post Accelerate threat modeling with generative AI.

We welcome your feedback and questions in the comments.
