posts.title: Analyze your Stripe data directly with your agent
posts.summary: You can now use natural language to create an investor slide deck highlighting where your business outperformed in the previous quarter, or build a custom dashboard to understand why your Stripe revenue changed.
posts.content:
As AI becomes a larger part of how teams work, users increasingly tell us they want to access and analyze their Stripe data directly with the agents they use every day.

Agents can now have structured access to your Stripe data to help you make faster, better business decisions. We introduced the ability for you to connect compatible agents such as Claude and Cursor to your Stripe analytics data via Stripe’s MCP or by using the Queries API and Reports API directly—now available for all Stripe users. With natural language prompts, you can do things like create an investor slide deck highlighting where your business outperformed in the previous quarter, or build a custom dashboard to understand why your Stripe revenue changed.

The Queries API is free for all Stripe users through January 31, 2027. After that, you’ll pay per credit of API usage, with no monthly subscription required. The Reports API will remain free.

How it works

To make use of your Stripe data, an agent needs to know which tables to use, how Stripe defines the relevant metrics, and how to construct the analysis. The Reports API has the modeled data schema of more than 300 tables, as well as built-in guidance for how the agent should use the tables, so you can get the most accurate and reliable analysis. If you want to better understand your subscriptions business, Stripe can route the agent to track monthly recurring revenue over time and attribute changes to upgrades, downgrades, churn, and anything else that is important for you to understand and take action on.

Once your agent has the relevant Stripe data, it can analyze the data alongside information from connected tools and relevant context from previous conversations. In Claude, you could bring together website activity from a PostHog connector, subscription data from Stripe, and context from earlier threads about a campaign to understand which customers clicked a button but later churned. 

This type of financial analysis often informs important business decisions and investor reporting, so results from an agent need to be clear and verifiable. For each analysis with our APIs, you can inspect the underlying SQL, confirm how the result was calculated, and edit the query as your needs change.

Example prompts to get started 

Explore and use your Stripe data with an agent using these example prompts, which you can copy or customize.

To answer accounting and finance questions:

  • “Reconcile each payout from the past three months to its underlying payments, refunds, disputes, fees, and transfers. Show any amounts that do not tie out and the transactions contributing to each difference.”
  • “Create an Excel file with all open and past-due invoices grouped by customer and invoice age from the last month. Flag customers with repeated collection failures.”

To track business growth:

  • “Build a monthly recurring revenue dashboard for me to monitor MRR, expansion, contraction, churn, and reactivation, then explain the largest month-over-month changes by product and plan.”
  • “How have our new promotions affected revenue this quarter?”

To understand and prevent fraud:

  • “Set up a Slack notification when fraud rates go higher than my predefined range. Show trends by payment method and dispute reason, then highlight the segments with the largest increases.”
  • “Find the payment segments with the highest chargeback rates over the past 90 days.”

To analyze payments performance:

  • “Give me a visual report on my payments business over the past quarter, with charts of payment volume, success rates, failures, refunds, and disputes. Show the most important trends by payment method and market, flag notable changes, and summarize where performance is improving or needs attention.”
  • “Find failed payments from the past 30 days that did not succeed within three days. Group them by decline reason and payment method.”

If you’re already connected to the Stripe MCP, you can get started by directly prompting your agent with one of the above examples. If you’re new to the Stripe MCP, open your agent and prompt: “Pull my Stripe data in” to get connected. 

If you want to access Stripe data programmatically from your own workflow, you can get started with the Queries API or Reports API directly.

posts.title: F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale
posts.summary: Facebook Feature Framework (F3) is Meta’s framework for authoring, compiling, and serving the machine learning features underlying ads ranking models, where a single request can require more than 20,000 features. We…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Xiaohe Dong, Jonathan He, Jesus Francisco Anaya Gonzalez, Purbesh Sahoo, Daniel Wang
  • Facebook Feature Framework (F3) is Meta’s framework for authoring, compiling, and serving the machine learning features underlying ads ranking models, where a single request can require more than 20,000 features. We first presented F3 at AI @ Scale 2020. 
  • F3 reduced execution computational costs by compiling all features into a single merged graph, but that graph also served as the release unit, so a single failure or invalid definition blocked the entire release pipeline.
  • This post introduces F3 Lightning, an infrastructure layer built on top of F3 to resolve this challenge by decoupling feature releases from shared execution, so each feature is compiled, validated, deployed, and rolled back independently.
  • The hardest part to solve was preserving F3’s efficiency improvements. Early per-feature release prototypes increased CPU usage because independent features no longer shared computation. We aimed to close this gap through four optimizations: stable computation identifiers, a single shared execution plan, one shared memory buffer across all features, and dense index mapping for direct array access.
  • With F3 Lightning, comparable extraction features now reach production ~3.6x faster than the prior F3, with no increase in infrastructure compute cost. This shorter release cycle also enables more model iterations in the same period.

A Primer on F3’s Shared Execution Architecture

Production machine learning systems rarely consume raw data directly. Before a model can make a prediction, its feature-serving system may need to read stored signals, filter events to a time window, count or sum values, normalize them, and combine intermediate results.

The simplest design to complete this work treats every feature as an independent function. That is easy to understand, but it becomes wasteful at scale, because features are not computationally independent. A seven-day click count and a seven-day impression count may read the same event source and apply the same time-window filter. A click-through rate feature may then reuse both results. Running each feature separately would repeat that filter, and every other shared step, on every request.

F3 approached this differently, by representing feature extraction as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each node performs one unit of work, such as reading an input, applying a filter, or calculating an aggregation. An edge means one computation depends on the result of another. The graph’s outputs are the feature values a model consumes.

Engineers author each feature independently in a high-level language. The F3 compiler turns each definition into a small graph, then merges the graphs for every feature a service uses into one merged graph (Figure 1). Where features share an operation, such as the seven-day filter above, the compiler collapses the duplicates into a single node. That shared work then runs once per request, not once for every feature that needs it. At runtime, feature extraction is a traversal of this merged graph.

The Shared Graph Made Every Release All-or-Nothing

F3’s merged graph shared computation efficiently, but it came with a major catch: The graph was also the release, and one malformed definition could hold back every other feature in the merged graph.

Figure 2 illustrates this challenge. It shows seven independently authored features, A through G, where five definitions are valid, but D and G contain unrelated errors. The “Attempt 1” build fails on D, so none of the seven features ships. After D is corrected, the “Attempt 2” build reaches G and fails again. Only after both definitions are fixed in “Attempt 3” does the complete merged graph make it successfully to production.

Failures became more frequent as F3 scaled. F3 originally served a few hundred features, and at that size merges succeeded and releases were largely smooth. Today that number is more than 20,000, and different feature types need their own checks depending on how they compute, so new features and modified features are held to different testing bars. A feature that a model already consumes needs model-related tests before it can be released. Those tests are computationally expensive enough that they run only in a later release stage, and, because the merged graph ships as one unit, every other feature in it waits for them too.

F3 Lightning: Making Each Feature Its Own Release and Sharing Computation

After F3 launched, we made several rounds of improvements to the merged graph. Each one brought back release speed for a while, but the gains eroded as more features landed, because all features still shipped together in the merged graph. So F3 Lightning was built to make every feature releasable on its own while preserving F3’s efficiency.

As illustrated in Figure 3, F3 Lightning introduced two changes to help achieve this:

  • Deployment granularity: Each feature is an independently releasable configuration. It is validated, shipped, and rolled back without affecting any other feature.
  • Efficiency parity: F3’s efficiency came from the merged graph, so giving every feature its own release removes the source of it. Matching that efficiency while keeping per-feature releases required several key optimizations in how F3 Lightning executes.

Deployment Granularity: How F3 Lightning Isolates Feature Releases

Isolation starts in the compiler, where each feature is compiled on its own into a single configuration. That feature configuration carries everything needed to extract that feature — every node it needs, in order, with nothing borrowed from a neighbor. If feature C has a problem, feature A still ships, because the two configurations have no relationship to each other.

Because features are no longer merged at release time, each one can be selected and released on its own schedule. The release path becomes an ordered queue instead of a batch that ships all at once or not at all. Changes are prioritized by what they unblock. A new feature that no model consumes yet can go out quickly on standard validation, while a change to a feature a live model already reads gets extra testing first.

Efficiency Parity: How F3 Lightning Preserved F3’s Serving Efficiency

Our first prototypes separated deployment only. Features shipped independently, but execution was no longer shared, so the prototypes used substantially more CPU than traditional F3. Each independently released configuration arrived at the serving process as its own graph and was executed separately, repeating every read, filter, and aggregation that F3’s merged graph had eliminated.

The fix was to bring shared execution back without bringing the merge back. At startup, F3 Lightning does not rebuild a merged graph. It takes the active feature configurations, consolidates the work they share, and arranges it into a single execution order. Getting back to parity took four steps: a compiler prerequisite followed by three startup optimizations.

Step 1: Stable Identifiers Make Shared Work Recognizable

To deduplicate execution, the runtime must recognize when two independently compiled configurations contain the same computation. Node numbers can’t do this, because numbering is local to each feature’s graph. The same seven-day filter might be node 2 in one configuration and node 7 in another, and inserting a single node renumbers everything after it. Traditional F3 never had this problem, because one compiler run saw every feature and could assign identifiers globally.

F3 Lightning instead has the compiler derive each identifier from what the work does, not where it sits: the operation, its parameters, and the identifiers of its inputs (see Figure 6). Because each input’s identifier already reflects everything upstream of it, the identifier captures the whole chain of work that produced the result. Where input order doesn’t affect the result, inputs are put in a standard order. Aggregations also include the properties that define their behavior, such as the time window and grouping keys. As a result, two features that define the same operation over the same inputs receive the same identifier, even if they were compiled and released weeks apart. If a computation’s meaning changes, its identifier changes with it.

Step 2: One Execution Plan Across Every Feature

At service startup, F3 Lightning builds a single execution plan across all active features, using a topological sort to place every node after the nodes it depends on. When several features contain a node with the same identifier, the plan keeps one copy and connects every consumer to it, so that computation runs once no matter how many features use it.

Merging guarantees each computation runs once, but the plan is still a graph that the executor walks pointer by pointer on every request. The same startup pass therefore flattens it into an ordered list, so each request runs a single forward pass down the list instead of traversing a graph.

Sharing one plan raises a risk: A single failing computation could affect every feature. To prevent this, if a computation fails or its input is unavailable, F3 Lightning marks everything downstream of it as not ready, and the executor skips that work. A failure affects only the nodes that depend on it, and independent branches keep running.

Step 3: A Shared Memory Buffer, Because Deduplication Was Not Enough

After steps 1 and 2 were complete, no computation ran twice, yet CPU use was still above traditional F3. The remaining compute cost came from memory layout. Each configuration carried its own request-time data container, so intermediate results were scattered across separate memory allocations. Walking the plan in order meant jumping between them, and each jump cost a cache miss.

F3 Lightning replaced those per-feature containers with one buffer per request. At startup, each feature’s references are rebound to slots in that buffer.

Three improvements follow from the single buffer:

Locality: Consecutive plan steps now touch adjacent memory, so the values a step reads are usually already in cache. This restores the sequential access pattern the merged graph always had. It also removes the per-feature allocation on every request.

One readiness vector: A single vector, stored apart from the values, replaces per-feature tracking, so the executor can check whether a value is ready without reading the value itself. The marker has to be separate because an empty list is a valid result, so “empty” can’t also mean “not computed yet.”

No duplicate copies: Most feature values are lists and maps, and consumers no longer get their own copy. The shared slot holds a reference to the producer’s result, so a computation used by 20 features is computed once and stored once. Single values (scalars) are still copied, because copying a small value is cheaper than following a pointer. This is safe because each buffer lasts only for one request, and the execution order guarantees each result outlives its last reader.

Step 4: Dense Index Mapping Removes the Last Per-Access Cost

Values now lived together, but finding one was still computationally expensive. Every access had to resolve an identifier, which meant hashing a key, probing buckets, and following a pointer. Lookups weren’t computationally efficient at Meta’s serving volume. 

The final fix applied the same principle as steps 2 and 3, doing the work once at startup. F3 Lightning assigns every unique identifier a consecutive integer slot and rewrites every reference in every configuration to point at those slots, so identifiers are used only during initialization. Reading a result becomes a direct array index into the shared buffer, with no hashing and no lookup table on the request path.

With F3 Lightning, comparable extraction features now reach production ~3.6x faster than on traditional F3, with no increase in infrastructure computational cost. That shorter release cycle means models can be improved and retrained more often in the same period. Building F3 Lightning also taught us three lessons:

Deployment and execution should have separate boundaries: If one artifact determines both how components run and when they ship, a failure in any one of them blocks all the others. Splitting the two jobs removed a trade-off between efficiency and release speed.

Work that never changes between requests belongs at startup, not on the request path: Three tasks were identical for every request: spotting shared work, deciding the order to run it in, and finding where each result is stored. F3 Lightning now does them once, when the service starts, so independent releases add no computational cost to individual requests.

Two designs can execute the same operations in the same order and still differ substantially in CPU computational cost: In F3 Lightning, we removed every repeated computation, yet CPU use stayed above traditional F3. Each feature still kept its own copy of the shared results, spread across memory. Consolidating them into one copy per result closed the gap. This is the least obvious result in the project and the one that generalizes furthest. On modern CPUs, where results live and how many copies exist can matter as much as how many computations run.

Acknowledgments

We would like to thank Sourabh Bansal, Ping Chen, Weitao Chen, Benjamin Dummitt, Junhua Gu, Henry Hu, Jing Huo, Joffrey Liu, Rocky Liu, Weixi Ma, Shuby Mao, Sandeep Pandey, Mihir Rastogi, Tim Sombuntham, Matt Steiner, Vivienne Sung, Ritwik Tewari, Vivek Trehan, Arnaud Venet, Ziheng Wang, Gautam Wilkins, Fan Yang, Qiao Yang, Jie Zheng and the entire team behind the development and productionization of F3, Meta’s Ads ML feature computation and serving platform, and F3 Lightning, the capability built on top of it.

posts.title: How to run a DR readiness engagement
posts.summary: This final post turns the DR framework into a repeatable engagement: a five-step sequence from kickoff and gap assessment through progressive validation to an updated recovery commitment, with a real before-and-after…
posts.content:
Part 3 of 3

The framework from Part 1 (three business decisions) and Part 2 (progressive validation) works at any pace. You can apply it over months as part of normal operations, or compress it into a structured engagement that moves from undefined targets to a validated recovery commitment in weeks. This post walks through how to run that engagement yourself, with concrete steps, outputs, and a before-and-after example from a real enterprise engagement.

Step 1: Kickoff (define the scope)

Bring three groups into one room: the application owner who knows the technical architecture, the business owner who understands the consequence of downtime, and the platform team that owns the shared services your application depends on. If a dependency is owned by a team not represented in the room, that’s your first action item before proceeding.

Ask these questions in order:

  • What does the user need to be able to do for this function to count as “recovered”?
  • Which applications, shared services, and accounts are in the path of that user journey?
  • Who owns each piece, and have they confirmed their recovery timeline?

The output artifact is a boundary map: a document listing every service and account in the recovery path, with an owner assigned to each and their stated recovery timeline recorded. This single artifact becomes the foundation for every subsequent step.

Step 2: Assessment (surface the gaps)

Run a structured review of each component in the boundary map. For each dependency, ask: does it recover in the target AWS Region, does it recover within the stated recovery time objective (RTO), and does an upstream service’s recovery target cap the RTO you can actually commit to?

  • A Well-Architected Framework Review against the Reliability pillar gives you a systematic way to surface single points of failure, missing health checks, and unverified quotas.
  • An Operational Readiness Review checks whether the runbook’s assumptions hold: are the resources pre-provisioned, do upstream dependencies recover within the target, and are there any manual steps that depend on a specific person being available?

The output is a prioritized list of dependency gaps with owners assigned and a target fix date for each. “Done” at this step means every gap has an owner, a planned fix, and a committed date. Gaps without owners don’t get fixed.

Step 3: Validation plan (structure the tests)

Build a test calendar that progresses through the levels from Part 2. A practical sequence for a first engagement:

  • Week 2: Tabletop exercise on the highest-consequence function. Confirm ownership, escalation path, and expected duration per step.
  • Week 4-6: Planned failover after gap remediation. Measure actual recovery time against the committed RTO. Verify data consistency against the recovery point objective (RPO).
  • Week 8-10: Surprise drill (if the planned failover passed). Test coordination without advance notice.

Don’t schedule a game day with fault injection until you’ve passed a planned failover cleanly. Each level builds confidence for the next. Attempting a higher level before the lower one passes cleanly wastes effort and produces noisy findings that obscure the real gaps.

Step 4: Execute and learn (close the loop)

Each test produces findings. Document them in a format that maps each finding back to the decision it informs:

  • Boundary findings (a shared service discovered mid-test that wasn’t in the recovery scope) → feed back into Decision 1.
  • Consequence findings (recovery took longer than the business can tolerate) → feed back into Decision 2, where the business owner either accepts the longer timeline or invests in a faster architecture.
  • Dependency findings (an upstream service whose recovery target capped the application’s own, a resource that wasn’t pre-provisioned) → feed back into Decision 3.

The output is an updated recovery commitment that reflects what you actually measured, not what you assumed. This document replaces the prior version and becomes the baseline for the next cycle.

Step 5: Ongoing cadence (prevent drift)

Recovery posture drifts as applications change. A new microservice adds a dependency nobody mapped. A team deploys a configuration change that shifts traffic routing. A quota that covered peak load 6 months ago no longer does. Schedule a quarterly review that checks: has the boundary changed (new shared services, new accounts)? Has the business owner confirmed they still accept the RTO/RPO targets? Have any dependencies changed their recovery behavior?

A trigger for re-engagement outside the quarterly cycle: any architecture change that adds a cross-account dependency or changes the failover path.

What this looks like in practice

In the enterprise engagement referenced throughout this series, the team applied this pattern across its portfolio of applications and accounts. The first exercise missed a contractual recovery commitment of 5 hours, taking more than twice that long. Root causes mapped to all three decisions: the boundary excluded a shared authentication platform (most downstream applications couldn’t authenticate users), the dependency chain included an upstream service whose recovery target capped what the applications calling it could achieve, disaster recovery (DR) resources weren’t pre-provisioned, and DNS failover depended on a manual step that took over 3 hours under coordination pressure.

Over 4 months, the team redefined the boundary to include shared platforms, documented the full dependency chain per application, reconciled each application’s target against its slowest dependency, pre-provisioned the recovery environment, and replaced manual DNS failover with automated routing built on Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) routing controls. ARC routing controls are on/off switches on a data plane that shifts traffic without depending on the Amazon Route 53 control plane, so a cutover doesn’t rely on modifying DNS records mid-event. This follows the Well-Architected guidance to rely on the data plane, not the control plane, during recovery (REL11-BP04), the same static-stability principle behind pre-provisioning. The second exercise passed. The organization operated a live customer-facing system from the recovery Region for the first time. Senior leadership cited the structured engagement as the factor that connected the two different outcomes.

Accelerating the timeline

You can run every step in this post with your own teams. If you want to compress the timeline, AWS Enterprise Support provides specific mechanisms that map to each step: a Technical Account Manager to facilitate the kickoff and maintain engagement momentum between sessions, Well-Architected and Operational Readiness Reviews for the assessment, specialist Solutions Architects for deep dependency analysis, and AWS Countdown for coordinated operational-readiness and engineering support during critical events, including planned failovers and DR game days. These are acceleration options, not prerequisites. The steps and outputs are the same either way.

The AWS Resilience Lifecycle Framework and AWS Resilience Analysis Framework provide the detailed practices behind each decision, and AWS Resilience Hub helps you assess applications against your defined RTO and RPO targets.

posts.title: Validating your DR commitment: From controlled test to real-world readiness
posts.summary: After you define your DR targets, testing tells you whether they hold. This post walks through a four-level progressive validation model (tabletop, planned failover, surprise drill, and game day) and shows how each…
posts.content:
Part 2 of 3

In Part 1 of this series, you defined three business decisions that shape your disaster recovery (DR) commitment: the recovery boundary, the business-anchored target, and the dependency-reconciled commitment. Those decisions give you a target on paper. Testing tells you whether it holds under real conditions.

This post covers a progressive approach to DR validation. Each level of testing surfaces a different class of gap, and each gap feeds back into the three decisions from Part 1 so your commitment gets stronger with every cycle.

Why a single test isn’t enough

A scheduled DR exercise with advance notice proves that the failover mechanism works. That’s a necessary starting point. You can confirm that traffic shifts correctly, data remains consistent in the recovery Region, and the application functions as expected after the transition.

A scheduled exercise doesn’t test the assumptions that only surface under pressure. It doesn’t show whether teams who haven’t rehearsed together can coordinate, or whether everyone agrees on who declares the failover and under what conditions. It also can’t confirm that you provisioned and validated your recovery environment before you triggered the failover. These are the conditions where real recoveries stall, and they’re invisible to a test where every team knows it’s coming and watches closely.

In the same engagement from Part 1, several applications had DR instances in a stopped state. The failover automation assumed it could launch instances, create database replicas, and scale container fleets on demand during the exercise. That approach worked only if the team confirmed two things in advance: that the recovery AWS Region had capacity for the requested instance types, and that the account quotas could absorb the full production load. The team didn’t verify these assumptions in advance.

The architecture was correct. The team didn’t verify those assumptions in advance, and it didn’t pre-provision the recovery environment. To close this gap, the team needs to pre-provision the recovery environment and configure auto scaling groups, confirm that its account quotas match production capacity requirements, and remove any runbook step that assumes your team needs to create resources during the event.

Four levels of progressive validation

The AWS Resilience Lifecycle Framework treats testing as a practice you deepen over time. The four levels below are a maturity model you can apply yourself, ordered from lowest-cost awareness to highest-fidelity validation. We’ve drawn it from patterns across the DR exercises we’ve seen. Each surfaces a different class of gap.

Level 1: Tabletop exercise. A facilitated walkthrough of the recovery plan without touching production. The goal is shared awareness and ownership clarity.

Questions to ask during the tabletop:

  • Who declares the failover, and under what conditions?
  • For each step in the runbook, who owns it and what’s their backup?
  • What’s the expected duration of each step, and what’s the total end-to-end timeline?
  • Which steps depend on a specific person being available?

In the same case study from Part 1, the first tabletop surfaced three boundary gaps: the shared authentication platform wasn’t in the recovery scope, a networking account owned by a different team had no failover runbook, and the DNS update step listed a generic team alias with no named owner.

Level 2: Planned failover. A scheduled failover with advance notice. The goal is confirming the mechanism works under known conditions.

What to measure:

  • Actual recovery time per application compared to the stated recovery time objective (RTO).
  • Data consistency validation in the recovery Region to confirm the recovery point objective (RPO).
  • Any step that requires manual intervention (potential automation candidate).
  • Any dependency that recovered later than expected.

In the same case study, the planned failover revealed the DNS misconfiguration: the shared platform’s Amazon Route 53 records still resolved to the primary Region 45 minutes into the test. Most downstream applications appeared healthy but couldn’t serve users. Actual recovery took more than twice the 5-hour target.

A successful planned failover produces a measured gap (or confirmation) between the RTO target you defined and your actual recovery time. That number is the starting point for every subsequent conversation with the business owner about whether the target is realistic.

Level 3: Surprise drill. A failover triggered without advance notice to the responding team. The goal is testing execution readiness, not capability.

This level finds the gaps that preparation hides: the runbook that only its original author can interpret, the step that depends on a specific person’s tribal knowledge, and the escalation path that nobody has practiced. In the case study, a later surprise drill revealed that only one engineer understood how to validate database consistency in the recovery Region. With that person unavailable, the team lost 90 minutes locating and interpreting the procedure.

Level 4: Game day with fault injection. An exercise where you inject specific dependency failures using AWS Fault Injection Service, which ships purpose-built scenarios such as “AZ Availability: Power Interruption” and “Cross-Region: Connectivity”. The goal is testing resilience under conditions you didn’t fully script.

You discover the dependency you assumed would be healthy, the monitoring gap that delays detection, and the cascade that your tabletop didn’t model. This is the closest approximation to a real event without waiting for one to happen.

What each level reveals

The tabletop finds the step no team owns. The planned failover finds the misconfiguration. The surprise drill finds the coordination failure. The game day finds the unmodeled dependency. Each level surfaces a different class of gap.

Run only the calm, scheduled test and you validate the mechanism while leaving the conditions that cause real recovery failures untested. The point isn’t to skip levels. You build confidence at each level before increasing realism. But stopping at the planned failover, a pattern we often see once the mechanism works, leaves team, process, and dependency gaps invisible until an event exposes them.

Closing the loop

Each test produces specific findings that map directly to the three decisions from Part 1.

  • A boundary gap (a shared service discovered mid-test that wasn’t in the recovery scope) feeds back into Decision 1.
  • A recovery that exceeds the time the business can tolerate feeds back into Decision 2, where the business owner either accepts the longer timeline or invests in a faster architecture.
  • A dependency that recovered slower than the target assumed feeds back into Decision 3 for a revised commitment that reflects what was actually measured.

In the same engagement, the first exercise surfaced all four patterns described across this series: a boundary gap (shared platform not in scope), a dependency gap (an upstream service whose recovery target capped the application’s own), a stability gap (resources not pre-provisioned), and a coordination gap (manual DNS failover). The team mapped each finding to a specific decision and a specific fix. Four months later, the second exercise passed. The organization operated a live customer-facing system from the recovery Region for the first time.

The value of progressive testing is not passing a single exercise. It’s building a practice where each cycle tightens the recovery commitment, and each finding has a clear path back to the decision it informs.

Where to start

If you haven’t run a tabletop yet, start there. Gather the owners of one critical business function and walk the recovery plan together. Ask: who declares the failover, what’s the first action, who owns each step, and what’s the expected duration of each. If the room disagrees with any answer, this indicates an opportunity to clarify and strengthen your recovery plan before touching production.

If you’ve passed a planned failover, consider whether a surprise drill would surface coordination gaps that preparation masks. In this engagement, the surprise drill cost the team 90 minutes that the planned failover never surfaced. Whatever level you’re at, document what each test reveals and feed it back into the three decisions. A posture that improves every test cycle is worth more than one that passes a single exercise and never evolves. In Part 3, we walk through how to structure a full DR readiness engagement: who to involve, what to produce at each step, and how to compress the timeline from months to weeks.

About the authors

posts.title: Three business decisions that define your DR success
posts.summary: A disaster recovery strategy is only as strong as the business decisions behind it. Before you choose an architecture pattern, three decisions shape whether recovery succeeds: what you're actually recovering, what the…
posts.content:
Part 1 of 3

A disaster recovery (DR) strategy is only as strong as the business decisions behind it. The architecture and failover mechanisms matter, but they execute against targets that you define. In our experience facilitating enterprise DR exercises, the difference between teams that meet their recovery targets and teams that don’t often comes down to three decisions made (or deferred) before the first architecture diagram: what you’re actually recovering, what the business needs from that recovery, and what your dependencies allow you to commit to.

This post helps you validate whether your current approach accounts for each one. It draws on a pattern from a real engagement where revisiting these decisions turned a missed recovery target into a successful test four months later.

This is Part 1 of a three-part series. It walks through those three decisions and shows how to make them before you choose an architecture pattern. Part 2 covers progressive validation testing. Part 3 covers how to run a DR readiness engagement. The approach builds on the AWS Resilience Lifecycle Framework and the AWS Resilience Analysis Framework.

Define the recovery boundary

The first decision is drawing the line around what “recovered” means. You cannot meaningfully define a recovery time objective (RTO) until you specify precisely what you need working for you to consider that objective met.

The Resilience Lifecycle Framework defines a business function as the end-to-end capability a user depends on (completing a transaction, filing a report, accessing an account). A single business function often spans multiple applications, accounts, and teams. When you set a recovery target at the application level without accounting for the shared services that the application calls, you might define the boundary too narrowly to deliver the capabilities your users require.

Here’s a pattern we observed in a DR exercise for a large enterprise customer. The customer tested dozens of applications across many AWS accounts. Each application had its own failover automation, and each one failed over correctly. But a shared authentication platform (running in a separate account, managed by a different team) used Amazon Route 53 simple routing pointed at the primary AWS Region. It had no health checks and no failover configuration. Because the team didn’t include it in the recovery scope, the platform remained in the primary Region while everything else moved. The result: Most of the downstream applications that depended on it couldn’t authenticate users. Although the team had successfully failed over the applications themselves, the business function (user login, transaction, confirmation) did not work. This single boundary gap, not the individual application architectures, was the primary driver of the missed recovery target.

The solution involved redefining the recovery scope rather than changing the architecture. The organization redefined recovery boundaries around business functions (what capabilities must you deliver to your users?) rather than individual applications (is this service running?). That single change pulled the shared authentication platform inside the scope and helped the team discover the dependency. A business impact analysis is the structured starting point for this work.

Anchor the target to business consequence

The second decision is settling what recovery means in terms the business owns. Business stakeholders strengthen RTO and recovery point objective (RPO) when they help set them. In organizations where these targets are defined by engineering alone, they can become disconnected from what the business actually tolerates. A 4-hour RTO means something different for a payments platform that clears interbank settlement than it does for an internal reporting dashboard, even when both share the same database engine and replication setup.

In the same engagement, the business carried a contractual recovery commitment of 5 hours. The business treated it as a firm commitment to their regulator. The engineering team treated it as a stretch goal based on the architecture’s theoretical capability. Neither side had validated whether 5 hours was achievable given the dependency chain. That disconnect only became visible when the first exercise took 9–11 hours. The target had never been tested against the actual recovery path, and the business stakeholder who owned the penalty had never been asked whether the engineering team’s assumptions matched theirs.

RPO is a statement about data loss. For a payments platform clearing interbank settlement, an RPO of 5 minutes might still be too wide if those minutes contain transactions that can’t be reconstructed. The question for the business owner is: Which records must survive a Regional impairment, and can you prove they will? The business owner uses that framing to decide whether asynchronous replication (with its window of in-flight data loss) is acceptable. The alternative is synchronous writes, with the latency cost that comes with them.

RTO is a statement about downtime tolerance. A 4-hour recovery time is a technical figure until someone attaches a consequence to each hour. For regulatory filings, the fourth hour might mean a missed deadline with financial penalties. For a storefront, every minute carries lost orders.

The AWS Resilience Lifecycle Framework recommends defining objectives around business outcomes directly (for example, the percentage of successful orders maintained when a component degrades). A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contract with a financial penalty. A service-level objective is a target you manage toward. Raising an SLA doesn’t make an application more resilient.

The output of this decision is a recovery requirement stated in language the business recognizes and engineering can build against: the function, the consequence of losing it, the data that must survive, and the tolerable downtime before the consequence lands.

Account for the dependency chain

The third decision is confirming that your recovery target accounts for everything in the critical path, not just the components you own. Your application recovers only as fast as its slowest dependency. If a service you call takes 4 hours to recover in the recovery Region, your achievable RTO is 4 hours regardless of your own architecture.

In the same engagement, one customer-facing application had committed to a 1-hour recovery target and had the architecture to meet it on its own. But it called a shared identity service, owned by a different team, to validate every user session. That identity service carried a 4-hour recovery target. No matter how fast the customer-facing application recovered, users couldn’t do anything until the identity service came back. The application’s real, achievable RTO was 4 hours, set entirely by a dependency its own team didn’t own and hadn’t accounted for when they committed to 1 hour.

This is why the dependency chain, not the application in isolation, defines the commitment you can make. Identify and document every service your business function calls, note the recovery target each one holds, and set your own target against the slowest link you depend on. Where another team owns a dependency, its recovery target becomes a commitment you need from them, in writing, not an assumption. The AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries whitepaper helps you reason about which dependencies hold during a Regional impairment, and which introduce risk. The distinction that matters is what your runbook asks a service to do. Reading existing data keeps working during an impairment: existing credentials still authenticate, and existing DNS records still resolve. Changing things is what carries risk, because creating or modifying AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and Route 53 records runs through control planes that live in a single Region. A recovery path that only reads existing state holds up. One that must create or change resources mid-event might not. That’s the case for settling those changes ahead of time.

Where you can, reduce the chain itself. When you pre-provision and run a dependency in the recovery Region before the event, you reduce how many services need to recover before you can restore your application. The shorter the chain of things that must recover in sequence, the closer your achievable target gets to the one you want to commit to.

Where to start

Start your validation by examining one business function. Assess whether: Is the recovery boundary drawn around the full user journey, including shared services in other accounts? Has a business stakeholder confirmed the consequence-per-hour attached to the current RTO and RPO? Does the target account for every dependency in the path, including global endpoints and any runbook step that assumes resource creation during failover?

If you can answer yes to all three with evidence, your targets are well-founded. If any answer is uncertain, you’ve identified where to focus next. In Part 2, we cover how to validate your answers through progressive testing that closes the distance between a controlled exercise and real-world readiness.

About the authors
