posts.title: Automating the full AWS DRS agent lifecycle: Install, heal, and offboard
posts.summary: Keeping a large Amazon EC2 fleet continuously recoverable with AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery is a lifecycle challenge. This post shows how to automate the full DRS agent lifecycle (install, heal, and offboard) using AWS…
posts.content:
If you protect a large Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) fleet with AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS), you manage the AWS Replication Agent across its whole lifecycle. You install it, keep it healthy and registered, and remove it cleanly when a server leaves disaster recovery (DR) scope. An enterprise IT customer with more than 300 Linux and Windows instances in DR scope ran into two of these problems while planning and validating a scheduled DR drill. Some agents had stalled after a network change, and some descoped servers were still replicating and adding to the bill. A server with a stalled agent can’t meet your recovery point objective (RPO), the maximum data loss you can accept after a disruption. The customer’s team checked replication status in the AWS DRS console before each drill, so a problem that started between drills could go unnoticed until the next one.

Working with that customer, we automated the install, heal, and offboard phases of the lifecycle. Most of the design choices in this post came from fixing those two problems. Each phase runs as an AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Automation document, started by Amazon EventBridge or on a schedule. A single EC2 tag decides which phase applies to an instance. Because the logic lives in the Automation documents, there are no AWS Lambda functions to maintain. When you take an instance out of scope, the automation records whether replication billing actually stopped.

You can find the SSM Automation documents, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, and deployment scripts in the aws-samples/sample-drs-agent-lifecycle-automation GitHub repository.

Solution overview

You apply a DR tag to each EC2 instance, and its value (yes, pause, or no) tells the automation what to do. Three SSM Automation documents divide the work. Onboarding installs and repairs the agent and keeps registration healthy. Healing responds when replication stalls, and offboarding runs teardown when you descope an instance.

AWS Systems Manager State Manager runs onboarding on a 30-minute schedule against tagged instances. Amazon EventBridge triggers healing when AWS DRS reports a stalled server, and offboarding when the DR tag changes. The automation runs primarily in your source AWS Region and calls the DR Region only where AWS DRS requires it.

Prerequisites

To deploy this solution, you need:

  • An AWS account with administrative access.
  • Two AWS Regions configured: a source Region (where your EC2 instances run) and a DR Region (where AWS DRS replicates to).
  • AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery initialized in both the source Region (for failback) and the DR Region (for replication).
  • Network connectivity between Regions with TCP 443 (AWS DRS API and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3)) and TCP 1500 (replication data) open. For private connectivity, use AWS Transit Gateway or VPC peering. Public endpoints are also supported.
  • (Optional) Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) endpoints for AWS DRS and Amazon S3 in the DR Region, if using private connectivity.
  • IAM permissions to deploy AWS CloudFormation stacks that create named IAM roles (CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM), Amazon EventBridge rules, and a State Manager association, and to register SSM Automation documents. You also need iam:PassRole on DRS-Automation-Role, because the Amazon EventBridge rules and the State Manager association use that role.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed and configured.
  • An instance profile on each source EC2 instance with the AWSElasticDisasterRecoveryAgentInstallationPolicy and AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policies, so that each instance is managed by Systems Manager. If your instances already have an instance profile, attach both policies to its role.
  • An existing Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic for notifications.
  • (Optional) An existing Amazon S3 bucket for audit reports.
  • Git, Bash 4 or later, and yq. The deployment scripts use yq to read config.yaml. macOS includes Bash 3.2, so install a newer version, for example with Homebrew.

You don’t need to create the automation’s IAM roles yourself. The CloudFormation templates create DRS-Automation-Role (which runs every lifecycle action) and DRS-EventBridge-Forward-Role (deployed with the DR Region stack), along with the Amazon EventBridge rules in both Regions and the State Manager association. Amazon CloudWatch metrics are published automatically.

One tag controls the entire lifecycle

After you deploy the solution, the value of the DR tag on each EC2 instance determines what the automation does:

DR valueStateWhat happensyesProtectedAgent is installed, failback tag applied, health maintained every 30 minutespauseQuiescedAgent stays installed, stalled alerts suppressed, offboarding blockedno or deletedDescopedReplication stopped, source server deleted, agent uninstalledAnything else (for example, DR=maybe, DR=true)MisconfiguredFail-safe: automation skips the instance and logs a SKIPPED_MISCONFIGURED status. No install, no heal, no teardown, preventing an unrecognized value from triggering the wrong action

The tag value is normalized (trimmed and lowercased) before evaluation. A value like DR=Yes normalizes to DR=yes and matches correctly.

Three SSM Automation documents divide the lifecycle:

  • DRS-Agent-Onboard runs every 30 minutes through State Manager against tag:DR=yes instances. It installs or repairs the agent, applies the AWSDRS:AllowLaunchingIntoThisInstance tag, and validates AWS DRS registration. The tag tells AWS DRS to launch recovery onto the original instance during failback and acts as the drift-correction backstop. State Manager re-evaluates tagged instances every 30 minutes. Each run catches instances that lost the Replication Agent, newly tagged instances that aren’t onboarded yet, and earlier runs that failed silently.
  • DRS-Agent-Heal fires when Amazon EventBridge receives a replication-stalled event (cross-Region forwarded from the DR Region). The rule filters on the STALLED state, so recovery transitions don’t trigger unnecessary runs. It inspects the replication error to distinguish agent-side failures from infrastructure issues. For agent problems, it restarts the service first, then reinstalls in place only if the restart doesn’t fix it. For infrastructure-caused stalls, it escalates to operators through Amazon SNS.
  • DRS-Agent-Offboard fires when Amazon EventBridge detects a DR tag change or deletion. The offboarding document first verifies safeguards: a tag re-check, a terminated-instance guard, and an optional approval gate. After those pass, it records replication state and stops replication. It then disconnects the source server, deletes it, uninstalls the Replication Agent, and removes the tags.

How the components connect

The solution operates primarily in the source Region. Cross-Region calls happen only where AWS DRS requires them (registration checks and teardown API calls target the DR Region).

The following diagram shows how the automation components connect across the source and DR Regions. State Manager and Amazon EventBridge operate in the source Region; AWS DRS replication and the stall-forwarding rule run in the DR Region.

Figure 1: AWS DRS agent lifecycle automation architecture across the source and DR Regions

In the source Region, State Manager runs the onboarding document every 30 minutes, and Amazon EventBridge rules start the heal and offboarding documents when their events arrive. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store holds the DR-event stand-down flag (/drs/control/event-in-progress). The DRS-Automation-Role IAM role runs every automation step. Amazon SNS delivers alerts, Amazon S3 stores per-event audit reports, and Amazon CloudWatch captures outcome metrics.

In the DR Region, AWS DRS manages source server registration and ongoing replication. AWS DRS emits replication events only in the DR Region, where the source servers are registered. An Amazon EventBridge forwarding rule filters replication-stalled events by the STALLED state. It then sends them to the source Region for healing. Staging subnets and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes, managed by AWS DRS, support the replication infrastructure.

For networking, AWS Transit Gateway (which connects VPCs across Regions) carries TCP 443 (AWS DRS API and S3) and TCP 1500 (replication data) between Regions. Amazon VPC endpoints for AWS DRS and S3 keep traffic on the AWS backbone without internet exposure. An Amazon Route 53 Private Hosted Zone (for DNS resolution within your VPC) resolves endpoint names to private IPs. This removes the need for --endpoint installer flags and protects failback compatibility.

Tag and rule examples

Run these commands after you deploy the solution. Tag an instance for protection:

aws ec2 create-tags --resources i-0abc123def456 --tags Key=DR,Value=yes

Descope an instance (triggers offboarding):

aws ec2 create-tags --resources i-0abc123def456 --tags Key=DR,Value=no

Or remove the tag entirely (also triggers offboarding):

aws ec2 delete-tags --resources i-0abc123def456 --tags Key=DR

The Amazon EventBridge rule that triggers offboarding matches this pattern:

{
  "source": ["aws.tag"],
  "detail-type": ["Tag Change on Resource"],
  "detail": {
    "changed-tag-keys": ["DR"],
    "service": ["ec2"],
    "resource-type": ["instance"]
  }
}

The Amazon EventBridge rule that triggers healing filters on the STALLED state so recovery transitions are ignored:

{
  "source": ["aws.drs"],
  "detail-type": ["DRS Source Server Data Replication Stalled Change"],
  "detail": {
    "state": ["STALLED"]
  }
}

Three layers protecting the RPO

The 15-minute RPO referenced throughout this post is a customer-configured target, not an AWS service guarantee. The architecture helps protect it with three complementary layers, each covering a different failure mode.

Layer 1: OS service auto-restart (seconds). The agent service uses systemd Restart=always on Linux and Windows Service Recovery. When the process stops, the OS brings it back automatically. On Linux, systemd restarts the service almost instantly. On Windows, the first recovery action fires after a configurable delay (30 seconds by default). This layer handles agent process crashes without any automation running.

Layer 2: Amazon EventBridge heal (minutes, not seconds). If the agent disappears or can’t maintain registration, AWS DRS detects the stall and emits a replication-stalled event in the DR Region. A forwarding rule filters on the STALLED state and sends it cross-Region to the source Region’s event bus. A matching receive rule triggers the heal document.

The heal document restarts the agent first (most stalls are transient). If restart fails, it re-runs the installer in place, preserving driver state to avoid a full-disk rescan. The restart path is the faster of the two, and total time depends on your environment and on AWS DRS stall-detection latency. The reinstall path takes longer because the agent must re-establish block-level tracking. Stall-detection latency also counts against the window, because lag must accumulate before the service marks a server as stalled.

Layer 3: State Manager backstop (up to 30 minutes). The onboarding document re-evaluates DR=yes instances every 30 minutes, catching drift and edge cases that faster layers miss. This exceeds the 15-minute RPO target, so it functions as a safety net rather than the primary defense.

Layer 2 requires the Amazon EventBridge data plane in both Regions to be operational, while Layers 1 and 3 run entirely in the source Region.

Onboarding: How ongoing convergence works

State Manager targets tag:DR=yes. Instances that already have the tag and instances you tag later are included automatically, without manual registration.

The onboarding document is idempotent. It skips healthy, registered instances. For instances that need work, it checks the stand-down flag and instance state, validates the operating system (Linux or Windows), and flags unsupported architectures as TAGGED_UNSUPPORTED. If AutoInstallEnabled is false, the run is audit-only.

For actual installs, a concurrency lock (flock on Linux, a named mutex on Windows) prevents races when multiple automation runs overlap on the same instance. This lock is built into the documents and needs no configuration. The State Manager association sets MaxConcurrency to 10 and MaxErrors to 100% in templates/state-manager-association.yaml. MaxConcurrency limits how many instances are processed at once. With MaxErrors at 100%, a failure on one instance doesn’t stop the run for the rest of the fleet. For larger fleets, raise MaxConcurrency gradually and watch for AWS DRS API throttling.

The failback tag (AWSDRS:AllowLaunchingIntoThisInstance) is applied only when the agent is confirmed present. Registration is assessed cross-Region, and if an instance stays in PENDING_REGISTRATION beyond a configurable threshold (default: 3 runs), the document escalates through Amazon SNS. Each execution writes an S3 audit record and emits a CloudWatch metric.

Healing agent issues within RPO

The heal document reads the source server ARN from the event and looks up the matching EC2 instance ID with drs:DescribeSourceServers in the DR Region. It then checks the stand-down flag and the tag state. Values other than yes suppress the heal with no action and no alert.

If restart doesn’t resolve the issue, the automation re-runs the installer in place as a fallback. It doesn’t uninstall first, so the existing replication driver stays intact where possible. Reinstallation can trigger a block-level rescan whose duration scales with total disk size. On large volumes, this might temporarily exceed the RPO window while the rescan completes.

Not every stall is an agent problem. Bandwidth throttling, undersized replication servers, or staging-area disk issues can also cause stalls. The automation escalates these non-agent stalls to your operators through Amazon SNS rather than attempting agent remediation. If the Replication Agent is still not functioning after reinstall, you receive a HEAL_FAILED notification with diagnostic details.

Only the AWS DRS agent service is restarted, not the EC2 instance itself. Your workloads keep running without interruption.

Offboarding with honest billing status

When you set DR=no or delete the tag, Amazon EventBridge fires a Tag Change on Resource event. The offboarding document applies several safeguards before teardown.

Terminated-instance guard: EC2 termination strips tags, generating the same event as a deliberate descope. The document sends an alert and stops. It doesn’t delete the source server, which contains the recovery point.

Tag re-check: If the tag has been restored, the document exits.

Approval gate: If AutoOffboardEnabled is false, the document sends a notification and stops.

State recording: Before modifying resources, it captures replication state, lag duration, and last snapshot time.

Recovery-instance check: Before completing teardown, the offboarding document checks for active recovery instances. If found, it flags them in the audit report and sends an SNS alert. Recovery instances incur separate EC2 billing that persists after source server deletion.

Adaptive retry: A maximum of 10 attempts with exponential backoff handles API throttling during bulk descope.

After teardown, the document checks what actually succeeded:

OutcomeMeaningCOMPLETEDSource server deleted, billing haltedBILLING_STOPPED_ORPHANReplication stopped but delete didn’t succeed. Operator must manually delete.FAILEDstop_replication didn’t succeed. Billing might still be active. Operator review recommended.NO_SERVERInstance was not registered as an AWS DRS source server. Clean no-op.

Because each outcome reflects what actually succeeded, you know whether replication billing has stopped or whether a source server needs manual follow-up.

Security: Least-privilege IAM roles

The solution creates two IAM roles and relies on one that you provide. SSM Automation and Amazon EventBridge assume the DRS-Automation-Role to run all lifecycle actions. Its permissions cover SSM, EC2 tags, cross-Region AWS DRS calls, SNS, S3, Parameter Store, and iam:PassRole on itself. The iam:PassRole permission only allows passing this role to Systems Manager. Run Command is limited to instances tagged DR=yes. In the DR Region, the DRS-EventBridge-Forward-Role can only put events on the source Region’s default event bus.

On each EC2 instance, the instance profile from the prerequisites lets the Replication Agent and SSM Agent reach their services. The automation stores no long-lived credentials. Each role receives temporary credentials when it’s assumed. When you use private connectivity, cross-Region traffic stays on Transit Gateway and VPC endpoints.

Deploy the solution

posts.title: Stripe on Stripe: What we learned moving $1B in vendor payments to Global Payouts
posts.summary: In early 2026, we began moving our vendor payments to Global Payouts, Stripe’s product for paying recipients in 160+ countries. New-market setup fell from six weeks to one, with a 99.9% payout success rate. Here’s what…
posts.content:
Stripe makes nearly 20,000 payments to vendors in more than 70 markets a year. Historically, we’ve made those payments through direct bank integrations connected to our enterprise resource planning (ERP) system. Where we didn’t have an integration, teams had to manually enter payments through bank portals.

That system worked but grew harder to support as Stripe scaled. Every banking relationship came with its own technical, contractual, and security requirements, and it took weeks to build an integration for a new market. When a payment failed, our operations and finance teams had to search across bank portals and the ERP to identify the problem and resend the money. 

Earlier this year, we began moving Stripe’s own vendor payments to the product we were building to help our users send money around the world: Stripe Global Payouts. Global Payouts enables businesses to pay recipients in more than 160 countries through a single API using local bank transfers, international wires, and stablecoins without requiring recipients to open a Stripe account. 

By October 2026, we had paid over $1 billion to more than 3,400 vendors in the US and UK using Global Payouts. The time it took to set up vendor payouts in a new market dropped from as many as six weeks to one. Our finance and treasury teams now save an estimated 20–30 hours a month with automated reporting and reconciliation, and payouts have maintained a 99.9% success rate. 

Using Global Payouts ourselves put us in our users’ shoes. Companies like Lyft, Scale AI, BMW, and Meta already use Global Payouts for use cases including marketplace earnings, freelancer payments, insurance claims, and customer reimbursements. Running our own vendor payments through the product showed us the pain points businesses hit when integrating and tracking payouts at scale and exposed gaps in vendor data, payment visibility, and high-value transactions—all of which we’ve since resolved. Here’s how we rolled it out and what we learned.

How we rolled out the migration

We began testing Global Payouts in February 2026, sending one low-dollar ACH or wire payment through each US payment flow. In March, we started a staged, four-wave rollout, increasing payment amounts only after nearly all eligible payouts in the previous wave had succeeded. By June, Global Payouts was handling the vast majority of Stripe’s domestic US vendor payments, measured by both payment count and value. 

What we learned using Stripe Global Payouts

Lesson 1: Validate vendor data before a payment reaches the banking system

Bank payments can fail for a lot of reasons, including insufficient funds, bank limits, and restricted accounts. Our previous bank integrations didn’t always catch incorrect or incomplete information when we submitted a payment. During Stripe’s migration, we discovered that recipient data problems were responsible for the majority of failures. A small mistake, like an incorrect postal code, might not become apparent until days later, when the bank returned the payment or the vendor contacted us.

Once we identified the most common reasons for failure, we moved those checks earlier in the payment flow. Our orchestration layer translates vendor and bank account records to the recipient and payout methods used by Global Payouts. The API checks that the required information is present and valid before any money moves. If there’s an issue, the error message identifies what needs attention. Our operations teams can now fix most issues in minutes, rather than having to retrace a failed payment days later.

Lesson 2: Sender-side visibility isn’t enough

Before Global Payouts, payment status information was spread across bank portals and our ERP. With Global Payouts, our teams can trace each vendor payment through a single API. Every payment has a unique reference number, and its invoice information is attached to the outbound payment as metadata. We can track the invoice and the payment from initiation through settlement.

However, in adopting Global Payouts, we found that the vendor’s bank statement didn’t necessarily provide the same context. The vendor might see that money had arrived but couldn’t always tell who sent it or which invoice it covered. A payment would be traceable in our systems but hard to recognize for the person receiving it.

To address the issue, we added customizable statement descriptors so businesses can attach recognizable information to recipients’ bank statements. This gives vendors more context to identify incoming funds and makes it easier for both the sender and recipient to reconcile the payment.

Lesson 3: Test transaction size, not just transaction volume

Global Payouts had to process tens of thousands of payments, but volume wasn’t the only dimension of scale. Some of our vendor payments were much larger than the system had been designed to handle. When a payment exceeded the existing limits, our operations teams had to process it manually. 

We raised the ACH and wire limits on the Outbound Payments API to $100 million. This allows more high-value vendor payments to run through the same automated workflow without bypassing the existing processes for approval, ERP recording, funding, reconciliation, and reporting.

Continuing to build

Global Payouts is now generally available in the US and UK. The product helps thousands of businesses send money to third parties in more than 160 countries, even when those recipients don’t use Stripe.

We’re now working to bring more of Stripe’s cross-border and cross-currency vendor payments onto Global Payouts. This includes expanding recipient-country coverage, supporting stablecoin payouts, and handling cases where a vendor’s address and bank are in different countries or a payment is sent in a different currency from the vendor’s bank account currency. 

We’re also developing AI-assisted capabilities for payouts and recipient onboarding through Stripe's Model Context Protocol, a standard way for agents to interact with Stripe. Businesses can delegate more of their workflow, like beginning recipient onboarding or initiating a payment, to agents while retaining control. They determine which Stripe data an agent can access, which actions it can take, and when a person needs to approve a payout. 

Learn more about Stripe Global Payouts or contact the team to get started.

posts.title: How BMW Group accelerated connected vehicle workloads on AWS Graviton
posts.summary: Learn how BMW Group migrated its connected vehicle platform from x86 to AWS Graviton. Using Karpenter, multi-architecture container builds, and Graviton-based CI/CD runners, the team moved workloads without disruption…
posts.content:
This post is co-written with Tomislav Lozancic, Hrvoje Lukavski from BMW Group, and Hugo Cardoso from CTW.

BMW Connected Company, a division within BMW Group, develops and operates premium digital services for BMW’s connected vehicle fleet of more than 24.5 million vehicles worldwide. Critical TechWorks (CTW), established in September 2018, focuses exclusively on developing software for BMW Group’s future connected vehicle fleet.

In 2024, BMW Connected Company began migrating its Connected Vehicle platform, known internally as Orbit, from x86 to Arm-based compute as part of a broader modernization strategy to advance BMW Group’s economic and environmental goals.

In this post, we share the methodology behind the migration, tooling and patterns that helped application teams move to AWS Graviton at their own pace, without service disruption.

Laying the groundwork

Before applications could adopt a new processor architecture, the platform needed a more flexible provisioning layer. The team adopted Karpenter, replacing fixed Managed Node Groups with dynamic, policy-driven node pools that could provision the right instance type automatically. You can read more about this migration in Transforming the BMW Connected Vehicle Backend with Karpenter.

With the compute foundation in place, the next challenge was supporting multi-architecture builds. Building, testing, and deploying the same application for two architectures without slowing teams down required extending the continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) platform. Build runners needed to target both x86 and Arm while producing dual build pipelines, as described in the following section.

Introducing Graviton-based CI/CD runners

The Connected Vehicle CI/CD platform facilitates over 130,000 builds and deployments daily through self-hosted GitHub Actions runners. You can read more about the evolution of this platform in An Engine of Efficiency: BMW Group’s CI/CD Modernization Journey with AWS.

To surface potential issues early and minimize disruption, the team first validated Graviton on a set of self-contained services. Dedicated Graviton runners operated alongside the existing x86 fleet during this phase. The price-performance advantage of Graviton was confirmed immediately, with lower cost per build minute and faster build times, justifying the business case for wider adoption.

Building on these initial results, the team designed the wider platform rollout around two complementary tracks.

  1. Dual build pipelines: Building and shipping both CPU architectures in parallel, giving applications a non-disruptive path to transition independently.
  2. Container hosting: Extending support into the centralized container platform, so applications could be hosted on Graviton.

The following figure shows the six-stage journey to adopt AWS Graviton. The stages are grouped into two phases: a build-foundation phase and a workload-migration phase.

Figure 1: AWS Graviton adoption journey across the Connected Vehicle platform

Supporting adoption

Getting teams onto Graviton depended less on policy than on removing friction. The following practices lowered the barrier to entry, beginning with the build pipeline.

1 – Multi-architecture builds

As outlined earlier, every container image needed to support both architectures before workloads could run on Arm-based instances. To achieve this, two complementary build approaches were used: emulated builds using Docker Buildx with QEMU, and native builds on Graviton-based runners.

Both approaches produce multi-arch images by publishing a manifest list (OCI image index) alongside the architecture-specific images. When a container runtime pulls a tagged image, it reads the manifest and automatically selects the correct variant for the node’s architecture. This means a single image tag serves both arm64 and amd64 nodes transparently.

2 – Mirroring base images

Public images are mirrored into a private Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) to achieve availability, immutability, and CVE compliance. To preserve multi-arch support during mirroring, the team uses Google’s Crane. Crane transfers images directly between registries and filters the manifest to only the required platforms, which avoids wasted storage from unused architectures.

Besides public images, custom application workloads also needed support for both architectures. Most Dockerfiles required no changes, because their base images and dependencies already supported multiple architectures. In some cases, an alternative or dependency with Arm support needed to be found. For the builds, two approaches were considered:

  1. Native build per architecture: Each architecture is built and pushed separately on a runner with the matching architecture, followed by a final job that creates and pushes the image index. In GitHub Actions, this means one runner per architecture plus one index-creation step. This approach is more reliable but requires a dedicated runner for each target architecture.
  2. Emulated builds from a single machine: Using Docker Buildx with QEMU, all architectures can be built and pushed from a single x86 or Arm runner. This streamlines the pipeline but introduces emulation overhead, often making builds significantly slower for compute-intensive workloads.

The team opted to support both approaches. For platform-scale adoption, Graviton runners were preferred because they ran arm64 builds natively. This avoided the QEMU emulation overhead and surfaced architecture-specific issues earlier in the pipeline. With GitHub Actions reusable workflows, teams can select the right fit for each use case. Dockerfiles use the QEMU path to avoid spinning up additional runners. Those with significant complexity, large dependency downloads, or long build times use native builds, where the overhead becomes problematic.

Graviton runner labels mirror the existing x86 labels, so adoption involves swapping x64 for arm64 in a single label.

3 – Defining Graviton NodePools

The following diagram shows the mixed-architecture Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster, including how on-premises systems connect and how the Graviton and x86 node pools coexist.

Figure 2: Mixed-architecture Amazon EKS cluster with dedicated Graviton node pools and opt-in scheduling

Dedicated Graviton node pools let teams adopt without friction across each environment. The pools are shared and general-purpose by default, not tailored to individual workloads. This keeps the underlying infrastructure model consistent and predictable while still allowing teams to migrate on their own schedule. Karpenter’s automatic scaling foundation supports efficient resource allocation and rapid provisioning for both Arm and x86 workloads.

To avoid accidental scheduling, the Graviton node pools use taints. Workloads must explicitly opt in using a node selector and matching toleration. This supports controlled rollout and predictable behavior:

nodeSelector:
  bmw.de/stateless-arm: supported
tolerations:
- key: "bmw.de/stateless-arm"
  operator: "Equal"
  value: "supported"
  effect: "NoSchedule"

With this in place, only Arm-ready workloads are scheduled on Graviton nodes, while other workloads continue to run on amd64 nodes without disruption.

4 – Phased rollout

Before supporting broad adoption for application workloads, the team first validated the migration path by running core platform services (Karpenter, Prometheus, and operational tooling). This platform-first approach identified compatibility gaps early, refined node pool configuration, and established rollback patterns. Teams had a proven reference model before they were encouraged to opt in.

A key design principle was minimizing rollback risk by keeping both architectures viable simultaneously. Dual-arch images and a dedicated NodePool mean every application can run on both CPU architectures. If issues arise, workloads fall back to x86 without image rebuilds or pipeline changes.

Kubernetes node affinity rules prefer Arm without forcing it, so workloads naturally gravitate toward Graviton instances:

{{/*
Workload node affinity
*/}}
{{- define "common.nodeaffinity" -}}
preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
- weight: 100
  preference:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: kubernetes.io/arch
      operator: In
      values:
      - arm64
{{- end -}}
{{/*
Workload node tolerations
*/}}
{{- define "common.tolerations" -}}
- key: bmw.de/arm
  operator: Equal
  value: supported
  effect: NoSchedule
{{- end -}}

If a full rollback is needed, the GitOps-based ArgoCD deployment model makes recovery straightforward by reverting to the previous version in Git and letting ArgoCD reconcile the cluster state.

Results

The migration delivered approximately $600,000 in annualized infrastructure savings and measurable performance improvements. After moving the NGINX-based ingress controller from x86 to Graviton, key results included:

  • CPU consumption decreased by approximately 57 percent, while maintaining the same ingress profile.
  • Price-performance improved by around 40 percent, as lower CPU consumption per request increased throughput capacity per dollar spent.
  • Scaling efficiency improved at peak loads, with workloads requiring less compute capacity to handle equivalent traffic volumes.

Today, more than 65 percent of the platform runs on Graviton across production environments, a shift that supports BMW Group’s sustainability goals by reducing compute energy demand.

Lessons learned

Migrating a platform of this scale surfaced practical lessons that shaped the team’s approach and would benefit others considering a similar transition:

  • Opt-in scheduling: Use taints, selectors, and tolerations to make sure that only ready workloads migrate.
  • Multi-architecture images: One manifest-based tag for both architectures keeps releases straightforward and rollback instant.
  • Platform-first adoption: Validate on shared infrastructure first to reduce risk before teams opt in.
  • Optimization of emulated builds: This approach is useful for straightforward pipelines. Compute-heavy builds should use native or cross-compilation paths instead, which avoids unnecessary QEMU overhead and long build times.

Conclusion

BMW Group migrated its Connected Vehicle platform to AWS Graviton, achieving over $600,000 in annual cost savings and a 40 percent improvement in price-performance. The more than 130,000 daily builds and deployments that power more than 24.5 million connected vehicles continued without disruption.

The migration succeeded because of deliberate, incremental choices: taint-based node isolation, multi-arch container builds, and Karpenter’s ability to provision the right instance at the right time. Each layer reduced risk while keeping the rollout optional for individual teams. What started as a platform experiment is now the default compute path.

To get started with Graviton-based workloads on Amazon EKS, see the AWS Graviton Getting Started guide. To learn how BMW Group adopted Karpenter at scale, read Transforming the BMW Connected Vehicle Backend with Karpenter.

posts.title: Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale
posts.summary: Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests). Now, we’re sharing the results and positive…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Sreeja Thummala, Sophie Zeng, Mark Harman, Weini Liu, Eric Liu
  • Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests).
  • Now, we’re sharing the results and positive impact we’ve seen with Catching JiTTests deployed into production.
  • Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” fully details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests.

Every code change improves our platform, but it also introduces new complexity. With hundreds of millions of lines of code constantly evolving at Meta, traditional testing can’t keep pace. Catching risks proactively, before code lands, enables us to identify risks earlier, respond more effectively, and deliver reliable experiences at scale.

Over the last year, we’ve shared our research into applying large language models (LLMs) to generate software tests. More specifically, we’ve shared our work with Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests), a novel testing approach where we leverage LLMs to catch bugs on the fly, even ones that traditional testing might not catch.

In the five months since we first unveiled this work, we’ve deployed our Catching JiTTests approach to determine its scalability and applicability to the wider industry. Today, Catching JiTTests are no longer a research prototype; they’re part of Meta’s infrastructure, and they’re helping our engineers catch more bugs with less load and a smaller chance of false positives.

The Advantage of Catching JiTTests

Most AI-based approaches to preventing bugs in code use LLMs and/or agentic AI to review code and detect faults based on prior experience. They work through the same review process that a human reviewer would, only faster. Catching JiTTests is a fundamentally different approach (Table 1): It generates executable tests that demonstrate a concrete behavioral difference introduced by the change. While it requires more computational steps, it catches classes of bugs that LLM- or agent-based code reviews might not.

How We Implemented Catching JiTTests at Meta

JiTTests are automatically generated and designed to fail, surfacing bugs in code changes (diffs) before they land in production. When they’re applied to a codebase as large as Meta’s, one challenge is distinguishing strong catches (i.e., true-positive failures that reveal real bugs) from weak catches (i.e., tests that may be false positives).

It boils down to a specific question: For every proposed diff, how can we automatically generate tests that find the most severe bugs before they cause severe issues, and do so with a high true-positive rate and without impeding the velocity of our engineers?

To address this, we developed two tandem workflows:

  • An “intent-aware” workflow that infers the intention and risks of a code change and targets test generation toward likely failure points.
  • A “dodgy diff” workflow that treats every code change as if it were a mutant/bug and generates tests to expose its behavioral differences without reasoning about intent. It implicitly asserts that a diff is buggy (hence the term “dodgy”).

To filter false positives, we employed a traditional rule-based approach combined with an ensemble approach we call “LLM-as-Judge,” which aggregates judgements from several state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs, all tasked with classifying weak catches as likely true or false positives.

We also maintained human review, with an eye toward reducing review load. Our goal is to maintain the consistency of human labeling but reduce the likelihood of an engineer being brought in to review a weak catch.

How It Works

The entire system workflow happens in five stages:

Stage 1: Targeting and Triggering 

The system runs overnight on spare capacity and targets diffs submitted the previous day that are deemed “risky” using a mechanism similar to Diff Risk Score (DRS) and trained on previous code changes. This helps ensure test generation is focused on diffs that are most likely to contain severe regressions.

Stage 2: Two Diff-Aware Test-Generation Workflows

The dodgy diff workflow treats each diff as if it were a mutant and uses mutation-guided LLM-based test generation to produce tests that distinguish the diff’s behavior from its parent. The goal here is to maximize the pool of weak catches and with it the chances of finding a strong catch among them.

At the same time, the intent-aware workflow uses an LLM to infer the diff’s intention using the code changes, diff title, and summary. The LLM then describes the “risks”— the ways an attempt to implement the intent could produce errors. It then uses those risk descriptions to construct mutants — each representing a bug that could be introduced while implementing the inferred intent.

Tests are generated to kill each mutant (i.e., distinguish mutant behavior from parent).

Those tests are then run on the actual diff. Any that fail are harvested as weak catches.

Stage 3: LLM-as-Judge Ensemble (Automated Assessment)

Once weak catches are generated, the system must determine whether each is a false positive or actually a strong catch (true positive).

The LLM-as-Judge ensemble consists of a collection of LLMs that review:

  • The weak-catch test-case code.
  • The test-execution outcome (failure code, message, execution trace).
  • The code changes between parent and child (the diff).
  • The inferred diff intent.

Stage 4: Rule-Based Assessor (RubFake)

We complement LLM-as-Judge with a more traditional, rule-based approach called Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment (RubFake).

LLM-as-Judge has rich semantics, but its judgements are non-deterministic and challenging to verify. By contrast, RubFake provides verified, deterministic judgments. Working together, RubFake and LLM-as-Judge produce an overall ranking of weak-catch candidates, with those ranked sufficiently highly being worthy of further consideration.

Stage 5: Human-on-the-Loop (Engineer Reach-Out)

Based on the ranking from LLM-as-Judge and RubFake, the system then decides whether to reach out to human engineers.

Rather than a human-in-the-loop approach, where a human engineer reviews every output, we’ve reduced friction through a human-on-the-loop approach, where human engineers set criteria and review outcomes at an aggregate level rather than supervising every output.

The Impact of Catching JiTTests at Meta

With the testing system in place, our goal is to get engineers to engage with its results.

As of this writing, 589 engineers at Meta (64% of our outreach) have engaged with Catching JiTTests. These engineers have reported that Catching JiTTests surfaces genuinely actionable findings, with a 60% rate of true positives.

In the first half of 2026, Catching JiTTests played a key role in catching 74 serious (SEV) privacy bugs at the diff stage, before they landed in production and lowering the overall occurrence of privacy SEVs by 20% during that timeframe.

Why It Matters

Agentic software development is helping engineers and developers across the industry write, review, and ship code faster than ever before. But faster deployment means there’s also a need for faster testing. Every bug caught before it reaches production is one that end users never need to deal with. We’ve shown that LLMs can provide an additional safety layer capable of catching what traditional tests may miss, demonstrating that AI-generated testing can scale enough to reduce organizational risk. 

Catching JiTTests is a solution that is scalable, both technologically and socially. Combining these tests with a human-on-the-loop approach helps ensure that engineers rarely need to read test code and only need to confirm whether an observed behavioral change was intended.

The approach is generalizable: Engineers define success criteria early, let AI execute the testing, monitor the outcomes at an aggregate level, and intervene at the policy level rather than per item.

Read the Paper

Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” which was presented at FSE 2026 and featured at Product@Scale, details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests in Meta’s infrastructure.

posts.title: Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design
posts.summary: This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval. In…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Haiyu Lu, Shuo Gu, Yang Yang (Tony), Jingwen Ren, Tianchen Ji, Qing Zhang, Wentian Guo, Haocheng Wu, Siqi Zeng, Yunchen Pu, Liang Wang, Chonglin Sun
  • This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval.
  • In production, the system scores every eligible ad with near ranking-level model performance at retrieval scale and surfaces the top candidates at over one billion ads per second, a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models (i.e., a 100x lift compared to the 2024 Meta Andromeda system).
  • For advertisers, this means better performance automatically from the retrieval system matching ads across a larger candidate pool, within the same latency budget. Since 2025, Meta Andromeda has delivered a 2.4% increase in conversions on Facebook.

Meta Andromeda is Meta’s machine learning system for personalized ads retrieval, the first stage of the ads recommendation pipeline. Retrieval narrows a vast pool of eligible ads down to a small set of strong candidates in milliseconds; a later, more computationally expensive ranking stage then scores those survivors in fine detail. 

Historically, the deep modeling quality of the ranking stage has been too costly to apply at retrieval’s scale. Building on the retrieval foundation established with Andromeda’s 2024 launch on the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip, this post shares how co-designing the model, system, and hardware together brings near ranking-level performance to the retrieval scale.

Challenges and Opportunities in Scaling Retrieval

The 2024 Andromeda deployment reimplemented retrieval with an end-to-end optimized retrieval implementation from custom AI hardware with hierarchical indexing and GPU-native operators to a purpose-built ML model, growing model capacity by four orders of magnitude. Since then, generative AI creative tools have helped advertisers rapidly create hundreds of millions of new ads, growing Meta’s ads candidate pool to an unprecedented scale. 

Scoring such a large ad candidate pool with a more accurate model at a much higher system throughput requires fundamental technology breakthroughs in model quality, system architecture, and hardware utilization jointly. 

Higher Model Performance Requires a New Architecture 

Ads retrieval has an outsized ROI on incremental quality: Small improvements in retrieval model performance can drive large gains in advertiser value. The rapid expansion of our ads candidate pool makes optimizing for hardware capacity ROI an increasingly critical factor. The 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval models have established a highly effective foundation with their GPU-optimized deep neural network architecture. To keep improving retrieval performance at a sustainable compute cost at our current scale, however, we must move beyond that paradigm. This requires a fundamental architectural evolution to push model performance boundaries significantly without a proportional increase in costs.

New System Bottlenecks at Billion Scale 

The 2024 Meta Andromeda system evaluates at tens of millions of ads per second per GPU card. Meeting the new business demand requires a throughput at multi-billion ads evaluated per second per card in the system. At billions of ads per second throughput, the memory bandwidth of passing ad tensors through memory hierarchy becomes the new bottleneck. Intermediate tensors between GPU kernels account for terabytes per second of memory traffic, and shipping ads between local CPU hosts and remote hardware accelerators evaluating models saturates the network link. This requires a new system co-design that unifies these fragmented, distributed workloads into a single GPU pipeline.

Pushing Towards the Hardware Limits 

With retrieval running on GPU, the important optimization question is “How close are we to the hardware ceiling, and how much room remains for future model growth?” Answering this requires pushing each component of the retrieval pipeline to the limits of the current hardware generation, a challenge that motivated a joint collaboration with NVIDIA.

Each of these challenges drove a corresponding advance.

Unlocking Retrieval Performance Through Model-System Co-Design

Next-Gen Retrieval Model Architecture — Retrieval Mixture-of-Experts 

The latest iteration of Meta Andromeda introduces three synergistic architectural innovations that bring large language model (LLM)-inspired mixture-of-experts (MoE) into the retrieval (see Figure 1). With this highly expressive yet inference-efficient architecture, a new retrieval performance-efficiency Pareto frontier has been established: model performance approaches ranking-level in a typical retrieval-then-ranking system, at approximately 300x fewer inference-time FLOPs than the 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval model.

On the user modeling side, we transitioned from a single user tower to an ensemble of specialized user towers as experts. This captures diverse, time-evolving, and contextualized user interests by integrating a vast array of high-fidelity signals: sequential ad engagement events, user-cohort representations, LLM-derived semantic features, and cross-surface co-engagement signals.

In the candidate ads tower, we employ a joint encoding strategy that incorporates real-time serving context, ensuring that downstream interaction models receive context-aware representations.

In the interaction overarch layer, the interaction model evolved from dense neural networks into an MoE attention-based gating network that dynamically routes candidates across the most relevant user experts, delivering near-ranking-level performance at a fraction of the FLOPs.

A defining property of the new architecture is that its performance is co-designed with the underlying hardware execution model. Model inference throughput has reached over 10 billion ads per second on a single GH200 GPU, and this efficiency allows model capacity to grow further, through richer feature interactions, additional expert sub-networks, and deeper architectures, without a proportional increase in GPU cost. Each incremental model advancement translates into greater advertiser value.

Co-Designing the Model and System Onto a Single GPU Pipeline

The 2026 Meta Andromeda pushes the model-system co-design to the next level with two innovations — a single GPU kernel fusing both model and system workloads per user-ad interaction and a strategy to co-locate per user request logics with per user-ad GPU kernels in a single GPU box. To this end, a highly optimized and fully fused GPU pipeline is built to host the entire end-to-end Meta Andromeda workflow.

Fused Kernel

At a high level, Meta Andromeda’s inference time per user-ad workload is a compact sequence of operations across model execution and system logics — gathering embeddings, executing user-ad interaction models, and scoring. The ~300x FLOPs reduction in the retrieval MoE gating architecture creates the necessary headroom and is less resistant to fully fuse both model execution and non-model system workloads into a single GPU kernel, compared to the 2024 launch where only operations within the model execution were fused. Consequently, the fused kernel now runs at over 10 billion ads per second on a single GH200.

This matters because retrieval workloads are fundamentally memory-bandwidth bound. At billions of ads per second, even a small intermediate tensor per ad multiplies into terabytes per second of high bandwidth memory (HBM) traffic. The memory workload of these intermediate tensors, not arithmetic, becomes the dominant bottleneck in multi-kernel retrieval pipelines.

The fused kernel eliminates this bottleneck entirely. Rather than dispatching multiple small GPU kernels for model and system operations, it executes the entire per user-ad computation in one pass. Intermediate results stay in GPU registers and thread block shared memory and are never materialized to HBM, achieving high utilization of the GPU’s peak memory bandwidth rather than wasting it on redundant intermediate traffic. 

Co-Location Strategy

Measured in isolation, the per user-ad fused kernel runs at multi-billion ads per second on a single GPU. However, per-user request operations such as the index matching (i.e., enforcing advertisers’ targeting rules) and top-K selection run on separate local CPU hosts and communicate with the fused GPU kernel scoring service on remote accelerators through the network connection. At multi-billion ads per second throughput, this traffic alone saturates the network link, making the network bandwidth become the bottleneck rather than GPU compute.

The co-design response was to collapse the system architecture to match the model architecture: co-locate index matching, scoring, and top-K selection on the same GPU. Instead of shipping large candidate lists across hosts, the system sends a compact request payload — user features and a targeting query — to a single GPU server, which runs the entire retrieval pipeline locally and returns only the final top-K results. This reduces network traffic by ~100x and shifts the system back to a GPU-compute-bound regime.

Moving index matching onto the GPU is not straightforward. Ads index matching evaluates complex advertiser-defined targeting logic across tens of feature categories, and must support real-time index updates as ads are created, modified, or expired throughout the day. Supporting this on GPU required redesigning the index structure for GPU-parallel execution while preserving the full fidelity of production targeting semantics.

A Single GPU Pipeline for Meta Andromeda

Combining the aforementioned two innovations, the fully co-located single GPU pipeline processes over one billion ads per second on a single GPU server while scoring every eligible ad in the candidate pool. This is a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models, and as the next section describes, significant headroom remains.

GPU-Accelerated Retrieval: The Meta-NVIDIA Collaboration

With the production pipeline running at over one billion ads per second, a natural question follows: How close is the system to the ceiling of the current generation hardware, and how much headroom remains for future model growth? In early 2026, Meta and NVIDIA launched a joint collaboration to answer this question — systematically optimizing each component of the retrieval pipeline to push throughput toward hardware limits. NVIDIA contributed optimized GPU kernels, and Meta integrated and benchmarked the full pipeline. Each component achieved 2x to 5x speedup over the baseline.

Interaction Network (Retrieval MoE Gating Network)

The optimized gating kernel improved by 5.3x, from 2.4 billion to over 10 billion ads per second, reaching ~85% of the GPU’s peak HBM bandwidth. At this throughput, the execution time / latency of the gating mechanism is just as fast as what a simple dot-product scoring kernel achieves on the same hardware — while the model is substantially more expressive. This is the co-design validation: the additional model complexity is essentially free on Tensor Core hardware. INT8 quantization achieved a further up to 2x throughput increase over the optimized FP16 kernels, with accuracy on par with 16-bit precision.

Index Matching

Through targeted GPU kernel optimizations, index matching throughput improved over 2x, reaching over 100 billion ads per second — an order of magnitude higher than the scoring network. This headroom means index matching can be re-run across multiple retrieval pathways without becoming a bottleneck.

End-to-End GPU Pipeline

Beyond individual kernels, the collaboration profiled the full retrieval flow and identified that data movement between pipeline components — not computation — accounted for a significant fraction of end-to-end latency. By co-designing data layouts across index matching and scoring to eliminate unnecessary indirection, the team removed this overhead. With all optimizations applied, the full pipeline benchmarks at multiple times the current production throughput on a single GPU server, with further gains expected as additional optimizations integrate into production.

Continuing Work on Next-Generation NVIDIA Platforms

Building on the Hopper results above, we are extending our optimization and co-design work to Grace Blackwell. Here, we are focusing on platform design optimizations that enable different CPU-to-GPU compute ratios, which our work so far suggests is an important factor for Andromeda-like workloads. We are evaluating how sensitive end-to-end application performance is to these ratios, using Grace-class CPU performance and Blackwell-class GPU performance for their respective parts of the workload.

More broadly, we are exploring how these findings extend to the next platform generation, where greater flexibility in CPU+GPU execution, resource ratios, and coupling could bring more of these architectural improvements to bear on Andromeda-like workloads.

These results confirm that the co-designed retrieval pipeline is not yet at its ceiling. With quantization unlocking further scoring throughput and index matching operating at an order of magnitude above the scoring network, the architecture is positioned to absorb significantly more model complexity — deeper interaction networks, richer feature spaces, and additional retrieval pathways — without proportional infrastructure growth.

The Path Forward for Ads Retrieval

The advances described here follow a single principle: The largest gains come from designing model, system, and hardware as one integrated stack, rather than optimizing each in isolation. The retrieval MoE gating architecture delivers near-ranking-level expressiveness at no additional serving cost. Fusing the entire retrieval pipeline onto a single GPU eliminates network and memory bottlenecks. And pushing the pipeline towards its hardware ceiling confirms substantial headroom remains.

Looking ahead, the co-design principle that drove these results applies equally to next-generation model architectures and hardware platforms, with the demonstrated headroom enabling continued scaling without proportional infrastructure growth.

For people who use Meta’s products, this translates directly into better ads that are more relevant to them, delivered within the same latency budget. For advertisers, it means better customer matches and more conversions. For Meta, it means increased business from advertisers and lower costs, as each GPU now evaluates more ads per second. As the volume of eligible ads continues to grow, driven by Advantage+ automation and generative AI creative tools, Meta Andromeda’s co-designed architecture scales to meet it.

posts.title: How the fastest-growing enterprises on Stripe scale globally
posts.summary: Despite slower global economic growth and greater geopolitical fragmentation, the fastest-growing enterprises continue to look beyond their home markets and are investing in tools and workflows that make expansion…
posts.content:
We analyzed more than 100 of the fastest-growing enterprises on Stripe and found that they processed their first cross-border transaction on Stripe 24x faster than the enterprise baseline. Despite slower global economic growth and greater geopolitical fragmentation, these enterprises continue to look beyond their home markets—and are investing in tools and workflows that make expansion faster and more repeatable.

To identify the fastest-growing enterprises on Stripe, we used a composite score that measures month-over-month payment volume growth, year-over-year performance, and recent momentum since 2025. We compared this cohort—which spans more than 10 industries across financial services, manufacturing, retail, technology, and others—against a broader set of more than 1,000 enterprises of a similar scale. We define an enterprise as an organization that has been active on Stripe for at least six months and that meets our internal benchmarks, including employee size and revenue.

Here’s what we learned about where enterprises find international demand, how they adapt payments to local preferences, and how they manage the accompanying fraud risk of expanding into new markets.

The fastest-growing enterprises have an outsized presence in emerging markets

Mature economies remain important sources of customer spending, but more of the world’s economic growth is expected to come from emerging economies. These markets are projected to grow by around 4% in 2026, compared to 1.5% for mature economies. And by 2035, emerging markets are expected to account for 65% of global economic growth. 

Surprisingly, the fastest-growing companies on Stripe already see outsized spend in emerging global markets. Compared with the enterprise baseline, they achieved 1.6x the share of cross-border payment volume in Brazil, India, and Argentina. 

They also reach customers across a wider range of markets. During its first year on Stripe, the median fastest-growing enterprise processed payments from customers in 25 countries—more than six times as many as the enterprise baseline. 

This suggests that a geographically diverse approach to expansion can help increase growth. Rather than following the traditional approach of sequential country-by-country expansion or a gradual test-and-learn approach, the fast-growing cohort expands to many mature and emerging markets in parallel.

The fastest-growing enterprises add more ways to pay with less work

Serving customers across so many countries means accommodating a wide range of payment preferences. A checkout that offers only one payment method—or omits the methods customers use locally—can reduce conversion by up to 15%. 

The fastest-growing enterprises are investing in a more localized payment experience. The median enterprise from the cohort offers 2x more local payment methods than the enterprise baseline. 

We also saw a pattern in how these enterprises manage their wider range of payment options. Adding a new payment method traditionally requires businesses to integrate, configure, and test it, then maintain it over time. Enterprises in the cohort are shortening that process, making it easier to add payment options as customer preferences evolve. 

For example, Facile.it—a price comparison service in Italy and a member of the fast-growing cohort—uses Stripe Checkout to add new payment methods in 80% less time than its legacy system required. 

Anthropic, a member of the cohort, also used Stripe Checkout to improve its checkout flow and offer a wider range of payment methods. It allowed Anthropic to easily offer payment options, such as credit cards, digital wallets like Apple Pay and Cash App Pay, and local payment methods that would appeal to the company’s increasingly international user base.

These examples show how the right infrastructure can help enterprises support rapid international growth without rebuilding their checkout for every new payment method or market.

The fastest-growing enterprises take a more targeted approach to fraud rules

Broader international reach can expose businesses to a wider variety of fraud patterns, which often differ by region and payment method. That risk exposure showed up in our analysis. In the first half of 2026, the fastest-growing enterprises saw an attempted fraud rate nearly 1.8x higher than the enterprise baseline. 

To help combat this fraud, more than half have implemented at least one custom fraud rule within Stripe Radar, our AI-powered fraud prevention product. This makes them more likely than the enterprise baseline to customize their fraud controls.

However, if we only analyze enterprises that use custom rules, the fastest-growing cohort maintains fewer rules per business than the baseline. This suggests a more deliberate approach to fraud management, with fast-growing enterprises relying on Radar’s default fraud models and adding targeted custom rules only where needed—rather than building extensive customized rule sets. 

How Stripe can help 

Enterprises use Stripe to expand into new markets and operate with less complexity. Stripe’s global selling solution brings together localized checkout, payments performance, money movement, tax compliance, and fraud prevention into one platform, so you can adapt to local customer preferences and regional risks for every new market.

Reach customers in more markets

  • Quickly launch a localized, optimized checkout experience across web and mobile with Stripe Checkout, including built-in support for 195+ markets, 135+ currencies, and 34 languages.
  • Automatically localize prices in 150+ markets, increasing cross-border revenue by an average of 17.8% with Adaptive Pricing.
  • Expand your customer base by offering relevant global and local payment methods, with built-in support for one-time payments, stablecoins, subscriptions, AI-powered fraud detection, localized currency presentment, and cross-border payments—all through a single integration. 
  • Launch in new markets faster without setting up local entities using Stripe Managed Payments, Stripe’s merchant of record solution that simplifies global selling.

Manage risk as you expand globally

  • Intelligently apply authentication to riskier transactions and as required by local regulations with adaptive 3DS, reducing fraud without adding unnecessary friction for legitimate customers.
  • Reduce fraud across supported payment volume globally, including bank debits, stablecoin payments, digital wallets, real-time payments, and cash vouchers, with Radar.

Learn more about how Stripe can help you go global faster, or contact us.

posts.title: Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI
posts.summary: By Praneeth Yenugutala , Victor Dusa , Anastasia Samoilova , Megan Ren , Justin Wei , Marcelo Mayworm At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems…
posts.content:
PensiveMaestroOrchestrationData EngineeringData ScienceNetflix Technology Blog14 min read·Oct 26, 2026

--

By Praneeth Yenugutala, Victor Dusa, Anastasia Samoilova, Megan Ren, Justin Wei, Marcelo Mayworm

At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines.

Our first answer to that problem was Pensive, an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro. It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic.

Rules work well for known patterns, but their coverage grows only when someone recognizes a new failure mode, understands the logs, writes a rule, and keeps it current as engines and log formats change. Over one three-month period, Pensive processed roughly seven million job-failure classifications, yet about half fell into the unknown bucket. We needed a way to expand coverage without giving up the deterministic parts of Pensive that already worked.

To solve this ambiguous and complex problem at Netflix scale, we invested in Pensive AI to add AI-assisted error extractions and focused diagnosis and remediation guidance to our data and ML practitioners. The goal was not simply to place a model in front of a large collection of logs. We needed bounded extraction, predictable evaluation inputs, responsive product behavior, and quality checks that could follow the system from local development through production. Those requirements shaped every layer of the design, which we will discuss in this blog. Pensive AI wraps AI around deterministic processes, which gives broader coverage, low latency, controlled AI costs, and easier maintenance across the software development lifecycle. Building on this foundation, we plan to explore more agentic debugging experiences, as Part 6 describes.

Early results are encouraging. AI error extraction now covers 100% of failures, including the failures that legacy Pensive classified as unknown. Failed step attempts where no one used Pensive AI averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions than attempts where someone did (an observational comparison, not a causal claim).

The two paths complement each other. Error extraction improves an existing capability and is always on. It lets the user of a failed Maestro workload quickly check the parts of the logs that may point to an immediate root cause. It has low latency and low cost, and it can help in a large share of cases. On-demand debugging enables a new capability. It looks at symptoms across the logs and adds the LLM’s own knowledge and reasoning for a deeper analysis, at slightly higher latency and cost. Extraction gives a fast first look at every failure, and on-demand debugging triggered by the user goes deeper when that first look is not enough.

Part 1: Finding the useful errors

Legacy Pensive rules are precise, but each one captures a particular log shape. A simplified rule looks like this:

- name: SparkContainerOOM
logSource: GENIE_STDERR
restartable: false
regex: "Container.*is running beyond physical memory limits.*Killing container"
summary: Spark AM container runs out of memory

With Pensive AI, we wanted to find useful errors that had no corresponding rule and adapt more easily when familiar errors changed shape after a platform upgrade. Data Portal (our UI for data pipelines) surfaces these extracted errors when available and links back to the source logs, giving practitioners a focused starting point for triage. That raises a question: how can we ask a model to identify an error without asking it to repeat a long stack trace token by token?

Producing output tokens is much slower than reading input tokens. A direct transcription approach would make long errors expensive and slow. Instead, Pensive numbers the lines of each log and gives the model a sequence of {lineNumber, text} records. The model identifies the first and last lines of the error span, and Pensive reconstructs the selected text from its own log copy, leading to lower cost and better latency. This way, the model always returns two integers (start and end line number), whether the selected logs span a few lines or hundreds of lines. The displayed content comes directly from the original log, reducing hallucinations. The model can still choose the wrong range, which is why extraction quality remains an integral measurement for our AI evals, as we will discuss later.

For orchestrated workflows, “Pensive AI Error Extraction” runs automatically whenever a step fails. A step attempt is one execution of a step within a Maestro workflow. Maestro already calls Pensive for a regex-derived error and restartability classification, so AI extraction runs in the same request and returns its results alongside the established fields. The overall Pensive response must return within Maestro’s hard 90-second post-processing timeout for a failed step attempt.

That deadline shaped the extraction path. Pensive extracts errors from the logs in parallel to reduce latency, and the per-log calls share one deadline set well inside Maestro’s timeout limit. A per-log extraction call that misses the deadline is excluded from the result, allowing the overall request to return on time.

The data contract between Pensive AI and the various consumers needed the same care. The legacy data model contained one flattened error string; AI extraction instead returns a list of errors, one for each log source, with deep links back to the originating logs. Changing the old field in place would have broken existing clients. We introduced the new data model beside the legacy non-AI error extraction data model and continued producing both. Data Portal, our user interface for monitoring and observing data pipelines, preferred AI errors when available and fell back to the legacy value when they were not during the rollout. That allowed a gradual rollout and ensured that historical failures still display an error, since we chose not to backfill the old data due to log retention issues.

The migration is still in progress today. The Data Portal UI surface used for failed Maestro steps reads the new AI extracted error field today, while the query editor (for editing and running SQL), Workbench notebooks (managed compute platform and UI to edit and run jupyter based notebooks) and some slack clients calling Pensive still use the legacy error extraction path. Each client needs a compatible schema change before it can consume the new data. Keeping both fields populated lets teams adopt the new behavior at their own pace without forcing a coordinated cutover as we continue evolving Pensive AI.

Part 2: Full failure diagnosis and the product experience

Beyond error extraction, we built Pensive AI Debugging, a tool that analyzes failed step attempts and provides root-cause analysis and suggested remediations. It is available through programmatic APIs, MCP, and the product UI (Data Portal), all backed by a common entry point across the Netflix Data Platform. This shared model supports consistent behavior and custom product experiences.

This diagnosis still has to arrive quickly and remain consistent across investigations. A debugging response can take tens of seconds or a minute to generate, compared with a few seconds for error extraction. We run full AI-based debugging on demand instead of automatically, which keeps costs under control because most failed steps are never opened. We treat the failed step attempt, not the person who triggered it, as the unit of work, so everyone investigating the same failed attempt sees the same diagnosis.

That choice gives us a stable unit of work for caching. We cache each debugging response by step attempt. A second request becomes a key-value read instead of another AI inference call. The cache also prevents duplicate work, reducing latency and lowering costs further. This also means that a debugging generated in the Data Portal is cached and immediately retrieved for the MCP path instead of incurring another AI inference call. A conditional write creates an in-progress record, one caller starts generation, and other callers wait for the shared result to avoid conflicts when concurrent requests come in for the same step attempt failure. If generation remains in progress past an abandonment timeout, Pensive treats the record as abandoned and reclaims it. Completed responses expire after 90 days to help control costs and optimize storage because debugging requests for much older workloads are uncommon.

Pensive AI supports multiple ways to initiate debugging responses. A caller can (1) read a cached response, (2) generate one if no cache entry exists, or (3) regenerate and overwrite an existing response. Those semantics support the product UI, programmatic access, and the evaluation harness while keeping the response associated with a single immutable workload failure.

For users, the most important behavior is that a long-running answer feels alive. Pensive streams the response as it is produced. The service emits server-sent events, and the GraphQL layer republishes them as a WebSocket subscription for the Data Portal client.

Get Netflix Technology Blog’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Remember me for faster sign in

Each event carries the complete response generated so far. That duplicates a small amount of text, but it keeps the client simple: it does not need a replay buffer or token reassembly logic, and the next event corrects the display after a dropped or late event. Generation is independent of the connection that requested it. A disconnect does not cancel the work, and the final answer still reaches the cache. A hard reload can show a loading state and poll for the completed result. Within the single-page application backing the Data Portal UI, active streams are maintained independently of view and component lifecycle, so navigation does not interrupt a response in progress.

Part 3: Measuring and improving the behavior we want

LLM-assisted systems need more than a demo or a few working examples. Before shipping in production, we need confidence in both error extraction and debugging guidance, and we need to know that we have not regressed on failures that legacy Pensive already handled. We built separate evaluation frameworks focused on the two distinct jobs.

Building labeled data is often the expensive part of evaluation. For error extraction, legacy Pensive’s hand-written rules provide reference labels for failures they recognize. They also serve as excellent ground truth in most cases. We run those rules over production logs and compare their extracted spans with Pensive AI’s output. This gives us a reliable regression set without relabeling every example by hand, though it is not an absolute ground truth (since our human-built rules could also have been stale). For now, we keep these rules frozen as a label source. This lets us continue to build comparison evals and run them on top of the existing system.

Stable inputs are essential for repeatable evaluation experiments where we A/B test new models/configurations or context injections to improve response quality. The logs Pensive AI uses can expire after as few as seven days or as many as 30 days. Production Pensive AI requests archive fetched logs to S3 object storage asynchronously during workload execution time so the upload is not on the user-facing critical path. Uploads do not overwrite an existing object, preserving the exact snapshot used to create an evaluation case. Evals use those archived logs, so score changes remain attributable to the system under test. The archive also prevents parallel experiments from overloading the source systems and lets us run them without affecting production. Cached S3 log inputs further reduce costs when running evaluations.

Concretely, we measure four complementary signals for error extraction:

  • Inclusion: An LLM judge compares the legacy Pensive error for a failure with the errors Pensive AI extracted and determines whether the known error is still represented, even when wording differs.
  • Precision: A second judge sees only the extracted AI errors and evaluates whether each is meaningful and actionable on its own.
  • Repeated noise: A script looks across the whole dataset for lines that recur too often. A generic status line may look harmless in one answer but become distracting if it appears in a large share of failures. Lines appearing in more than about 30% of workflows are candidates for explicit exclusion. In practice, the exclusion list has only three lines, each of which otherwise appeared in nearly every extracted error.
