  • Latency: We record the latency of every extraction call. Quality scores alone cannot reveal when an apparent improvement requires too much additional work, which often correlates with increased AI costs.

This combination gives us an actionable feedback loop. Prompt changes can reduce general noise, while the dataset-level view exposes the stubborn boilerplate that prompt changes do not eliminate. Existing rules act as a regression floor, and archived logs give us a repeatable way to compare changes. At Pensive AI’s scale, model and system choices must satisfy quality, latency, maintainability and cost constraints together.

To seed the debugging ground-truth dataset for evaluation, we mine internal engineering-support Slack threads and use an LLM to identify threads that link to an orchestrated workflow, describe a resolved problem, and match the class of issue Pensive AI handles. A second model synthesizes a reference debugging response from the relevant discussion. Paired with logs from that workflow failure, it becomes a concrete evaluation row in our evals dataset. This approach works only retrospectively, because Pensive AI in production aims to provide debugging guidance before such a Slack discussion happens.

We also made the debugging generation process visible. Tracing follows the request through Pensive, with child spans for each log fetch and extraction tool call. Our tracing backend based on Braintrust brings the prompt, completion, tool calls, and latency into a single view. During early product development, that visibility helped us inspect low-performing debugging responses in context instead of guessing which input or operation caused them. Tracing helped us improve the responses and fill context gaps even before we had comprehensive evals. In production, the API and UI return the trace identifier with the response, so feedback can lead directly to the trace for in-depth analysis.

Part 4: Keeping quality in the release path

Evaluation is not only for experiments with LLM orchestration, models, prompts, or context changes. Changes to log selection, trimming logic, or a source system can change what the model sees and therefore change extraction quality. We use the same evaluation harness and evaluators throughout local development and Pensive AI deployment so those effects are visible before users encounter them.

posts.title: Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing
posts.summary: Serdar Cellat , Yuchen Xie , Bernadette Marcu , Blaid Burgess , Cody Jarrett , Carlos Pereira , Qing Shi , Samuel Carvajal , Manuel Pamplona , Dorothy Jung , Feiko Ritsema , Benjamin Klein , Alex Woo , Eugene Lok , Anna…
posts.content:
Netflix Technology Blog4 min read·Oct 26, 2026

--

Serdar Cellat, Yuchen Xie, Bernadette Marcu, Blaid Burgess, Cody Jarrett, Carlos Pereira, Qing Shi, Samuel Carvajal, Manuel Pamplona, Dorothy Jung, Feiko Ritsema, Benjamin Klein, Alex Woo, Eugene Lok, Anna Pulido, Rebecka Swe, Sanford Holsapple, Ranjith Kumar Shetty

Introduction

At Netflix, a crucial part of our mission is ensuring our content looks stunning on any device. Vertical formats are increasingly important for Netflix, as we have 1.2B followers across our social media accounts, and have recently rolled out Clips, our vertical video feed in the Netflix mobile app. Traditionally, creating vertical assets meant editors and producers manually reframed horizontal videos in editing tools, a process that doesn’t scale as our catalog and use cases grow. To support both our in‑app feed and external marketing campaigns at scale, we built an automated multi‑ratio video cropping system, tightly integrated into our internal production tools, that can generate high‑quality vertical and other aspect‑ratio variants with minimal manual effort.

Our Video Resizing Approach

Converting cinematic 16:9 footage into mobile‑friendly aspect ratios takes more than a simple center crop. Filmmaking often involves dynamic character blocking and complex camera movement. We need an intelligent “virtual camera” that can follow the key action, respond to how each scene is composed, and produce crops that feel as intentional as the original shot.

Get Netflix Technology Blog’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Remember me for faster sign in

We address this challenge by framing video resizing as a tracking and temporal optimization problem. Our pipeline processes each asset in three main stages, designed to produce 9:16, 4:5, and 1:1 crops in a single pass, without incurring additional computational overhead.

Shot Detection and Splitting

First, we segment the video into atomic shots using a neural‑network–based shot boundary detector. In many cases, shots contain multiple characters conversing on opposite sides of the frame. To better handle these scenarios, we use an Active Speaker Detection based approach to logically split a single continuous shot into multiple sub‑shots. This allows our virtual camera to cut and re-focus on different speakers as the conversation flows. Our Active Speaker Detection leverages an internal face detector and LipFlap to reliably identify active speakers in both live‑action and animated titles.

Focus Region Discovery

Once shots and sub‑shots are defined, we identify the most important region in each frame. We combine face detections with visual saliency maps to filter and prioritize the faces that should be in focus. In scenes with multiple characters, we further rank faces using signals such as active speaker status and relative size. Our model aggregates these cues with shot‑level content understanding to establish a continuous “focus region” for the virtual camera.

Temporal Reframing

Once we’ve established the focus region, the next challenge is deciding how the crop should move over time. Tracking the focus region on a strict frame-by-frame basis would produce a shaky, distracting viewing experience, so we apply a set of heuristics that consider how the focus region moves over the course of a shot. When its displacement is small, we lock a static crop window that consistently covers the relevant area. When there is significant motion, we compute a dynamic tracking window and smooth its path so that any panning feels intentional and cinematic.

Tooling and Workflow Integration

We integrated the resizing algorithm directly into our internal Clips tool, so editors and producers can access it as part of their existing workflow. The interface enables them to automatically generate multiple aspect‑ratio versions of a clip with smart reframing. A unified in‑app module provides intuitive shot‑reframing controls, allowing users to review the algorithm’s crops, and quickly make targeted adjustments where needed.

For more complex shots or custom campaigns, producers can export the resizing parameters as XML and load them directly into external timeline editors such as Adobe Premiere. This allows agencies and external partners to start from the algorithm’s framing decisions instead of recreating crops manually or relying on tools like Premiere’s Auto Reframe. In our internal test, our resizing algorithm outperforms Auto Reframe on a curated evaluation set, so the XML export effectively brings those higher‑quality crops into external workflows. By bringing automated resizing and manual refinement into a single place, this pipeline significantly reduces production time and manual effort while preserving creative control.

Conclusion

Our work on multi-ratio video resizing is one step in a broader effort to make content creation more scalable, without compromising creative intent. By pairing algorithm-driven reframing with editor-friendly tools, we’ve reduced the time teams spend on repetitive resizing tasks and unlocked faster experimentation across mobile feeds and marketing campaigns. As we continue to broaden these capabilities to new formats and workflows, our goal remains the same: to give creatives more time to tell great stories, and to deliver a consistently high-quality viewing experience for our members and fans.

posts.title: Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
posts.summary: By Roberto Perez Alcolea , Java Platform Team Quasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decision At Netflix, shared Java…
posts.content:
JavaSoftware EngineeringApi DesignDeveloper ToolsCode AnalysisNetflix Technology Blog9 min read·Oct 23, 2026

--

By Roberto Perez Alcolea, Java Platform Team

At Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed.

The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it.

Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.

Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next:

  • Does any consumer still call this method?
  • Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations?
  • Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact?
  • Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign?

At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds.

Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally.

We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions:

  1. What changed in the library’s public API?
  2. Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed?

The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing.

From API Changes to Consumer Impact

Existing techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive.

Quasar builds on SCIP, an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently.

On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change.

During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings through its REST and GraphQL APIs and MCP server; follow-up usage queries provide dependency-version breakdowns and source locations. A separate compatibility-impact assessment can also follow implementations and their callers when a producer supplies a changed JVM symbol.

Consider this simplified API change:

public interface Client {
- Result getLegacyValue(Request request);
+ Result getValue(Request request, Options options);
}

For a detailed compatibility-impact assessment of this removal, a producer-side tool supplies the old method descriptor. Quasar constructs its canonical symbol identity. This abridged excerpt from the direct-reference portion of Quasar’s Amazon Athena query shows the essential match:

SELECT c.change_id, 'DIRECT_REFERENCE' AS evidence_kind,
       r.scm_type, r.org, r.repo, r.dep_version, r.file_path
FROM requested_changes c
JOIN quasar.symbol_refs r
  ON r.symbol_canonical = c.target_canonical

requested_changes contains the API changes submitted by the producer. The SQL excerpt finds repositories that call the removed method. Quasar also checks implementations and calls through them, so it can count each affected repository once. It returns sample dependency versions and file locations to help investigate the result.

For the Client change, this tells the producer which repositories still use getLegacyValue, which versions they use, and where some of those calls occur. That helps the producer decide whether to coordinate a migration before removing the method.

Bringing the Analysis Before Release

Version-to-version comparison is valuable when planning an upgrade or writing a migration guide. Producers benefit even more when feedback arrives during code review.

For pull-request analysis, Quasar stores API definition snapshots keyed by commit. Given a base and head commit, it classifies symbols as added, removed, or signature-modified. Removals and modifications then become candidates for consumer-impact analysis.

Get Netflix Technology Blog’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Remember me for faster sign in

An incompatible change is not automatically a high-risk change. Quasar reports the observed impact so the producer can decide what to do; it does not enforce a release policy. “No references observed” means only that Quasar found none in the indexed population. Reflection, configuration, dynamic loading, stale branches, or incomplete indexing can hide consumers. The result needs to show whether the requested commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated.

Pull-request review requires indexed snapshots for the exact base and head commits. If either is unavailable, Quasar reports that it cannot compare them; it does not substitute a default-branch snapshot. This keeps a missing comparison from looking like a clean API diff.

Return to our Client change. This illustrative report brings together signals available through Quasar's API comparison, consumer-usage queries, and library-level criticality. It is not a literal response from one API:

{
  "change": "REMOVED",
  "symbol": "Client#getLegacyValue(Request)",
  "affectedRepositories": 137,
  "versionDistribution": [
    { "version": "4.2.1", "repositories": 86 },
    { "version": "4.1.7", "repositories": 38 },
    { "version": "3.9.4", "repositories": 13 }
  ],
  "sampleConsumerLocations": [
    {
      "repository": "checkout-service",
      "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/checkout/CheckoutClient.java",
      "lines": [84, 129]
    },
    {
      "repository": "client-wrapper",
      "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/client/ClientAdapter.java",
      "lines": [57]
    }
  ],
  "libraryCriticality": {
    "tier": 1,
    "basis": "highest-tier downstream application"
  },
  "comparison": {
    "baseShaFound": true,
    "headShaFound": true
  }
}

The repository count is symbol-specific: in this example, 137 indexed repositories refer to the removed method. The version distribution reveals a dominant cohort on 4.2.1 and a smaller long tail still on 3.9.4. A producer can inspect affected repositories and retrieve indexed file paths, with line numbers where the index provides them. The JSON shows only two sample locations to keep the example readable. The filePath and lines shape mirrors Quasar's query contract. The tier is broader context about the library, inherited from its highest-criticality downstream application; it does not imply that all 137 callers are Tier 1.

Together, those signals change the producer’s plan. Instead of merging the removal and waiting for failures, the producer can retain and deprecate the old method, publish a migration path, coordinate a broader migration, and track the long-tail versions before removal. File paths and available line numbers turn that scope into a concrete work list for engineers or coding agents. The same API diff paired with weak or stale evidence would lead to a different action: refresh the indexes before deciding. The value is not merely detecting the removal; it is choosing a proportionate next step.

A Polyglot Foundation with SCIP

The shared SCIP format also lets Quasar index several language ecosystems. Each language indexer resolves its own code, while Quasar can use the resulting symbol identities to find references across repositories.

Conceptually, client-lib indexes Client#getLegacyValue(Request) as a definition, while checkout-service indexes a reference to the same symbol. Quasar can then connect the library API to its consumer across repositories.

Relationships are especially useful when generated code separates the API a producer owns from the symbols consumers invoke. For example, Quasar can trace a Protobuf definition through its generated Java members to the repositories that use them, even when consumer code never names the .proto element.

SCIP records symbols and their references; it does not determine whether an API change violates an ecosystem’s compatibility rules. Today, Quasar compares indexed JVM and Protobuf API definitions and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java to find affected repositories. A separate JVM compatibility-impact path uses breaks identified by a producer-side tool to query affected repositories. Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust support usage queries, but Quasar does not yet assess their breaking API changes.

Moving Risk Assessment Earlier

Today, Quasar surfaces API-change findings on pull requests, including observed consumer counts and confidence. Producers can use its other queries to inspect dependency versions and source locations, with library criticality as broader context. Together, those signals support a decision before merge.

We want to move that context earlier. An agent writing library code should recognize when it is changing a public symbol and consult Quasar before the change becomes a pull request. Quasar’s APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration provide an access path, but access alone does not create awareness. The coding workflow must also recognize public API edits so the agent knows when to query impact and when to involve the producer.

Earlier guidance will not replace pull-request analysis. The PR assessment will still verify the concrete diff and catch changes that were not recognized during coding. Coverage, freshness, ambiguity, unsupported platforms, and truncation must travel through both checks in machine-readable form. An agent should not turn “no observed usages in the available index” into “safe to remove.”

Today, agents can query Quasar through MCP when prompted. We are working toward making that context part of the coding workflow, then using identified call sites to prepare migration changes. Quasar supplies semantic evidence, an agent reduces migration toil, and the library producer remains responsible for API and release decisions.

What We Learned

Building this workflow led us to four practical lessons.

  • Separate compatibility from reach. A removed method can break the API contract even when Quasar finds no callers. A list of affected repositories and their library versions shows the migration work ahead. Producers need both signals to choose a release path.
  • Make the evidence inspectable. A repository count is more useful with sample call sites and a version breakdown. The result also needs to show which commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated. Otherwise, “no usage found” can be mistaken for proof that nobody is affected.
  • Keep usage and compatibility separate across languages. SCIP lets Quasar find symbol references in several ecosystems. Deciding whether an API change is breaking requires compatibility rules or a trusted producer-side signal for that ecosystem.
  • Bring evidence to the producer while choices are open. Pull-request findings can prompt a producer to retain an API, publish a migration path, or coordinate consumers before merge. Moving the same evidence into the coding workflow could shape the edit earlier. After release, it still helps locate consumers that need to migrate.

Today, Quasar indexes JVM, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust code for cross-repository usage analysis. It compares JVM APIs and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java. Producers can review change findings through Quasar’s REST and GraphQL APIs or its MCP server, then investigate affected repositories and call sites. We are extending this foundation toward more ecosystem-specific compatibility checks, deeper code-review integration, and agent-assisted consumer migrations that keep release approval with the producer.

Quasar is internal to Netflix, but the pattern is portable: index code semantically, retain API definitions, compare them at the point of change, query affected consumers, and report the quality of the evidence. Library producers need more than a compatibility verdict. They need to know who may be affected and have enough time to act before release.

A huge thank you to the Java Platform team at Netflix. Their expertise, collaboration, and support made this work possible

Related Talks

  • From Lag to Lightning: Transforming Dependency Update Timelines explores how Netflix shortened dependency-update timelines.
  • Netflix’s Journey to Confident Automated Code Changes discusses building confidence in automated changes at scale.

posts.title: Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform
posts.summary: Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in…
posts.content:
ContainersKubernetesIsolationCompute PlatformVirtual MachineNetflix Technology Blog26 min read·Oct 22, 2026

--

Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker

You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years.

For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host.

We will walk through why shared-kernel isolation runs out of road for certain workloads, how we measure isolation rather than asserting it, the options we weighed (microVMs, gVisor, EC2, and more shared-kernel tuning) and why a dedicated VM inside Titus won, how the mode is built on the Titus federation layer and autoscaling, and what we have seen along three axes: isolation, fleet efficiency, and the operational cost of keeping the fleet patched.

The cost of good neighbors

Multi-tenancy is a tradeoff. Packing many containers onto a large bare-metal instance keeps utilization high, but it also means those containers share a single Linux kernel and the underlying hardware. Titus isolates them with the tools the kernel provides: cgroups cap CPU, memory, and disk; namespaces give each container its own view of the system; seccomp and AppArmor restrict the system calls a container can make; the Completely Fair Scheduler divides CPU time; the iocost controller meters disk IO; and traffic shaping meters each container’s slice of the network. Each container also gets its own identity, IAM role, and security groups, so tenants are isolated for security and resource management.

These mechanisms provide isolation for what the kernel can partition. They cannot fully partition what is shared in hardware. A group of cores shares a last-level cache and a path to memory, so a container that suddenly pulls a lot of data from RAM evicts a neighbor’s cache lines and slows it down, even when both stay inside their CPU limits. There is no cgroup for memory bandwidth or cache residency, as there is for CPU shares. The interference is real, it is hardware, and it does not show up as either container exceeding its quota.

A noisy neighbor and a co-located app each stay within their cgroup CPU and memory limits, but both draw on a shared last-level cache and memory bandwidth that lack cgroup fences. The noisy neighbor takes most of it, so the co-located app stalls and its tail latency rises even though no one exceeded a quota.

We have written about this before. Predictive CPU isolation of containers at Netflix moved some placement decisions out of the kernel and into a service that forecasts each container’s CPU demand and re-pins containers to cores to reduce cache interference, formulated as a combinatorial optimization solved every minute. Noisy Neighbor Detection with eBPF instruments the kernel scheduler to surface per-container run-queue latency, so we can see a victim being starved in close to real time. And Mount Mayhem traced container-startup slowness to a global kernel lock amplified by modern CPU cache topology. Each of these raised the floor for everyone on the platform, and we are continuing that work.

A decade of shared-kernel isolation, at Netflix and across the industry, has not made co-tenancy invisible, because a noisy neighbor is not one problem but a family of them. Almost every physical resource a host shares is its own axis of interference, and a cgroup can fence very few of them:

  • CPU performance indeterminacy. Co-located threads contend for the run queue, so scheduling latency rises even while a container remains within its CPU quota. Separately, a neighbor with a large working set evicts a tenant’s last-level cache lines and saturates memory bandwidth, neither of which a CPU share can partition.
  • Network bandwidth and packets per second. Per-container shaping competes for link bandwidth, and receives processing runs in softirq context, charging one container’s packet work to whatever CPU a neighbor is running on. A flood of small packets exhausts a core’s softirq budget long before any bandwidth cap is reached.
  • Storage bandwidth and IOPS. A neighbor saturating a device’s queue serializes everyone’s I/O, and on cloud block storage, the per-volume and per-instance throughput ceilings are a shared budget in their own right.
  • Long tail. Page-cache reclaim, NUMA and cross-socket interconnect traffic, TLB-shootdown interrupts, PCIe and GPU contention, package-level power and thermal throttling, and contention on kernel global locks (the class of problem behind Mount Mayhem) each degrade neighbors in their own way.

What unites them is that they are physical, shared, and below the level a quota can reach. A platform can cap how much CPU time or memory a container is granted; it cannot hand each tenant its own slice of the memory bus, its own softirq budget, or its own portion of the last-level cache.

Of these, the network dimension has bitten hardest in our experience. Per-container bandwidth shaping uses a hierarchical token bucket (HTB) queueing discipline that serializes traffic with a global lock to account for each container’s bytes and packets. Under a flood of small packets from a single container, contention for that lock can burn kernel CPU and starve co-located containers of the time they need to process their own traffic, resulting in TCP retransmits and tail-latency spikes on services that did nothing wrong. The mechanism meant to prevent noisy neighbors becomes one.

The workloads most exposed to this are stateful, high-throughput streaming jobs: real-time data pipelines and stream processors that continuously move large volumes of data and maintain in-memory state. When one of these is perturbed, recovery is not cheap. A stream processor that falls behind or loses its place may have to restore from a checkpoint and pause processing for many minutes to catch up. For these jobs, intermittent interference from a neighbor is not a small slowdown that averages out; it is a stop-the-world event that pages an on-call engineer. The same teams report, accurately, that they never saw this on a plain EC2 instance.

Why we kept coming back to the VM

Full VM isolation, where a workload gets its own host and kernel, is the standard our customers are already happy with. The question was not whether VM isolation works; it was how to offer it without giving up what makes Titus worth using. We weighed four paths.

  1. Keep improving shared-kernel isolation. This helps every workload on the platform, needs no opt-in, and we are still investing in it (more on the roadmap below). Its limitation is structural. Each round of tuning narrows the gap without closing it, because the underlying hardware remains shared. Cache, memory bandwidth, and the kernel’s own shaping and scheduling locks are not things a container boundary can fully contain. Shared-kernel isolation is the right default and the wrong promise for a workload that cannot tolerate a bad minute.
  2. microVMs (Firecracker, Kata Containers). Lightweight VMs boot in about 150 milliseconds by emulating far less hardware than traditional VMs, which is why they power serverless platforms. They were the most appealing alternative on paper, and we carefully reviewed them. Three things made the cost hard to justify. First, the hardware virtualization they rely on is available only on bare-metal instances or through nested virtualization, and nested virtualization was not ready on the instance types we run at Netflix at the time, so adopting microVMs broadly would have constrained us to a narrow slice of the fleet. Second, there is no managed microVM service we could build on, which means we would have to run and maintain a virtualization layer ourselves: patching the hypervisor, live-migrating guests, and qualifying emulated devices. That is exactly the kind of operational surface we prefer not to own when we can avoid it. Third, even setting those aside, microVMs add virtualization overhead on CPU- and IO-bound work and do not support GPUs. Excellent isolation, but at a price in flexibility and operational load we were not willing to pay.
  3. gVisor. A user-space kernel that intercepts system calls provides sandbox-grade isolation without a hypervisor, thereby avoiding the bare-metal constraint. The catch is performance and dependency. Intercepting syscalls in user space adds overhead on IO-heavy paths, which are precisely the workloads we most need to protect, and the open-source project lags behind its internal counterpart in fixes and is effectively maintained by a single vendor. The isolation we would gain came with a throughput tax on the exact jobs we were trying to help.
  4. Move the workload to EC2. It is possible to run containers directly on EC2 instances. The problem is that the application team takes back the operational load that Titus exists to carry: choosing instance types, patching hosts, and sizing and scaling the fleet. For a team that came to Titus precisely to avoid those things, this is a regression in the experience, and the move between Titus and EC2 has historically been a one-way door that teams are reluctant to cross.

Spectrum of isolation options from lighter and more shared to stronger isolation: shared-kernel containers, then gVisor, then microVMs (Firecracker or Kata), then a full VM as used by single-tenant Titus, which is highlighted. Each option is annotated with its launch latency, overhead, and the entity that operates it; single-tenant Titus is a dedicated EC2 instance with no additional virtualization overhead.

There is also a question of what kind of isolation we actually need. microVMs and gVisor are built for security isolation between mutually distrusting tenants, the case where one tenant might actively try to attack or escape into another. Among Netflix teams, that threat model is more than the situation warrants. What these workloads need is resource and performance isolation: a guarantee that a neighbor cannot steal their CPU, cache, memory bandwidth, or network, not protection from a hostile co-tenant. A dedicated EC2 VM delivers exactly that, with hardware we do not have to emulate and a kernel we do not have to sandbox. We pay for the isolation we need rather than for a stronger security boundary.

microVMs and gVisor asked for a large, bespoke investment with real risk in order to approximate something we could get directly: a VM. Using EC2 to run containers provides the VM, but takes away the managed experience. So we took the direct route and brought single-tenant VM isolation into Titus itself, under the existing API and the existing shared-responsibility model.

How single-tenant Titus works

The idea is simple to state: a single-tenant task runs on its own EC2 instance, sized to fit it, with nothing else scheduled alongside. That instance is still a Titus container host that the Compute/Platform team owns and patches. The team running the workload sees the same Titus API and the same deployment path. Nothing about how they package or ship the job changes.

Side-by-side anatomy of a multi-tenant Titus, where multiple teams’ containers share one Linux kernel and the hardware beneath it and contend with one another, versus a single-tenant node where one task plus its platform sidecars owns the whole machine with no co-tenants.

Most of the work happens in the federation layer, the part of Titus that decides where a job runs (which cell, which capacity) before it is scheduled onto a node.

When a job is eligible for single tenancy, three things happen.

  1. Federation decides eligibility and the envelope. Eligibility is governed by an allowlist maintained by the Compute/Platform team; a team opts in by targeting a single-tenant workload group rather than flipping a flag in the public API. For an eligible task, federation tags it as single-tenant and records the set of instance families it may run on, ensuring consistent performance across the workload. Consolidating this decision in federation follows the same principle we use for routing in general: placement intelligence belongs in one place, above the individual cells, where it can account for capacity and availability across the region.
  2. Autoscaling provisions a dedicated node. Given a pending single-tenant task, our autoscaling implementation launches the smallest instance that satisfies the task’s requested CPU, memory, and GPU from the allowed families for the task just in time. Taking the tightest fit keeps the unused remainder of each dedicated node small. The next section covers this in detail.
  3. The scheduler enforces one task per node. Single-tenant pods are configured with pod anti-affinity to prevent colocation with other pods, along with a priority class that exempts the task from preemption. Single-tenant nodes are also tainted to prevent unrelated workloads from being placed there, with only single-tenant workloads tolerating this taint. We also disable defragmentation/repacking for these nodes, so a single-tenant task is never relocated to repack the fleet. Together, these mean a single-tenant task has its host to itself for its entire life, undisturbed by a neighbor or by the platform’s own bin-packing.

Two design choices are worth dwelling on. First, single tenancy is allowlisted on purpose. If it were a free checkbox in the API, most teams would tick it, because who wouldn’t want a quieter host? And the efficiency that multi-tenancy exists to provide would erode across the fleet. Keeping the Compute/Platform team in control lets us direct dedicated isolation to workloads that need it and steer the rest toward shared capacity, while keeping the public API surface small as we learn. Second, we do not silently resize anyone’s job to fill its node. The job keeps the resources it requested; we recommend sizing it close to a node shape so the dedicated instance is well utilized, while keeping the workload portable and running identically whether in single-tenant mode or not, regardless of the host’s dimensions. Moving in and out of the mode is a configuration change, not a rewrite.

A few perpetrators, a lot of collateral damage

posts.title: Trends from Money20/20 2026: The rise of “hidden” financial services
posts.summary: As fintech products become increasingly capable, the infrastructure behind them fades into the background. Three trends from Money20/20 show how stablecoins, agents, and always-on money are changing financial services.
posts.content:
Onstage at Money20/20 USA this week, Airtm Chief Product Officer Arshi Singh made the case that financial infrastructure works best when customers don’t have to think about it. “If we expect our user to understand the stablecoin infrastructure, then we are not doing our job right,” she said.

Speakers from Robinhood, Citi Treasury and Trade Solutions, the Solana Foundation, and other companies reinforced that idea throughout the event, which brought more than 11,000 payments, fintech, and business leaders to Las Vegas. Customers need access to useful financial products without requiring them to understand—or manage—the infrastructure underneath. That can mean using a stablecoin wallet inside a familiar application, setting clear limits on what an AI agent can buy, or accessing financial services outside banking hours.

Making those products easy to use requires enterprises and fintechs to use the right infrastructure behind the scenes. Three trends at Money20/20 showed what that looks like.

The next 100 million stablecoin users might never download a crypto wallet

Stablecoin adoption might not depend on persuading consumers to download a crypto product. Instead, businesses are embedding stablecoin wallets into the mobile apps, websites, and other products people already use. In most cases, users won’t need to understand the infrastructure underneath. 

Amira Valliani, head of payments growth at the Solana Foundation, described two emerging models: dedicated crypto wallets that give users access to a wide range of assets, and “hidden” or white-labeled wallets embedded inside another product. These hidden wallets might support stablecoin payouts, for example, without presenting users with an explicitly crypto-branded experience.

“I don’t know about a single feature that will bring on 100 million users,” said Valliani. “But I do think what’s going to happen is we’re going to have a few killer integrations that bring on the next 100 million users.”

A mobile-device manufacturer, for example, could add stablecoin-powered international money transfers to the wallet app already available on its phones, rather than ask customers to adopt a separate financial app. This can help make an existing product more useful, increase engagement, and add financial capabilities without becoming a traditional bank.

As stablecoin wallet functionality becomes more integrated throughout the existing financial ecosystem, consumers increasingly associate the experience with the application they use, rather than the infrastructure behind it. "I think crypto basically just fades into the background,” said Nitesh Nath, founder and CEO of DFlow. “[The wallet and application] become the same thing.”

Companies that simplify the underlying complexity can have an advantage. Customers want to be able to sign up quickly, access funds right away, and complete transactions without learning the language of crypto. By building these capabilities into familiar products, fintechs can reach new users without requiring them to adopt a separate crypto product—or even know that a stablecoin wallet is involved.

Always-on money is creating new financial products

Around-the-clock settlement with stablecoins allows fintechs and financial institutions to design credit, investment, treasury, and earnings products that respond to demand in real time, including outside traditional banking hours.

Citi Treasury and Trade Solutions offered its vision for helping institutional clients fund activity across markets with different operating calendars. Ryan Rugg, global head of digital assets for Citi Treasury and Trade Solutions, described a broker-dealer that wanted to buy US equities during Chinese New Year, when banks in Singapore were closed for the holiday. Traditionally, the company would have had to forecast its needs and send money to the US in advance. With tokenized deposits, it could move the funds when they were needed.

Always-on payment rails can also support new lending models. Valinor Digital used stablecoins to create a financing facility that lets prediction-market businesses access capital in real time, including overnight and on weekends. 

“The economy doesn’t shut just as the banks do,” said Valinor Digital Cofounder and CBO Lily Yarborough. The facility gave borrowers access to capital when demand arose, while giving lenders an opportunity that would have been difficult to serve on a traditional banking schedule.

Consumer fintechs are using the same infrastructure in different ways. Robinhood used on-chain lending markets to let customers earn potentially higher returns on their stablecoins than through its traditional cash product. Airtm uses stablecoins to help digital workers outside the US and Europe receive earnings from companies in those markets, then connects those funds to local options for saving, spending, and withdrawing. 

This 24/7 money movement can reduce the need to forecast and prefund accounts, align financing with real-time demand, and make financial services available across more hours and markets. This helps financial products to operate on the schedules of the businesses and people they serve.

Agentic payments require machine-readable consumer intent

A payment credential can show that an agent has access to a consumer’s funds, but it can’t show what the consumer authorized the agent to purchase. Businesses need a structured record of the consumer’s instructions, such as what the agent can buy, how much it can spend, and when the permission expires.

However, natural language instructions leave room for interpretation. For example, a consumer might request a cheap pair of headphones that will arrive quickly.  The agent still has to define “cheap,” “quickly,” and even “headphones.” The agent might make a reasonable inference from the customer’s spending history and still complete a purchase the customer did not intend.

Rather than asking consumers to manage the payment mechanics themselves, payment providers are building those boundaries into the transaction. Shirley Zhou, product lead for Link at Stripe, described a process in which an agent submits a spend request specifying the amount, seller, and purpose of a proposed purchase. The buyer can approve the request before the agent completes the purchase, with the spend request information also informing fraud models. Link’s wallet for agents also offers free purchase protections when an agent uses Link to complete an eligible purchase on their behalf. For qualifying Link transactions, accidental damage, lost items, price drops after they buy, no-fee returns, and return guarantees are covered. 

Other financial companies are developing ways to carry consumer intent through the agentic transaction. American Express, for example, described a model where the issuer receives the customer’s purchase instructions earlier in the transaction lifecycle and can set controls based on what the customer asked for. Permissions for longer-running tasks may also need to remain visible, adjustable, and revocable. A buyer could authorize several purchases within a set budget, ask an agent to monitor an item for a price drop, or allow it to act until a specified date.

The financial infrastructure for these agentic payments remains largely out of sight, while the consumer retains control over the decisions that matter.

How Stripe can help

Customers increasingly want products that help them make better use of their money. Delivering those experiences means connecting traditional and stablecoin rails, preserving customer preferences across agentic channels, and maintaining trust as AI takes on more responsibilities tied to personal finance. 

Stripe brings these capabilities together in one stack. Businesses can embed wallets, issue cards, enable payments, and move money between fiat and stablecoins without exposing users to the underlying complexity. 

Stripe also supports OUSD, Open Standard's recently launched stablecoin for global money movement and settlement across payment networks. With more than $800 million in circulation, OUSD allows businesses to receive, hold, send, and spend funds with Stripe Treasury; build and operate a global card program with Stripe Issuing; and pay recipients worldwide with Stripe Global Payouts. 

Stripe’s agentic commerce solution can also help businesses make payments available to agents while preserving details they’ve spent years honing, like authorization, fraud controls, and branded checkout.

To learn how Stripe can support your stablecoin or agentic commerce strategy, contact us.

posts.title: Stripe survey: Four trends reshaping how SaaS platforms compete in the AI era
posts.summary: AI is creating more SaaS competition, and platforms are feeling the pressure. A Stripe survey of 200 platform leaders shows how they plan to evolve pricing, grow revenue, and retain customers.
posts.content:
AI is making software faster and cheaper to build, lowering barriers to entry and intensifying competition for SaaS platforms. That growth is clearly visible on Stripe, where the number of new platform businesses has increased more than 180% year over year.

We surveyed 200 platform leaders across North America and Europe, half of whom use Stripe, and found that 57% are concerned about losing customers to AI-driven competitors. Leaders are reworking how they build products, set prices, and retain customers to protect margins and make their products harder to displace.

Our survey identified four ways SaaS platforms are adapting: 

  1. Deploying AI internally and in customer-facing products
  2. Testing usage- and outcome-based charges alongside subscriptions
  3. Rebalancing their revenue mix around how their customers operate
  4. Offering embedded finance products to strengthen retention

1. Platforms are pursuing AI efficiency and AI products in parallel

Platforms are applying AI on two fronts: inside their own operations and in the products they sell. Internally, 81% have used AI to accelerate research and development over the past 12 months, and 58% are rebuilding workflows around agents. At Granum, for example, agents automate tasks across customer-facing teams, helping support staff handle 23% more tickets and onboarding specialists serve 34% more customers.

On the product side, 79% have added AI features to existing products over the past 12 months. Canva recently took that approach with Canva AI 2.0, a conversational, agentic workspace within its design suite.

These investments are already paying off. Forty-five percent of platform leaders say their AI investments have lowered operating costs. At GoodLeap, those costs have fallen even as payment volume has increased.

2. Seat-based pricing is losing ground, but not going away

Platforms adding AI are testing pricing tied to usage and outcomes as they look for ways to cover inference costs. Forty-four percent plan to make multiple pricing changes in the next 12 months.

Seat-based pricing will remain part of the mix, but fewer platforms expect it to be their primary model, falling from 16% in 2026 to 11% in 2027. Horizontal platforms are moving away from seats faster. By 2027, just 7% expect seats to remain their primary pricing model, compared with 14% of vertical SaaS.

The key difference is how closely growth has been tied to customer headcount. Horizontal platforms have traditionally grown by selling more seats to larger customers. But fewer seats may be needed as agents take on work that people used to do. Vertical SaaS platforms typically sell only a handful of seats to each merchant, but they’re still tied to people using the software.

Seat-based pricing still gives SaaS platforms a predictable base. One in four plan to keep per-seat fees, then charge separately for agent work based on credits, usage, or outcomes. Zendesk, for example, now charges for resolutions alongside its subscriptions. Another 7% plan to treat agents like seats, charging a base fee plus a license for each agent. The range of approaches suggests that no single metric captures every kind of agent work.

3. Horizontal and vertical platforms are split on leading revenue models

Our survey found a split in expected revenue models by platform and customer segment. Among horizontal platforms serving midsize and enterprise businesses, just 3% expect  embedded finance—including payments, financing, financial accounts, and card issuing—to generate the largest share of revenue in 2027. That figure rises to 34% among vertical platforms serving micro and small businesses. That reverses for usage and hybrid pricing: 60% of the horizontal cohort expect these models to lead revenue, compared with 22% of the vertical cohort.

The gap likely comes down to merchant needs. Small businesses are more likely to want payments and working capital built into the software they already use. Vertical platforms can offer these services because they sit close to the transaction. Larger businesses usually have their own payments and financing infrastructure. But they also need more software to run their complex operations, so software fees can make for a steadier revenue source for horizontal platforms.

4. Embedded finance is emerging as a core retention strategy

Beyond its revenue potential, embedded finance can help platforms retain customers. Sixty percent of platforms say it will be very important or mission-critical to retention over the next 24 months.

Embedding payments and financial services deepens merchant relationships and makes a platform harder to replace. Payments also generate proprietary transaction data, which more than half of surveyed leaders named as a top competitive advantage. Platforms can use payments data to offer financing and let merchants manage more of their finances in one place.

More platforms on Stripe are following that playbook. As of September 2026, the number of active platforms offering Stripe Capital nearly doubled year over year.

Hear from SaaS leaders

Stripe helps more than 19,000 platforms onboard new merchants, accept payments, and grow revenue. Join SaaS leaders across verticals at our SaaS Platform Summit on Tuesday, November 3, in San Francisco to learn how they’re updating their pricing, products, and business models for AI.

Methodology

Stripe surveyed 200 C-suite and director-level leaders at SaaS platforms across North America and Europe in March 2026. Respondents represented startups operating for one to two years, early-stage companies operating for three to five years, established companies operating for six to 10 years, and mature companies operating for more than 10 years. The sample was evenly divided between vertical and horizontal SaaS platforms. Half of the respondents were businesses on Stripe.

posts.title: Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
posts.summary: Prasanna Vijayanathan , Renzo Sanchez-Silva When Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure…
posts.content:
Knowledge GraphObservabilityOntologyGenaiNetflix Technology Blog13 min read·Oct 16, 2026

--

Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-Silva

When Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded.

This post is about that search for the needle.

The Four hours before a fix

Consider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it?

As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner.

The MELT Layer

“What caused the issue?”

Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to.

The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer:

The timeline of an investigation

So how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again?

In our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover.

The disagreement underneath

The instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow.

It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle.

Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas, our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found.

The difficulty is that they do not agree on what they are talking about. A thing that is an application in one system is a service in a second and a cluster in a third, with names differing by a suffix, a casing convention, or a rename only a couple of people remember (SMEs, ring a bell?). Joining across them requires a human carrying the mapping in their head, and that person becomes the bottleneck in such cross-domain investigations. The hard part of end-to-end observability is probably better understood as a data modelling problem.

What we lacked was an explicit, machine-readable agreement about the entities in our operational world.

The Ontology

This agreement has a name: an ontology. Ontology is a formal specification of types, the properties they carry, and the relationships they may have. Its unit is the triple, one fact expressed as subject, predicate, object. Consider the following example triples.

api-gateway   rdf:type       ops:Application .
api-gateway   ops:ownedBy    "Team Bedrock" .
api-gateway   ops:deployedIn "us-east-1" .

INC-5377      rdf:type       ops:Incident .
INC-5377      ops:affects    api-gateway .
INC-5377      ops:severity   "SEV 2" .

In the example here, we have already encoded six facts, and can answer in one query, a question that used to span three tools.

“Which incidents affected applications owned by Team Bedrock in us-east-1?” is a single query in place of looking up incidents, Spinnaker and Radar.

We call our ontology layer, The Observability Ontology. It acts as the schema, rule set and shared agreement that standardizes how different systems understand entities like applications, services, incidents, deployments, etc.

We built it on the W3C stack for this: RDF for the data model, OWL for the ontology, SHACL for validation, and SPARQL for querying. These standards are well specified and widely implemented, which keeps the model portable across graph stores.

The data from the ontology itself, is stored as a knowledge graph, persisted to QuipuDB, our homegrown RDF graph database, a distributed quad store based on redb, a Rust-based embedded key value db. Data here is generated by parsing raw telemetry, logs, and incident discussions into triples (subject-predicate-object facts).

Every harvest also produces a full Turtle serialization for archival, making it human-readable and diff-friendly, which has proven more useful for debugging than we expected.

Our ontology is organized into twelve namespaces, each owning one operational domain:

There are two decisions about this ontology that mattered while we built it, so they’re worth sharing.

The first is that we refused a generic Service type. “Service” means four different things across our tooling, so applications resolve to exactly one type, ops:Application, and every one of them is validated against our software catalog of roughly 49,000 entries before the entity is created. Unvalidated strings like usernames, team names, dependency names scraped from network topology, never become applications. We also cap dependency edges in both directions, because one popular service can carry thousands of reverse dependencies and would otherwise dominate the graph.

The second decision concerns what we chose to model. Incident chat carries the reasoning behind an incident. The hypotheses tried and discarded, the mitigation that worked, who knew why, is all context in the incident’s Slack channel and that knowledge evaporates when the channel goes quiet. So a 200-message, 50-person, 15-service incident channel becomes a structure, converting the operational chaos of an incident into ordered triples:

Creating determinism from non-determinism

Building this graph means using tools that are inherently stochastic. LLMs summarize discussions. Fuzzy matching resolves service names. A probabilistic engine proposes causal chains. None of these produce the same output twice with certainty, but what comes out at the end of our system is a deterministic graph that answers a SPARQL query the same way every time.

Get Netflix Technology Blog’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Remember me for faster sign in

The ontology is the mechanism that creates this determinism through its pipelined approach. We think of the pipeline as a ladder that drives entropy down, where entropy means the proportion of information still trapped in unstructured form. For example, at the start of this pipeline, an LLM could say anything, but it cannot emit a triple that violates the type system. We constrain the output space tightly enough and a stochastic process yields a deterministic contract:

# The model may produce any prose. Its output MUST fit these predicates:
category  IN ["incident", "question", "discussion", "decision"]
sentiment IN ["positive", "neutral", "negative", "urgent"]

# Result — a deterministic triple:
thread:123  slack:category          "incident" .
thread:123  slack:isIncidentRelated "true"^^xsd:boolean .

There are five layers that get us down this ladder. Any single step of this ladder is non-deterministic. But in aggregate, the chain becomes deterministic. That inversion is the whole trick. We describe them below:

Enrichers: Agents as entropy reducers

We use what we call, enrichers, to reduce entropy across the knowledge graph. Dozens of enrichers run over the graph. Each one of them takes noisy input and emits typed triples, and each reads what earlier enrichers wrote. The contract for an Enricher is deliberately narrow:

class Enricher:
    async def _enrich_async(self, ...):
        raw    = await self.fetch(...)      # 1. read noisy input
        result = self.analyze(raw)          # 2. process (may be stochastic)
        graph.add((uri, RDF.type, OPS.X))   # 3. emit TYPED triples
        graph.add((uri, OPS.pred, Literal(result.value)))
        return EnrichmentResult(success=True, triples_added=count)

Three invariants that are standard across the enrichers:

  • every entity carries an rdf:type,
  • every URI follows a single naming scheme, and
  • the catalog gates every ops:Application.

Two operational choices are worth naming here, as well. The enrichment pipeline runs sequentially — load the graph, add triples, and save.

This sequencing removes an entire category of race conditions at a cost in wall-clock time we are happy to pay. And calls out to external systems like metrics, logs, events and the rest could be best-effort, so a slow downstream API doesn’t block the graph harvest, albeit some degradation. To that end, we are also working to translate these separate systems into the ontology, such as the Metrics Ontology and the Alerts Ontology, so everything could be queried from the Ontology itself.

The Correlation Engine: finding the correlation chains

The correlation engine assimilates the vast number of signals from diverse input sources and condenses them into causal or correlatory chains of events. Today, the engine reads thirteen signal types, including log errors, metric anomalies, slow and failed traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, config changes, experiments, autoscaling, commits, end-to-end bottlenecks, and error patterns. It then searches for paths among them. Some ordered pairs are known to be causal and carry a high prior weight. For example, deployment before log error, config change before metric anomaly, failed trace before incident, and so on. Others, which show high correlation are considered correlation chains. Such chains are scored on temporal proximity and severity, inside a ten-minute window, with anything under 0.6 confidence getting discarded.

The role of the engine here is to propose with evidence, not to make conclusions. Hence, the engine stores its chains along with the graph records that were used to create them.

A 0.87 chain in the above example, is a strong hypothesis for a human or an agent to check, and the graph records the confidence alongside the claim so that consumers can understand why a chain is what it is and weigh their options to make decisions.

The knowledge flywheel

Each harvest cycle turns the same four steps, and each rotation leaves the graph richer for the next. This is the Knowledge Flywheel, leading to continuous enrichment and improvement of the context about our system, stored in the knowledge graph.

Observe collects the signals. Enrich adds typed triples. Infer finds patterns invisible in the raw data. Adapt feeds knowledge back, so that established patterns become detection rules. The compounding result of the four phases leads to a self-improving system. A causal chain discovered in one incident becomes a known pattern for the next, and the ontology gradually stops being a schema and starts being a memory.

Consider the example above. When we first see an incident in api-gateway caused due to a timeout and resolve it, we convert this knowledge into entries to the ontology. This becomes encoded knowledge. As we go through multiple cycles of this encoding, the graph starts learning patterns. After N cycles, patterns become wisdom — “api-gateway deploys cause 40% of SEV-2s” and “30% of deployment issues in api-gateway come from Connection Timeouts”. Surface this as an insight and we proactively start reducing incidents, not just react quickly to new ones.

Putting the graph to work

On top of the graph sits AutoRCA, our internal agentic AI solution, built with a set of specialist agents coordinated around one question. Walking the home page regression from the top of this post, the agentic system’s reasoning chain might look something like this:

Each specialization to the inputs is built by people who understand their respective domain deeply. That division of labour only works if the specialists can pass findings to one another without having to agree on the terms of communication or even have knowledge of each other. The ontology acts as the interface. Each specialist learns one vocabulary — the graph’s. A team writing specialized use cases for how they use traces record their findings as triples about an ops:Application, the logs specialization reads triples about that same ops:Application, and neither needs to know the other exists. A new specialist learns the same vocabulary once and can immediately read everything the other six have written.

Set against the investigation we opened with, the change is narrower than it might sound. The alert still fires at 3:30pm, an engineer still has to weigh the evidence, and the fix still has to be written by someone who understands the code. The hour or two that used to go into assembling context — finding the owning team, reconstructing what shipped, correlating information from different parts of the system, recalling that something similar happened last quarter — all that work is the part the ontology and the graph absorbs. We are early enough that the ranked hypotheses are sometimes wrong, which is why each one carries the evidence that produced it. But when the engineer now starts the investigation, they are already holding the picture that used to take half an afternoon to assemble.

If you want to build one of these

A fair amount of what we have built, we learned by getting it wrong first. Based on this experience, these are the principles we would carry into a second attempt.

  • Model identity before anything else. Choose one authoritative catalog per entity kind and validate against it before creating an entity.
  • Treat the ontology as code. Version it, review it, test it, and let changes arrive as pull requests. Treating the ontology as code lends itself to agentic development and lets teams scale and contribute to it.
  • Separate concepts from instances.

posts.title: New ways for fintechs to move money and expand globally
posts.summary: We’re introducing three updates to help fintechs launch products and grow internationally more easily: simpler payout management with Stripe Global Payouts, support for stablecoin cards in more countries, and unified…
posts.content:
Many of the world’s leading fintechs use Stripe to build and scale, including 32 of the Forbes Fintech 50 (and counting). As these businesses expand into new markets, they need to deliver the same fast, reliable experience everywhere while supporting local payment methods, navigating local compliance requirements, and integrating new banking partners. 

We’re introducing three updates to help fintechs launch products and grow internationally more easily: simpler payout management with Stripe Global Payouts, support for stablecoin cards in more countries, and unified APIs for building global financial products. 

Here’s what’s new.

Send payouts to recipients in more than 160 markets

We’ve expanded Global Payouts to more markets and made it easier to set up and manage. Businesses can now send instant stablecoin payouts to recipients in 160 markets and traditional currency payouts to recipients in more than 100, directly from the Stripe Dashboard.

Fintechs can also use Global Payouts programmatically—by embedding hosted forms or integrating with flexible APIs—to enable use cases like loan disbursements, remittances, investment withdrawals, and neobank cash-outs within their products. Turo, for example, uses Global Payouts to send claims payments. The company has processed over $160 million, with a 99.5% payout success rate.

Issue stablecoin cards in more countries

Stripe is launching stablecoin card issuing in 27 EU countries, bringing availability to more than 65 countries worldwide. We plan to expand to 100 countries by the end of 2026. With stablecoin cards on Stripe Issuing, fintechs can offer cards that draw from stablecoin balances held in a custodial wallet, noncustodial wallet, or Stripe financial account. When cardholders make a purchase, Stripe automatically converts their stablecoins into the local currency at the point of sale; merchants can accept these payments just like a traditional card payment.

Fintechs can use Issuing to launch a global stablecoin card program that works across markets with one integration, rather than connecting separate providers for card issuing, currency conversion, KYC and KYB verification, fraud management, and customer support. 

Stripe Issuing already powers more than 400 million cards worldwide across commercial and consumer card programs. Stablecoin cards extend that infrastructure to fintechs and platforms building with stablecoins, enabling them to scale globally and reach a larger customer base.

Add financial capabilities with a unified stack

Stripe Treasury is the building block that connects business earnings with the tools to manage and move money.  

Stripe Treasury allows businesses to settle Stripe earnings, hold funds, convert currencies, spend with cards, and send outbound payments. Fintechs can also bring these same capabilities to their customers by embedding Treasury’s financial tools and services into their platforms.

Stripe Treasury, Global Payouts, and Issuing are all part of Stripe’s unified stack for fintechs, meaning they easily integrate with one another and KYC information can be shared, reducing compliance work and additional user verification steps. They are also compatible with Open Standard’s OUSD stablecoin and Tempo’s blockchain, helping businesses access the benefits of stablecoins while still being interoperable with fiat infrastructure.

Grow your business on Stripe

Over 1,500 fintechs on Stripe serve customers in more than 200 countries and territories. With Stripe’s unified stack, they don’t need to integrate and manage multiple vendors. Instead, they can use a single integration to build global financial products that support money movement, storage, and payment use cases while they continue to expand across markets.

Contact the team to get started.

posts.title: Advancing Generative Recommendation Inference: our collaboration with NVIDIA on TensorRT LLM
posts.summary: At Spotify, every surface and interaction is personalized to you as a user: the content on the Home page, the... The post Advancing Generative Recommendation Inference: our collaboration with NVIDIA on TensorRT LLM…
posts.content:
At Spotify, every surface and interaction is personalized to you as a user: the content on the Home page, the next song that plays, and more recently the ability to talk to Spotify. 

Traditionally, this content is provided by recommendation systems that require multiple steps for candidate retrieval and ranking, and perhaps individual systems per surface. Generative AI is fundamentally changing this. We have been exploring how to provide recommendations via a Large Personalized Language Model in real time, across multiple surfaces.

This shift, however, presents unique engineering challenges, particularly when moving from a proof of concept to a scalable, production-grade inference architecture. 

Spotify’s journey into LLM-powered recommendations

Beam search

In January 2026, Spotify introduced LLM-powered technology to its podcast recommendations. The work is grounded in recent advancements in generative recommendation architectures, specifically the foundational methods introduced in the PLUM paper . At Spotify, we have applied these concepts to build a specialized generative recommendation system for podcasts, aimed at delivering deeply personalized listening experiences. Our specialized architecture, detailed in our "Deploying Semantic ID-based Generative Retrieval for Large-Scale Podcast Discovery at Spotify" paper  employs beam search to explore multiple token sequence paths simultaneously for candidate generation. 

Beam search is a technique that allows exploration of an LLM’s output space with the goal of identifying highly probable token sequences. This technique navigates a decision tree of potential recommendations by keeping the most promising 'beams' or sequences active at each step, with the goal of identifying the highest-scoring podcasts for personalization. For this reason, these top sequences constitute semantic IDs that are then translated to catalog items to serve recommendations to users.

Our initial release relies on vLLM as an inference engine. vLLM is one of the most widely adopted open source inference engines, particularly strong at supporting modern model architectures for high-throughput  inference deployments. However vLLM’s support for beam search is limited compared to traditional completion requests – its beam search implementation doesn’t extract the maximum performance from GPU devices.

Specifically, vLLM's beam search implementation operates outside the core GPU engine, which introduces CPU-side bottlenecks and additional GPU work due to the recomputation of partially filled KV blocks.

For our January launch, these limitations meant we couldn't fully utilize high-end GPUs, so we opted for lower-tier accelerators to manage costs while keeping the system at a more optimal load point. 

Candidate scoring

Another inference technique we’ve been exploring is candidate scoring. Candidate scoring uses a model's log probabilities to evaluate and rank a set of candidates. 

A naive way to perform this type of inference is to adopt a “fan-out” approach and run inference on each candidate separately, for each request then we extract the related logprobs, before aggregating them to achieve the desired ranking operation.

This type of inference is generally available in most open source inference engines, however a more efficient technique has found its way into SGLang, thanks also to work from Linkedin’s engineering team. For this reason we’ve been utilizing SGLang as well to access this feature at inference time with an efficient candidate masking technique that allows us to score multiple candidates in a single request.

Personalization

The most important part of Spotify recommendations is our ability to personalize based on user preferences and interactions. In our traditional recommendation systems, we have used dense user embeddings to accomplish personalization at scale. As we have experimented with LLM-based recommendations, we have explored a few approaches to enable personalization in this new paradigm.

Plain User Text

This approach entails converting user listening and interaction history to text to place in the prompt for the LLM. The major issue with fully text based user history is the amount of text required to accurately represent the user. Prompts become extremely large, resulting in large inference latency that is too long for our request budget as well as higher GPU usage. Plain User Text is used sparingly, generally for smaller cases like the user’s most recent real time streams.

User Semantic Ids

Similar to the PLUM paper mentioned earlier, we explored representing user history as a semantic id. This approach extends the model vocabulary with user semantic id tokens, which are easily added to prompts using a handful of text tokens, keeping prompts short and easily servable with no custom inference requirements. The LLM was fine tuned using the user semantic id space and extended vocabulary, and at inference time, a user semantic id is added to the prompt. While early results were promising, this approach requires further experimentation and research before it's ready for production. 

Soft Tokens

The most successful method we have used for personalizing LLM requests is based on our existing user embeddings. The general approach is outlined in a white paper called Embedding to Prefix created by Spotify Research. Overall, the idea is to learn a projection from an existing embedding space into an LLM’s embedding space as a single soft token.  The LLM is fine tuned using a subset of the weights to be able to use this soft token to personalize recommendation outputs. At inference time, a user vector is projected into the LLM embedding space and inserted into the prompt before executing the initial forward pass. We have used this approach successfully for podcast recommendations and are currently integrating and evaluating it for various tasks with our internal LLM model.

Expanding LLM-powered recommendation systems
